file: 1997/1997-09-15_75 extra copies_discuss_huge surprise_mordac_request computer upgrade_the rufuser.gif
title: Mordac Eats the Request Form

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac the Refuser. I am here to discuss your request for a computer upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crinkle!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Mmphh!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Chomp chomp chomp

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: We lotht thuh pahper-wuhk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a huge surprise. Luckily I made seventy-five extra copies.

situation: Mordac the Refuser arrives to discuss Dilbert's request for a computer upgrade, holding the request paperwork. He stuffs the papers in his mouth and chews them up, then claims with a full mouth that the paperwork was lost. Dilbert, who anticipated this, produces a big stack of seventy-five extra copies.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically feigns surprise at the 'lost' paperwork because he knew Mordac would destroy it, so he has already made a huge stack of backup copies.
summary: A gatekeeper from IT destroys a computer-upgrade request by eating it, but the employee came prepared with a mountain of duplicates.

file: 1997/1997-09-23_third date_vendor_client_obligated_feisty_oysters_sale first_kill client.gif
title: Vendor's Lunch Date With Client

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Do you realize this is our third date?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: We're not dating. I'm a vendor and you're my client.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: You always say the only time we can meet is during lunch. That way I'm obligated to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: You're feisty. I'd better get the oysters.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: (thought) Make sale first. Then kill client.

situation: A bald, bespectacled client sits across a restaurant table from a woman vendor. He treats their lunch meetings as dates, but she insists they are strictly business and calls out that he only meets her at lunch so she has to pay. When he cheerfully decides to order oysters, she silently fumes.
punchline: The vendor must keep smiling and close the deal while privately fantasizing about murdering the client who flirts with her and runs up expensive lunches on her tab.
summary: A saleswoman putting up with her lecherous client's free lunches plots his demise as soon as the contract is signed.

file: 1997/1997-11-20_dogbert research_small dog_with glasses_bureau of dogs_50 dollars_file complaint.gif
title: Complaining to the Bureau of Dogs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Research Co.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: First question: What would you losers do if a small dog with glasses took advantage of you?

transcript.speaker: Focus group man
transcript.text: We would complain to the... um... whoever handles that sort of thing!

transcript.speaker: Focus group woman
transcript.text: Yeah!

transcript.speaker: Focus group man
transcript.text: It costs fifty bucks to file a complaint?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And ten bucks to borrow a pen.

setting: Dogbert Research Co. focus group room, then the Bureau of Dogs office
situation: Dogbert runs a research session and asks participants what they would do if a small dog with glasses exploited them. They confidently say they would complain to whoever handles such things. In the last panel, a participant is at the Bureau of Dogs, run by Dogbert, where complaining costs fifty bucks plus ten more to borrow a pen.
punchline: The complaint office is run by the very dog being complained about, who charges absurd fees to complain, so the victims are exploited all over again.
summary: A group that vows to complain about a scheming little dog discovers the complaint bureau is run by that same dog, who bills them for every step.

file: 1997/1997-07-28_great news_sell product line_strongest comepetitor_not viable_amazingly stupid_integrating line_work here.gif
title: Competitor Offers Their Doomed Product Line

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great news! Our strongest competitor offered to sell us their product line.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously they think their products are not viable. We'd have to be amazingly stupid...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you'll be in charge of integrating their product line with ours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...to work here.

situation: The Boss excitedly tells Dilbert that their strongest competitor has offered to sell off its entire product line. Dilbert points out that the competitor must believe its products are not viable, and that buying them would be amazingly stupid. The Boss ignores this and assigns Dilbert to integrate the products, which prompts Dilbert to finish his sentence with 'to work here.'
punchline: Dilbert's unfinished remark that 'we'd have to be amazingly stupid' gets completed as 'to work here,' implying the company's own foolishness is the very reason the doomed acquisition is happening.
summary: A rival company's eagerness to dump its products is hailed as a bargain by management, and the employee wryly implies that only a foolish company would take the deal.

file: 1997/1997-03-19_confides in alice_crush on dilbert_desiring engineer_report_tech writer_wrong situation.gif
title: Tech Writer's Forbidden Crush Reported

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: Alice, I think I'm developing a crush on Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is that so wrong?

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: Apparently it is.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: I have a report of a tech writer desiring an engineer.

setting: Office meeting table or break room
situation: A tech writer confides in Alice that she is developing a crush on Dilbert, and Alice gently asks whether that is so wrong. Immediately a red-costumed devil carrying a giant spoon appears with a report, accusing a tech writer of desiring an engineer.
punchline: The workplace's rigid caste system treats a tech writer's crush on an engineer as a literal sin, with a devil arriving to punish it.
summary: A woman's innocent confession about liking a coworker summons a pitchfork-style punisher who treats cross-department romance as damnation.

file: 1997/1997-02-14_raise didn't go_secretary_didn't do paperwork_initite disciplinary actions_disciplinary action forms.gif
title: Secretary Refuses Disciplinary Paperwork Request

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My raise didn't go through because your secretary didn't do the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I demand that you initiate disciplinary actions against her!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll try, but...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, could you get me one of those disciplinary action forms?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Sure, right after my ski trip to hell.

setting: The Boss's office and Carol's desk
situation: Dilbert complains to the Boss that his raise was not processed because the Boss's secretary skipped the paperwork, and demands she be disciplined. The Boss agrees to try, then asks that same secretary, Carol, to fetch him a disciplinary action form against herself. Carol sarcastically refuses, saying she'll do it after a ski trip to hell.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to discipline his secretary depends on her cooperation, and she sarcastically says it will happen when hell freezes over.
summary: A man seeking justice for a missed raise learns that punishing the culprit requires the culprit's own help.

file: 1997/1997-10-21_sport memorabilia_baseball_autographed_babe ruth_autographed later_sports.gif
title: Babe Ruth Autograph Coming Tonight

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sports memorabilia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the best price I've seen for a baseball autographed by Babe Ruth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I don't see where the autograph is.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It gets autographed later tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take this and three of the Honus Wagner cards.

situation: Dilbert is browsing a sports memorabilia store run by Dogbert and admires a baseball supposedly autographed by Babe Ruth at a great price. He notices there is no autograph on the ball, and Dogbert explains it will be signed later tonight. Dilbert, undeterred, buys it along with three Honus Wagner cards.
punchline: Dogbert is openly selling forged memorabilia, since Babe Ruth is long dead and the autograph will be faked that night, and Dilbert happily goes along with the scam.
summary: A dishonest shopkeeper admits his celebrity-signed baseball hasn't actually been signed yet, and the customer buys it anyway.

file: 1997/1997-08-19_recruiting on campus_twelve comapnies_copies_resume_true tables_interview_interviewee.gif
title: Cocky Applicant Gets Brushed Off

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Recruiting on campus

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: I have better offers from twelve companies. Why should I work at yours?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll see what I can do for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have enough copies of my résumé?

situation: Dilbert is interviewing a college student at a campus recruiting session. The student boasts of twelve better job offers and demands to know why she should work for Dilbert's company. Dilbert calmly says he'll see what he can do, then hands her his own résumé and asks if she has enough copies, reversing the roles.
punchline: Dilbert turns the tables by treating the arrogant applicant as a hiring helper, implying his own job prospects are so shaky he wants her to circulate his résumé to those twelve companies.
summary: A confident graduate brags about her many job offers, and the interviewer responds by quietly asking her to help him find a new job.

file: 1997/1997-07-08_broke herd_dancer_do your stuff_flirting_powerful_woman_chick magnet.gif
title: Ratbert Proves He's a Chick Magnet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you're such a chick magnet, let's see you do your stuff.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Okay. I'll wag. They love that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's working! You broke one out of the herd. She's coming this way.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Be careful. I don't know how powerful this is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grumble

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'll bet you work out a lot. I'm a dancer.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

situation: Dilbert sits on the grass and challenges Ratbert to prove he is a chick magnet. Ratbert wags his tail, and a woman from a nearby group heads over. She ends up petting and flirting with Ratbert while Dilbert looks on grumbling.
punchline: Ratbert's cute-pet charm actually works on women, leaving the human Dilbert ignored and jealous while Ratbert is overwhelmed by his own success.
summary: A skeptical Dilbert dares his pet to attract women, and the little creature's tail-wagging works so well that a dancer fawns over him instead.

file: 1997/1997-10-27_disturbing pattern_soultions_problems_try last_old rags_due respect.gif
title: With All Due Respect, Boss Insulted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I've noticed a disturbing pattern. Your solutions to problems are always the things you try last.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: With all due respect, are you using your skull to store old rags or what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a good thing you said "with all due respect."

situation: The Boss tells Alice that her solutions to problems are always the last things she tries. Alice snaps back with an insult about his head being stuffed with old rags, prefaced by 'with all due respect'. The Boss, now standing in the doorway, tells her it's a good thing she added that phrase.
punchline: The Boss naively believes that prefacing an insult with 'with all due respect' makes it acceptable, so Alice gets away with calling him stupid.
summary: A manager criticizes an employee's problem-solving, she retorts with a barbed insult wrapped in politeness, and he treats the courteous-sounding preface as if it excuses everything.

file: 1997/1997-11-19_dogbert research co_focus group_carefully screened_loser choices_opposite_what recommended_skipped jury duty_liver transplant.gif
title: Focus Group of Loser Choices

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Research Co.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You've all been carefully screened for this focus group.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Each of you has a pattern of making "loser choices." I'll tell my clients to do the opposite of whatever you recommend.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Fun! I'm glad I skipped jury duty to be here.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I rescheduled my liver transplant!

setting: Conference room at Dogbert Research Co.
situation: Dogbert, running a market research firm, addresses a focus group seated around a table. He reveals that the participants were chosen because they consistently make bad decisions, so his clients will do the opposite of what they recommend. The participants proudly cite their own poor choices, such as skipping jury duty and postponing a liver transplant to attend.
punchline: The participants prove they were perfectly screened for bad judgment by gleefully admitting they put a pointless focus group ahead of a civic duty and a life-saving operation.
summary: A research firm deliberately recruits people with terrible judgment for its panel, and the attendees immediately confirm their credentials with absurd life choices.

file: 1997/1997-06-18_catbert_evil hr director_complaints_unnecessary_meetings_family_ridiculous.gif
title: Catbert Reveals Boss's Meeting Addiction

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: People are complaining that you schedule unnecessary meetings as a substitute for a family.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's ridiculous! Come to my next meeting and see for yourself.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Okay, I will.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I got us a family cat. How was your day, dear?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sob

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, then an office cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells the Boss that employees are complaining he holds pointless meetings because he has no family. The Boss denies it and invites Catbert to attend his next meeting to see for himself. In the last panel the Boss treats Dilbert, who sits sobbing at his computer, like a spouse, saying he got them a family cat and asking how his day was.
punchline: The Boss proves the complaint true by treating his employee as his spouse and claiming a cat as their family, showing that his meetings and work relationships really do substitute for a family life.
summary: A boss insists he doesn't use meetings to fill a family void, then absurdly greets a miserable employee as his spouse and announces a pet for their imaginary household.

file: 1997/1997-04-11_argument_new org chart_promotion for intern_startegies_pretend  its work.gif
title: Intern Promoted Above Dilbert on Org Chart

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't care what it "looks" like on the org chart! You're an intern, not my boss!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I just saw the new org chart. Congratulations on your promotion, Asok!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Let's go make some strategies and pretend it's work!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Not so loud. The L-U-S-E-R might hear.

situation: Dilbert angrily tells Asok that an intern cannot be his boss, whatever the org chart shows. Phil then congratulates Asok on his promotion, and Asok cheerfully suggests they go make strategies and pretend it's work. Phil nervously shushes him, spelling out 'loser' so Dilbert, hunched in his cubicle, won't hear.
punchline: Phil and Asok treat Dilbert, now Asok's subordinate, as a loser and openly joke that management 'strategy' is just pretending to work, while spelling the insult as if that makes it polite.
summary: After a reorganization puts a young intern over him, a sulking engineer becomes the subject of whispered mockery from his new boss and a colleague.

file: 1997/1997-03-26_plan too much_bias for action_posters_proclaim commitment_measure once_cut twice.gif
title: Measure Once, Cut Twice Poster

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We plan too much. From now on we'll have a bias for action.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want posters that proclaim our commitment to action. And I want them soon!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Measure once. Cut twice."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Told you.

situation: The Boss announces that the company plans too much and will now have a bias for action. He demands motivational posters proclaiming this commitment, and soon. Wally presents a poster with the slogan 'Measure once. Cut twice,' and the Boss approves of it.
punchline: The slogan inverts the carpenter's proverb 'measure twice, cut once,' so the poster endorses sloppy, error-prone work, and the clueless Boss likes it anyway because it sounds action-oriented.
summary: A manager ditches planning for hasty action and happily approves a motivational poster that celebrates doing the job wrong.

file: 1997/1997-07-25_dogbert_find people_laugh nervously_smack with flyswatter_wouldn't be hobby_no reason.gif
title: Dogbert's Flyswatter Hobby Needs No Reason

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wish me luck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For what?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to find people who laugh nervously every time they talk. Then I'll smack them with my flyswatter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the reason would be?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It wouldn't be a hobby if it had a reason.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch, then Dogbert heading out
situation: Dogbert, wearing a backpack and carrying a flyswatter, announces he is heading out to hunt for people who laugh nervously whenever they talk. Dilbert, sitting on the couch with a remote, asks why. Dogbert replies that having a reason would stop it from being a hobby, and walks off.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the need for justification by pointing out that a hobby is defined by being pointless, so smacking nervous laughers is its own reward.
summary: Dogbert sets off with a flyswatter to whack habitual nervous laughers and explains that a pastime with a purpose would not count as a hobby.

file: 1997/1997-11-12_many fcators_features_usage_secret pact_useful information_gave information.gif
title: Engineers Withhold Everything, Even the Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Well, that depends on many factors involving features and usage.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Do you engineers have a secret pact to withold all useful information? You haven't answered one question and it's already... um...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Two o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We hear you gave information to Marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just the time of day. He would have found out anyway!

setting: Conference room and office lunch table
situation: Dilbert is asked questions by a marketing representative and gives only vague, evasive answers. The frustrated marketer accuses the engineers of a pact to withhold information, then asks what time it is, and Dilbert tells him. Later Wally and Alice confront Dilbert at lunch for leaking information to Marketing.
punchline: The engineers' culture of withholding is so strict that telling Marketing the time of day is treated as a betrayal that needs defending.
summary: An engineer who refuses to give straight answers to marketing is chastised by his coworkers for revealing the current time.

file: 1997/1997-01-18_business like christianity_faithful and obidient_obtain bliss_afterlife_reincarnation model_higher level  employment_bio degrade_become wd40_dinosuar.gif
title: Careers as Reincarnation, Retirees as WD-40

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Businesses used to be like Christianity; if you were faithful and obedient, you could obtain bliss in the afterlife of retirement.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now it's more of a reincarnation model. If the worker learns enough in his current job, he can progress to a higher level of employment elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: These analogies aren't working for you, are they, Bob?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: My hope is that one day I will biodegrade and become "WD-40" oil.

setting: A therapist's office, with Bob the dinosaur on a couch and Dogbert beside him
situation: Dogbert, acting as a therapist, explains to Bob the dinosaur how employment used to work like a religion with retirement as heaven. He then says it now works like reincarnation, where learning on the job lets you move up to a better job elsewhere. Bob replies that he hopes to biodegrade into WD-40 oil, which shows the analogies mean nothing to him.
punchline: Bob the dinosaur takes the reincarnation talk literally and hopes to become WD-40 oil, since dinosaurs are the source of fossil fuels.
summary: A dog therapist compares careers to afterlife beliefs, but his dinosaur patient only dreams of decomposing into lubricant.

file: 1997/1997-02-26_off site meeting_overworked_invite staff_discuss mission statement_sack race_state trooper_shoot any animal.gif
title: Boss Plans Off-Site, Ignores Workload

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you set up our off-site meeting so we can talk about how overworked you are?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was thinking we should invite the rest of the staff, too. We can discuss our mission statement, maybe have a sack race.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you know that if you're a state trooper, you can shoot any animal that's been hit by a car?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert, who is busy at his computer with a phone cord wrapped around him, to organize an off-site meeting about how overworked Dilbert is. The Boss then expands the plan to include the whole staff, a mission statement discussion and a sack race. He finishes by sharing an unrelated and oddly violent trivia fact while Dilbert silently keeps working.
punchline: The Boss wants a meeting about Dilbert's overwork, but he makes Dilbert do the planning, turns it into a pointless team-building event, and then drifts into irrelevant trivia, showing he will do nothing to actually reduce the workload.
summary: A manager has his overloaded employee organize a retreat about being overloaded, bloats it with games and slogans, then wanders off into random trivia.

file: 1997/1997-11-26_insatlling isdn line_digital phone_different process_slap fight_awkward.gif
title: ISDN Installer's Awkward Slap Fight

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Installing an ISDN line

transcript.speaker: Installer
transcript.text: These digital phone lines require a very different installation process.

transcript.speaker: Installer
transcript.text: You'll have to show me your SPIDs now.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What happened after the slap fight?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then it got awkward.

situation: A phone technician installs an ISDN line in Dilbert's home while Dilbert sits on the couch. The technician announces that Dilbert must now show him his SPIDs, a technical ISDN term. In the last panel Dilbert is disheveled and Dogbert asks what happened after the slap fight.
punchline: The technical request to show his SPIDs sounds like an inappropriate demand, so Dilbert's rumpled state and the implied slap fight and awkward aftermath suggest he misunderstood it as something far more personal.
summary: A routine phone line installation turns into a misunderstanding when the technician's jargon-laden request sounds like something entirely different.

file: 1997/1997-03-28_profits down_morale down_anti management cartoons_hang cubicle walls_mission statement.gif
title: Blaming Cartoons for Low Morale

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Profits are down. Morale is low. What is the root problem?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's got to be those anti-management cartoons the employees hang on their cubicle walls!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they aren't even funny.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This one has our mission statement.

setting: Boss's office, then an office cubicle
situation: The Boss sits at his desk pondering why profits and morale are down, and decides the culprit must be the anti-management cartoons employees pin up in their cubicles. He then inspects a cubicle wall, complaining the cartoons aren't even funny. Wally, standing in his cubicle, points to a clipping and says it contains the company's mission statement.
punchline: The only thing on the wall mocking management is the company's own mission statement, implying the mission statement itself is the joke and the real root cause of low morale is management.
summary: A manager blames employee cartoons for his company's troubles, only to be shown that the funniest thing on the wall is his own corporate mission statement.

file: 1997/1997-03-22_invented quantum computer_solve complex equations_chaos theroy_shift destiny_possibly killing inhabitants_shift happens.gif
title: Quantum Computer Kills Other Universe

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've invented a quantum computer, capable of interacting with matter from other universes to solve complex equations.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to chaos theory, your tiny change to another universe will shift its destiny, possibly killing every inhabitant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fire it up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shift happens.

situation: Dilbert proudly explains that he has built a quantum computer that draws on matter from other universes to solve complex equations. Dogbert points out that, by chaos theory, even a tiny interference could wipe out every inhabitant of another universe. Dogbert then tells him to fire it up, and Dilbert answers with a pun.
punchline: Dilbert shrugs off the possible destruction of an entire universe with the pun 'Shift happens', a play on a vulgar saying, showing a cheerful disregard for consequences.
summary: An engineer cheerfully switches on his universe-tampering machine after being warned it may annihilate another reality.

file: 1997/1997-05-15_over slept_big meeting_no makeup_newt gingrich.gif
title: Unmade-Up Boss Looks Like Gingrich

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, no! I overslept... No time to apply makeup before my big meeting!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, does everyone understand their tasks?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll get right on it.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Absolutely.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder why they were so respectful today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's Newt Gingrich!

setting: Bedroom, then an office meeting room
situation: The Boss oversleeps and panics that he has no time to put on makeup before an important meeting. He runs the meeting anyway, and his employees are unusually quick to agree and obey. The Boss wonders why they are so respectful, while Dilbert whispers that he looks like Newt Gingrich.
punchline: Without his makeup the Boss resembles Newt Gingrich, then Speaker of the House, so his staff treat him with the deference due a powerful politician and he never realizes why.
summary: A boss skips his morning makeup and puzzles over his staff's sudden obedience, unaware they mistake him for a famous politician.

file: 1997/1997-05-01_sign agreement_5 year after_wally_doesn't work anyway_boss_contract.gif
title: Non-Compete Agreement Is Easy for Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You want me to sign an agreement that I won't work for a competitor for five years if I leave here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No problem. Here you go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is too easy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I haven't done any work here for five years, so how hard could it be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: New game?

situation: The Boss asks Wally to sign a non-compete agreement promising not to work for a competitor for five years after leaving. The Boss thinks Wally agreed too easily, while Wally privately reasons that he hasn't done any work at his current job in five years, so he can simply keep not working.
punchline: Wally is so notoriously lazy that a five-year promise not to work elsewhere costs him nothing, since he already does no work.
summary: A legal restriction on future employment barely troubles an employee whose current output is already zero.

file: 1997/1997-04-16_joking and grumbling_life insurance_catered lunch meetings_discuss feelings_mad cow burger_chicken bone surpise.gif
title: Lunch Meeting With Deadly Menu

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's been a lot of joking and grumbling since the company took out life insurance policies on all of you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So we're having these catered lunch meetings to discuss your feelings.

transcript.speaker: Caterer
transcript.text: Do you want the Mad Cow Burger or the Chicken Bone Surprise?

situation: The Boss tells his staff that the company has taken out life insurance policies on them and that people have been grumbling about it. To address their feelings, he holds catered lunch meetings. The caterer then offers the employees a choice between two dangerous-sounding meals.
punchline: Rather than easing employees' fears about the company profiting from their deaths, the lunch menu offers food hazards that could actually kill them, implying management is trying to cash in on the policies.
summary: Management responds to worry over staff life insurance by serving lunches that seem designed to make the payouts happen.

file: 1997/1997-02-20_bold commando_relocates pc_thwarting union rules_moving computer_police catch dilbert_jailtime.gif
title: Commando Computer Mover Goes to Jail

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The bold commando stealthily relocates his PC at night, thus thwarting burdensome union rules.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Freeze, miscreant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope this works.

transcript.speaker: Inmate
transcript.text: You don't look like Johnny Cash to me.

setting: Office at night, then a jail cell
situation: Dilbert, dressed in black like a commando, sneaks through the office at night carrying his PC to move it himself and avoid union rules. A uniformed guard catches him at gunpoint, and Dilbert ends up in a jail cell. A tough-looking inmate remarks that Dilbert doesn't resemble Johnny Cash.
punchline: Dilbert's hopeful plan to be treated like Johnny Cash at a prison show backfires, since he is simply an ordinary inmate facing the same hard-bitten cellmates, and the joke also mocks the extreme lengths he goes to just to move his own computer.
summary: A black-clad Dilbert sneaks his own computer across the office to dodge union restrictions and gets thrown in jail, where a gruff inmate is unimpressed.

file: 1997/1997-09-26_didn't use brain_already knew_car pool_staff meeting_steak alive.gif
title: Wally's Brain-Free Week Streak

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't use my brain this week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I listened to things I already knew; I waited for people who were late; I was a passenger in my car pool.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's start the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes!! Keeping the streak alive!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: Wally proudly lists all the ways he avoided thinking during the week, such as listening to things he already knew and waiting for late colleagues. When the Boss announces the start of the staff meeting, Wally cheers because he expects it to extend his streak of not using his brain.
punchline: Wally treats the staff meeting as another guaranteed brain-free activity, implying meetings are so pointless they require no mental effort at all.
summary: A cheerfully lazy employee celebrates a week of zero mental effort and looks forward to a meeting that will keep his streak going.

file: 1997/1997-08-02_elbonian audit_flexible_holy week_more spce_open minded_share cubicle_wedgies.gif
title: Wedgies During Elbonian Holy Week

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll need to share your cubicle with the Elbonian audit team until we get more space.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is their holy week so I expect you to be open-minded and flexible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, how do you celebrate the holy week?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Wedgies, mostly.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he must share his cubicle with a team of bearded Elbonian auditors in tall white hats. He urges Dilbert to be open-minded and flexible because it is their holy week. When Dilbert politely asks how they celebrate, an Elbonian cheerfully answers that it is mostly wedgies.
punchline: Dilbert's request to be open-minded about a foreign religious observance turns out to mean he will be the target of their ritual wedgies.
summary: A manager's plea for cultural tolerance backfires when the visiting auditors reveal their holy-week tradition involves physically tormenting their host.

file: 1997/1997-12-11_lower opinion_time bombs_ruin magic_kill me_one kiss_no tongue.gif
title: Engineer Ruins the Magic Instantly

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Sooner or later you'll say something that will lower my opinion of you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grunt.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Men are like time bombs. At any moment you'll say something that will ruin the magic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Aaargh!! Kill me!! Kill me!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll give you one kiss, no tongue.

setting: Outdoors on a date, with the couple walking arm in arm
situation: Dilbert's date warns him that sooner or later he will say something that lowers her opinion of him, comparing men to time bombs. Dilbert answers that he is an engineer, and then offers her a clinically worded romantic concession. She is horrified and begs to be killed.
punchline: Dilbert proves her time-bomb theory almost immediately by treating a kiss like a negotiated, limited-scope deliverable, which is exactly the unromantic engineer behavior she feared.
summary: A woman predicts her date will eventually kill the romance, and he promptly does it by offering a stingy, specification-style kiss.

file: 1997/1997-01-29_schedule_future unplanned network outages_include schedule_sick days_volcanic eruptions_earth quakes_hurricanes.gif
title: Schedule of Unplanned Network Outages

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you requested, here is a schedule of all future unplanned network outages.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I took the initiative to include a schedule of all future sick days, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and hurricanes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the point when you realize how stupid your request was and we have a good laugh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does CNN know about this?

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a schedule of all future unplanned network outages, as the Boss requested. He adds that he also included future sick days, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and hurricanes. Dilbert says this is when the Boss should realize how stupid the request was, but the Boss takes it seriously and asks whether CNN knows about the predictions.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically mocks the impossible request by offering to predict other unpredictable events, but the clueless Boss believes the predictions are real and worries about the news coverage.
summary: An employee ridicules his manager's demand to forecast random failures by also forecasting natural disasters, and the manager naively thinks it's newsworthy.

file: 1997/1997-03-31_project reuirements_was for nothing_believes you did work_homemade cookies.gif
title: Wally Exploits Coworker's Wasted Work

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, I forgot to tell you that all of the project requirements changed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What?!! All my work was for nothing?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He actually believes you did work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I'll get some homemade cookies out of this!

setting: Conference room, then the hallway outside the meeting
situation: At a meeting table, a coworker casually tells Wally that all the project requirements have changed. Wally loudly acts outraged that his work was wasted. Afterward he tells Dilbert his plan to milk the coworker's guilt for homemade cookies, and Dilbert is surprised the coworker believes Wally ever did any work.
punchline: Wally never did any work on the project, so he fakes outrage over the changed requirements to guilt the coworker into giving him free treats.
summary: A staged show of anger over wasted effort turns out to be a scam to score baked goods from a gullible coworker.

file: 1997/1997-05-21_folded arms_important one_physically impossible_third project_finish both products.gif
title: Do Both, Then Add Third

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is physically impossible for me to finish both of my projects on time. Which one is more important?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm... If I absolutely HAD to choose between them, I'd say... Do them both on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. When you do that with your arms, it creates the illusion that you're thinking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What you need is a third project.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that he cannot finish both of his projects on time and asks which one takes priority. The boss refuses to prioritize and insists he do both on time, then remarks on how Dilbert's gesturing hands make it look like he is thinking. He finishes by assigning Dilbert a third project.
punchline: Instead of helping prioritize, the clueless boss ignores the impossibility and piles on even more work, mocking Dilbert's pleas along the way.
summary: A worker pleads for guidance on which of two impossible deadlines matters more, and his oblivious manager responds by handing him another assignment.

file: 1997/1997-03-29_banning cartoons_anti management_hurt morale_banning humor_raise morale_not funny.gif
title: Boss Bans Anti-Management Cartoons

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm banning the posting of anti-management cartoons in the office. They hurt morale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're banning humor to raise morale?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there something wrong with that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the subject of today's cartoon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you see how it's not funny?

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert that he is banning anti-management cartoons from being posted in the office because they hurt morale. Dilbert questions the logic of banning humor to raise morale, and the Boss sees no problem. Dilbert points out that this very policy is the subject of today's cartoon, and the Boss smugly says it isn't funny.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly proves his own point is absurd by treating the cartoon mocking his policy as evidence that anti-management humor isn't funny, while ignoring that he is the joke.
summary: A manager outlaws satirical comics to boost spirits, then dismisses the very strip lampooning his decision as unfunny.

file: 1997/1997-10-06_men_communicate_only talks_sports_computers_job_tv_sex_jokes_greek mythology_date_likes_dislikes_business.gif
title: Date Rules Out Every Conversation Topic

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I like men who know how to communicate...

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: But not a man who only talks about sports, or computers, or his job, or TV, or sex, or jokes, or his accomplishments...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would leave... Greek mythology... and... you

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: No Greek stuff.

setting: A restaurant table on a date
situation: Dilbert sits at a restaurant table across from a blonde woman on a date. She says she likes men who communicate, then rules out nearly every topic a man might discuss. When Dilbert works out that only Greek mythology and her are left, she vetoes the Greek mythology too.
punchline: By banning every possible conversation topic, the date leaves Dilbert with nothing to talk about, so her demand for good communication can never be satisfied.
summary: A woman demands a man who communicates well, then eliminates every subject he could possibly bring up.

file: 1997/1997-05-09_product requirements_design prodcut_doomed projects.gif
title: Designing Doomed Products Without Requirements

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, we don't have time to gather the product requirements ahead of time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to start designing the product anyway. Otherwise it will look like we aren't accomplishing anything.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Of all my projects, I like the doomed ones best.

situation: The Boss tells Wally there is no time to collect product requirements, but orders him to start designing the product anyway so the team appears productive. In the last panel Wally relaxes behind a newspaper with his feet up on his desk, thinking about the project.
punchline: Wally knows a project started without requirements is doomed to fail, so he happily does no real work, since nothing he does will matter.
summary: Told to build a product before anyone knows what it should do, Wally settles back with a newspaper and quietly welcomes a project destined to fail.

file: 1997/1997-05-04_first salesperson_noah_sell ark_animals_yacht_sales babble_disguise motives_pioneered lame joke_weather_reach quota_blaming engineering_greatest innovation.gif
title: Noah, the First Salesperson

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Who was the world's first salesperson, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Some people say it was a guy named Noah.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Noah's last name was Content.

transcript.speaker: Noah
transcript.text: I have a big, curly stick and I don't even know why.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: His job was to sell an ark cruise to animals.

transcript.speaker: Noah
transcript.text: Did I say ark? I meant yacht.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: He invented something called sales-babble to disguise his motives.

transcript.speaker: Noah
transcript.text: We'll partner to leverage our value-adds in a win-win proposition.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: He pioneered the lame joke.

transcript.speaker: Noah
transcript.text: How's the weather up there? Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: When he couldn't reach quota, he got creative.

transcript.speaker: Noah
transcript.text: Strap this to your head and don't ask questions.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: But his greatest innovation he called "blaming engineering."

transcript.speaker: Bear
transcript.text: I can't find the honey spa.

transcript.speaker: Noah
transcript.text: Think fast.

setting: Dogbert's living room, then a retelling of the biblical ark story
situation: Dogbert tells a story about Noah being the world's first salesperson, with the ark portrayed as a misleadingly marketed 'yacht cruise' sold to animals. Noah uses jargon, lame jokes, and sketchy sales tactics, then hits quota by strapping a horn to a cat to pass it off as a unicorn. When the bears discover the promised honey spa doesn't exist, he blames engineering.
punchline: Noah is cast as the archetypal salesperson who overpromises, uses meaningless buzzwords, fudges the product, and deflects blame onto engineering when customers discover the product doesn't match the pitch.
summary: Dogbert retells the flood story as the origin of sales, complete with deceptive marketing, empty jargon, and finger-pointing at the engineers.

file: 1997/1997-03-03_combine words_ecosystem_engagement manger_ratbert_seem smart_walmart.gif
title: Ratbert Bluffs With Buzzword Bingo

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, I'm going back into the consulting business and I need you to be my engagement manager.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll seem very smart if you randomly combine the words on this list and make many references to "Wal-Mart."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It's like "Wal-Mart." Migrate your value into the white spaces of the ecosystem.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Wow! That's one smart rat!

setting: Dogbert's office and a client conference room
situation: Dogbert announces he is returning to consulting and makes Ratbert his engagement manager. He coaches Ratbert to sound smart by randomly combining buzzwords from a list and repeatedly mentioning Wal-Mart. At the client meeting, Ratbert recites meaningless jargon and the listeners are impressed.
punchline: Meaningless buzzword salad plus a Wal-Mart reference is enough to make a rat sound like a brilliant consultant, mocking how easily clients are impressed by jargon.
summary: A dog trains a rat to pass as a sage consultant by stringing together fashionable jargon, and the clients fall for it completely.

file: 1997/1997-01-21_perfromance review_alleged misdeeds_lower rating_fit bell curve_selling crack.gif
title: Bell Curve Forces Fabricated Misdeeds

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't sign this performance review! It's full of alleged misdeeds that you invented to lower my rating!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but I think it reflects the sort of things you might do. I had to make all the reviews fit a bell curve.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I am NOT selling crack from my cubicle!!!

situation: An employee storms into his manager's office, refusing to sign a performance review because it accuses him of misdeeds he never committed. The Boss calmly admits he invented the offenses because he had to force all the reviews to fit a bell curve. The employee, now reading the review, angrily denies one of the accusations: selling crack from his cubicle.
punchline: The Boss openly admits that the negative review items are made up just to satisfy a forced bell-curve ranking, and the invented accusation turns out to be absurdly serious.
summary: A manager cheerfully concedes he fabricated an employee's offenses to satisfy a mandated ratings distribution, leaving the worker to deny a ridiculous drug-dealing charge.

file: 1997/1997-01-02_million dollars_ten thousand_separate business cards_value added support.gif
title: Splitting Budget Into Business Cases

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need a million dollars but I only have authority to sign for up to ten thousand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Break it into a hundred separate business cases.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for your value-added management support.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was nothing.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a million dollars, but the boss can only approve up to ten thousand. The boss simply suggests splitting the request into a hundred separate business cases so each falls under his limit. Dilbert thanks him for his 'value-added' help, and the boss says it was nothing.
punchline: The boss's only contribution is advising Dilbert to circumvent the spending limit, so his 'value-added management support' really is nothing.
summary: A manager who can't approve a big expense just tells his employee to chop the request into many small ones, and gets thanked sarcastically for his useless help.

file: 1997/1997-09-02_dogbert_company emperor_wheelbarrows_salary_downsized_buzz saw dogbert_parent company_money.gif
title: Emperor Dogbert Downsizes Everyone

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Company Emperor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell the employees to get wheelbarrows to carry my salary out of here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Turn out the lights when you're done. You're all downsized. Shoo!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The media loved him

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Can we call you "Buzz Saw Dogbert"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I bought your parent company today. You're downsized. Shoo!

setting: Executive office, with Dogbert standing on a filing cabinet
situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and holding a scepter, becomes company emperor and orders the employees to carry out his enormous salary in wheelbarrows. He then lays off the entire staff. When reporters admiringly ask to nickname him "Buzz Saw Dogbert," he reveals he has bought their parent company and downsizes them too.
punchline: Dogbert's ruthless, indiscriminate layoffs earn him media praise, until he turns the same downsizing on the media outlet itself.
summary: A crowned canine tyrant pockets a gigantic paycheck, fires the whole workforce, and then buys and axes the press that was fawning over him.

file: 1997/1997-01-27_catbert_evil hr dircetor_lower base salary_necktie_wally.gif
title: Catbert Cuts Salary Because He Can

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We've decided to lower your base salary, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I realize this will be a hardship. But if you hand me your necktie I'll show you why this is being done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What did he say was the reason?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Because I can."

setting: Catbert's H.R. office and a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Wally from atop his desk that his base salary is being lowered. He offers to explain the reason if Wally hands over his necktie, which he apparently takes. Afterward Dilbert, holding the necktie and a coffee mug, asks Wally what the reason was, and Wally, holding a little plant, reports the answer.
punchline: The supposed justification for the pay cut is nothing but an arbitrary display of power, and Wally had to give up his necktie just to hear it.
summary: A malicious personnel chief slashes an employee's pay and demands a tie in exchange for an explanation that turns out to be pure spite.

file: 1997/1997-02-04_intranet web page_mother visit_mpeg file_video of birth_html_covered video_fire wall_nick name_dilberts mother.gif
title: Dilbert's Mom Hears Work Nickname

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent all week tweaking HTML for my intranet web page. You should see it, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I converted the video of my birth into an MPEG file. Anyone behind the fire wall can view it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: You should hear the nickname they have for you at work!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should hear the one I have for you right now.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on couches
situation: Dilbert visits with his mother and proudly tells her about the intranet web page he spent a week tweaking. He explains he has put a video of his own birth online for anyone behind the company fire wall to view. His mother, appalled, says he should hear the nickname his coworkers now have for him, and he snaps back with an insult of his own.
punchline: Dilbert's mom is mortified by his posting his birth video for coworkers to watch, and he responds with a nickname for her, implying the mother-son rudeness goes both ways.
summary: After boasting about putting his birth video on the company network, a man is scolded by his mother about his coworkers' nickname for him and fires back with a rude name of his own.

file: 1997/1997-07-15_pointless presentation_trade show_usual time wasting_filler_morres law_netscape_comparison_ironically_impassioned reminder_awards.gif
title: Alice Mocks Boss's Cliched Presentation

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've prepared your pointless presentation for the trade show.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's got the usual time-wasting filler: a graphic of Moore's Law, a "Netscape" comparison, and ironically...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ...it ends with an impassioned reminder to think in new ways.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I should give out some awards, too.

situation: Alice reads aloud the trade show presentation she has written for the Boss, openly describing it as pointless and full of time-wasting filler. She lists its standard contents, including a Moore's Law graphic and a Netscape comparison, and notes it ends with a plea to think in new ways. The Boss, missing the sarcasm, responds that he might hand out awards as well.
punchline: The presentation is a pile of buzzword cliches that ends by urging innovation, and the oblivious Boss is not insulted but inspired to add even more cliched conference fluff.
summary: A sarcastic employee previews the stale, formulaic talk she wrote for her boss, who cheerfully suggests padding it further.

file: 1997/1997-03-09_cheetah_drew lines_feel bad_mock you_morale of the story_opinions mattered_pure adrenaline_shrunk everything_sprang into action_totally worthless_trampoline.gif
title: Dilbert's Unreadable One-Page Org Chart

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're probably wondering how my day was.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was terrible...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Until I did this!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It all started when I deluded myself into thinking my opinions mattered.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I sprang into action like a cheetah on a trampoline!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I drew lines and boxes and arrows for hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was pure adrenaline.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Suddenly, trouble struck! It wouldn't fit on one page!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I shrunk everything until it was totally unreadable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it fit!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The moral of the story is that you don't have to feel bad just because you're totally worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd mock you but the challenge is gone.

situation: Dilbert comes home and narrates his day to Dogbert, who is reading a newspaper on the couch. He explains how he spent hours drawing a diagram of lines, boxes and arrows, then shrank it until it was unreadable so it would fit on one page. He concludes with a bleak moral, and Dogbert says he'd mock him but there is no challenge left.
punchline: Dilbert is so defeated and self-deprecating that he is proud of a diagram nobody can read, and even Dogbert can't be bothered to mock someone who has already done it himself.
summary: After a day of futile diagram-making, Dilbert cheerfully admits his own worthlessness and leaves his sardonic dog with nothing left to ridicule.

file: 1997/1997-12-27_wally the role model_art sarcasm_bosses own word_disciplined for insubordination_lips_resources_adding value_would be delighted.gif
title: Wally Teaches Safe Sarcasm

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally the role model

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's an art to sarcasm, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you use your boss's own words, you can't be disciplined for insubordination.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And do this with your lips.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today I focused my resources on adding value to the product process. Our shareholders would be delighted to know that.

situation: Wally coaches young Asok on how to be sarcastic without getting in trouble, advising him to repeat the boss's own words and to purse his lips. At a meeting, the boss reads out a buzzword-filled statement about adding value and delighting shareholders, which Wally and Asok are positioned to receive.
punchline: Wally's sarcasm technique is to quote the boss's meaningless corporate jargon back at him, which is safe because it can't be called insubordination, and the boss's own jargon is already ridiculous enough to sound sarcastic.
summary: A veteran slacker shows a newcomer how to mock management safely by parroting their own empty buzzwords back at them.

file: 1997/1997-10-28_boss_doesn't know_being insulted_with all due respect_intangible benefits_insulting_monkey face.gif
title: With All Due Respect, Insult the Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I discovered that our pointy-haired boss doesn't know he's being insulted if you say "with all due respect" first.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I love the intangible benefits of this job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: With all due respect, is that your face or is a monkey climbing down your collar headfirst?

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's doorway
situation: Alice tells Wally and Dilbert that the Boss can't recognize an insult if it is prefaced with "with all due respect." Wally, thinking to himself how much he enjoys the perks of the job, steps up to the Boss and tests the trick by insulting his face. The Boss stands there listening, apparently oblivious.
punchline: Wally gleefully exploits the Boss's obliviousness by delivering a blatant insult behind a polite phrase, which the Boss doesn't recognize as an insult.
summary: A coworker reveals a loophole for mocking the clueless boss, and Wally promptly puts it to creative use.

file: 1997/1997-02-16_leadership seminar_manager motivates employees_14 hour days_filthy sadist_pointy haired imbecile_leader_unpopular decions_training engineers.gif
title: Leadership Seminar Trick Question

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Grumble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grumble.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Grumble.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Leadership seminar

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: What would you call a manager who motivates employees to work fourteen hours a day?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A filthy sadist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pointy-haired imbecile.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Umm... No... That's not what I'm looking for.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think he means what do we call him to his face.

transcript.speaker: Alice, Dilbert, Wally
transcript.text: Leader.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Right! And what do you call someone who can make unpopular decisions again and again?

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: I hate training engineers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A filthy sadist?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait, it might be another trick question.

situation: Dilbert, Alice and Wally are grumbling on their way to a leadership seminar. The trainer asks what to call a manager who gets people to work fourteen-hour days, and the engineers answer honestly with insults. Alice realizes the trainer wants the polite label they would use to the boss's face, and they say 'leader'.
punchline: The engineers' honest opinions of overbearing managers are exactly what the trainer doesn't want, and they stay cynical enough to suspect even the next question is a trap.
summary: Cynical engineers keep giving blunt, insulting answers at a management seminar until they learn the diplomatic word the trainer was fishing for.

file: 1997/1997-07-10_incredibly sexy_fuzzy guy_dogebrt_dillbert_in touch with feelings_make me doubt_scientific methid.gif
title: Dilbert Is Not In Touch

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Wow. You're an incredibly sexy man. It's too bad I met this little fuzzy guy first.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: But looks aren't everything. Studies show that women want a man who is in touch with his feelings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: AAGH!! I hate my life!!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Gee. That's enough to make me doubt the scientific method.

situation: A woman pets Dogbert while telling Dilbert he is incredibly sexy, but says she met the little fuzzy guy first. She adds that studies show women want a man in touch with his feelings. Dilbert then cries out that he hates his life, and she says this makes her doubt the scientific method.
punchline: Dilbert's emotional outburst is exactly the sensitivity studies say women want, yet it fails to impress her, so she jokes that it undermines science.
summary: A woman who prefers Dogbert to the handsome Dilbert watches him vent his misery and decides the research on what women want must be wrong.

file: 1997/1997-08-30_dogebert_systems adminitrator_evil system_private_compiled binder_off color humor_unkind references_naughty propositions_heading_sing.gif
title: Dogbert Blackmails Wally Over Email

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Network Systems Administrator

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wally, did you know your e-mail system isn't private?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've compiled a binder with all of your off-color humor, unkind references to co-workers, naughty propositions, and admissions of theft.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Where is this heading?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like you to sing that question while hopping on one foot.

situation: Dogbert, working as the network systems administrator, tells Wally that company e-mail is not private. He reveals a binder he has assembled from Wally's own messages, full of offensive jokes, insults about co-workers and confessions of theft. When Wally nervously asks where this is going, Dogbert uses the blackmail material to demand a humiliating performance.
punchline: Instead of demanding money or favors, Dogbert's blackmail payoff is the petty, silly request that Wally sing his question while hopping on one foot.
summary: Armed with a binder of incriminating emails, the network administrator dog gleefully coerces an employee into a ridiculous act.

file: 1997/1997-01-09_mail order bride_elbonian_expectations low_avoid disappointement_powder snout_pig lady.gif
title: Low Expectations for Elbonian Mail-Order Bride

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My Elbonian mail-order bride has arrived.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I must keep my expectations low to avoid any disappointment.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Bride
transcript.text: Where's the ladies sty? I desperately need to powder my snout.

setting: Wally's home or an unspecified room with a shipping crate
situation: Wally opens a large shipping crate containing his mail-order bride from Elbonia, and tells himself in thought bubbles to keep his expectations low. When the bride emerges, she is a pig in a purple dress and yellow hair ornament, who asks for the ladies' sty to powder her snout.
punchline: Even with his expectations set deliberately low, Wally's Elbonian bride turns out to be an actual pig, proving that Elbonian goods and the mail-order process are worse than he could imagine.
summary: A man unpacks a crate holding his imported bride and is stuck with a pig in a dress who needs to freshen up her snout.

file: 1997/1997-10-13_mutual fund_investors_know alternatives_huge market_invest_index fund_wag hard.gif
title: Mutual Fund for Clueless Investors

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting a mutual fund for investors who aren't bright enough to know their alternatives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be a huge market. Otherwise most people would invest in index funds.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's an index fund?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ouch, ouch! You're making me wag too hard!

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert announces he is starting a mutual fund aimed at investors too unaware to know their other options. Dilbert sarcastically remarks that the market must be enormous, since otherwise most people would choose index funds. Dogbert, who has never heard of index funds, asks what one is, and is shown wagging his tail so hard that it hurts.
punchline: Dogbert's question reveals he is as ignorant of index funds as his intended customers, and his painfully vigorous tail-wagging shows he's delighted at having found a gullible market.
summary: A scheming dog plans to sell investment products to the uninformed, then reveals he doesn't know the cheap alternative himself.

file: 1997/1997-01-01_catbert_evil hr director_window cubicle_naps_on walls head.gif
title: Catbert Naps on Dilbert's Head

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally, I pulled some strings to get you moved to a window cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's for my own benefit. I plan to take naps while lying in the sun on top of your head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every day this job teaches me I can get used to anything.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Wally he arranged a move to a window cubicle, then reveals the real reason: he wants to nap in the sunlight on top of Wally's head. In the last panel, Dilbert is at his computer with Catbert asleep on his head, resigned to the situation.
punchline: Dilbert has become so conditioned by his awful workplace that he calmly accepts a cat sleeping on his head as just another thing he's gotten used to.
summary: A scheming HR cat disguises a self-serving favor as a perk, and the beleaguered employee who ends up as his sun-bathing cushion shrugs it off with weary acceptance.

file: 1997/1997-08-05_blueprints_new cubicle_window view_hot by window_breeze.gif
title: Cubicle With Beam And Window

transcript.speaker: Facilities Worker
transcript.text: According to the blueprints, your new cubicle has a support beam in it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least I have a window view.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's 108° by the window. But at least there's a breeze from the people who walk by and laugh.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't let me slow your search for someone who's interested.

setting: Office cubicle area and Dilbert's new cubicle by a window
situation: Dilbert carries a box of belongings while a man holding blueprints tells him his new cubicle has a support beam in it. Dilbert comforts himself that he at least gets a window view, but he ends up sweating in the 108-degree heat beside the window. He complains to Dogbert, who sits on a couch and sarcastically dismisses his whining.
punchline: Dilbert's only consolation is the window, but it makes him sweat in the heat, and even his cooling breeze comes from coworkers laughing at him, while Dogbert sarcastically shows zero sympathy.
summary: A man given an awful cubicle with a pillar in it tries to find a bright side, only to bake by the window while the sole breeze is passersby mocking him.

file: 1997/1997-01-03_one hundred business cases_level of approval.gif
title: Million Dollars, Hundred Business Cases

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Per your instructions, my request for a million dollars has been broken into one hundred business cases.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Each one is for ten thousand dollars, which is your exact level of approval authority.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I meant I can approve anything UNDER ten thousand dollars... so if you wouldn't mind...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Killing you? No, I wouldn't mind a bit.

situation: Dilbert arrives carrying a huge stack of paper and explains that, following the Boss's instructions, he split a million-dollar request into one hundred business cases of ten thousand dollars each. The Boss points out that his approval authority only covers amounts strictly under ten thousand, and asks Dilbert to mind something. Dilbert, misreading or deliberately twisting the Boss's trailing request, cheerfully says he wouldn't mind killing him.
punchline: After Dilbert's malicious-compliance workaround of the approval limit fails on a technicality, the Boss's trailing 'if you wouldn't mind...' lets Dilbert reply that he wouldn't mind killing him, revealing his true feelings.
summary: A big request is chopped into pieces to fit exactly at a manager's spending limit, and when the manager objects, the employee's reply turns darkly hostile.

file: 1997/1997-04-12_critical_dept phone list_list alphabetically_sort phone number.gif
title: Phone List Sorted By Number

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, I don't mean to be critical about the department phone list you put together...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it's traditional to list people alphabetically, not sorted by phone number.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because what possible use...?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Incoming call from... let's see... It's Wally... I can ignore it.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

situation: Dilbert politely complains to Carol, the department secretary, that the phone list she compiled is sorted by phone number instead of alphabetically. As he asks what possible use that could be, his phone rings and he looks at the number on it. He then realizes the number-sorted list lets him identify the caller as Wally and ignore the call.
punchline: Dilbert's own phone rings just as he asks what use a number-sorted list could be, and it turns out to be useful for identifying and ignoring callers like Wally.
summary: A man criticizes a coworker's oddly organized directory, then promptly discovers it helps him dodge an unwanted call.

file: 1997/1997-09-17_reverse psychology_goal_opposite of wants_space shuttle launch_alice desk.gif
title: Reverse Psychology Against IT Department

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not using reverse psychology! I really don't need anything from the Information Technology Department.

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: Curse you! You know our goal is to give you the opposite of what you want. If you want nothing we must give you everything!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please tell me how you got them to do this.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Watch me launch the space shuttle!

situation: Alice tells an IT technician she needs nothing from his department. Furious, he explains that IT's policy is to give users the opposite of what they ask for, so he must give her everything. Dilbert then asks how she managed this, and she is shown at her desk using the lavish equipment to launch the space shuttle.
punchline: Because IT perversely does the opposite of whatever users request, Alice exploits it by asking for nothing and ends up with every piece of equipment imaginable.
summary: By declaring she needs no help, Alice tricks a spiteful tech department into showering her with gear, which she gleefully uses on a space shuttle simulation.

file: 1997/1997-07-17_finest executives_created statements_core values_help community_producing state of the art_business soultions_didn't skimp_nine executives.gif
title: Ten Executives Wrote Core Values

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ten of our finest executives got together and created a statement of our core values.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "We help the community and the world by producing state-of-the-art business solutions."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm glad we didn't skimp and try to do that with only nine executives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah. It might have sucked.

situation: The Boss proudly announces that ten top executives collaborated to write the company's core values statement, then reads it aloud. It is a bland, generic line about producing business solutions. Wally and Dilbert respond with sarcastic relief that the committee wasn't smaller.
punchline: The mission statement is so trivial and generic that Wally and Dilbert sarcastically imply it would have been terrible if produced by fewer executives, mocking the idea that ten executives were needed for such a vapid result.
summary: A boss reads out a hollow corporate values statement crafted by a committee of ten, and his employees sarcastically praise the staffing level.

file: 1997/1997-06-27_good idea_nurture passion_rebellious employees_sarcastic employees_startegies_wearing culottes.gif
title: No Rebels, Only Sarcastic Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, we'll nurture the passion of our rebellious employees and form strategies around them.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: We don't have any rebellious employees. The last one got fired for wearing culottes on casual day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) It was such a good idea in my head.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: We still have some sarcastic employees. Can you work with that?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces a new strategy of nurturing rebellious employees, but a bald coworker points out there are none left because the last one was fired for a trivial dress code matter. The Boss's grand idea deflates, and the coworker offers sarcastic employees as a substitute.
punchline: The company fires anyone who shows even mild nonconformity, so the boss's plan to harness rebellion is impossible, and the best fallback is the sarcastic staff who survive by mocking quietly.
summary: A manager's plan to build strategy around rebel employees collapses when it turns out the company already purged them over absurd trivia.

file: 1997/1997-08-08_open book management_repurchasing stock_unpaid overtime_ignorance is bliss_highly motivated.gif
title: Open Book Management Reveals Stock Buybacks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I appreciate your new "open book management" philosophy...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, I've learned that we're repurchasing stock while I'm working unpaid overtime.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yet I remain highly motivated because I understand that income and equity are distinct concepts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who said ignorance is bliss? Ha!

situation: Dilbert thanks his boss for the company's new open book management policy, which has let him see the financials. He points out that the company is buying back its own stock while he works unpaid overtime, then sarcastically claims he stays motivated because income and equity are different things. The boss, speaking from off-panel, gleefully remarks on ignorance being bliss.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic gratitude exposes that transparency only shows employees how much the company spends on shareholders while they work for free, and the boss is delighted by the idea that his staff's ignorance keeps them content.
summary: A worker's thanks for newly revealed company finances turns into a sarcastic complaint that cash goes to stock buybacks while his overtime goes unpaid.

file: 1997/1997-11-10_cubicle police_living organisms_stack of paper.gif
title: Cubicle Police Topple Paper Stack

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Police Officer
transcript.text: I'm with the cubicle police. This is a safety violation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's perfectly safe unless you tap it with a flashlight or a dog jumps on it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This plays right into my theory that cubicles are living organisms.

situation: A uniformed cubicle police officer with a flashlight and a police dog cites Wally for a dangerously tall stack of papers on his desk. Wally calmly insists it is safe unless poked by a flashlight or jumped on by a dog, which are exactly what the officer has. The stack then collapses and buries Wally, and Dilbert observes it as evidence for his theory about cubicles.
punchline: Wally's stack is only safe under conditions the safety inspector immediately creates, so the pile collapses on him, and Dilbert smugly treats the cubicle's apparent revenge as proof that cubicles are alive.
summary: A pretend law enforcement visit to a cluttered desk ends with an avalanche of paperwork, which a bystander blames on the cubicle itself.

file: 1997/1997-11-11_stack of paper_cubicle cop_body_enrolled_workshop_temporary solution_three days.gif
title: Hiding a Body in Quality Workshop

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I heard that a stack of your papers fell over and killed a cubicle cop.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mmm.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What did you do with the body?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I enrolled it in the quality workshop next door.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a temporary solution.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The workshop is only three days.

setting: Office break room or conference table during lunch
situation: Dilbert, Alice and Wally sit eating at a table. Alice has heard that Wally's towering stack of papers fell and killed a cubicle cop, and asks where the body went. Wally calmly says he enrolled the body in the quality workshop next door as a stopgap.
punchline: Wally disposes of a corpse by hiding it in a mandatory quality workshop, implying such workshops are so dull and unproductive that a dead body would blend right in among the attendees, and the only flaw is that the workshop is short.
summary: A co-worker's accidental paper-avalanche killing is casually covered up by signing the corpse up for a training class.

file: 1997/1997-02-22_abandon logic_manage cliches_one bird_always right handed_actually inprovement.gif
