title: Boss Manages By Garbled Cliches

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to abandon logic and manage by cliches.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It won't be easy, but I'll take it one bird at a time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And remember, the customer is always right-handed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is actually an improvement.

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert that he will stop using logic and instead manage by cliches. He then mangles the sayings, mixing up 'one bird at a time' and saying the customer is always 'right-handed' instead of 'right'. Dilbert, sitting at his computer, remarks that this is actually an improvement.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan observation that the Boss's nonsensical, garbled cliches are better than his usual logic-based management implies his normal decisions are even worse.
summary: A manager vows to run things with mangled proverbs, and his employee dryly notes it beats the manager's normal thinking.

file: 1997/1997-02-13_haven't submitted paperwork_raise_show up_talk to boss_too busy_secretary needs secretary.gif
title: Secretary Too Busy for Paperwork

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, do you know why my raise hasn't showed up in my pay yet?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I haven't submitted the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm too busy to do it. Maybe you should talk to my boss about getting me a secretary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, you are the secretary.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: That'll cost you another month.

situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the boss's secretary, why his raise has not appeared in his paycheck. She admits she never submitted the paperwork because she is too busy, and suggests he ask her boss to get her a secretary. When Dilbert points out that she is the secretary, she responds by delaying his raise by another month.
punchline: Carol, the secretary, is too busy to do her own job, and when Dilbert calls this out she punishes him by delaying his raise even further.
summary: A secretary who has neglected a colleague's raise paperwork blames her workload, then retaliates with more delay when he points out the obvious.

file: 1997/1997-09-28_boss zone_donuts on hair_executive retreat_failure_one month_project_six phases_uncertainty_approval.gif
title: The Boss Zone Guarantees Failure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get my approval at each phase. Finish in one month.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's see... You're on vacation next week. Then you're traveling. Then there's your executive retreat...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ... It takes three weeks to get on your calendar... and the project has six phases...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What we have here is guaranteed failure.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You've left nothing to chance on this one.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I mean, normally there's a bit of uncertainty, but you've... Oh.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You've slipped into the "Boss Zone" where you can't see or hear employee input.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's weird. I lost ten minutes, and when I woke up, my doughnuts were gone.

setting: The Boss's office, then a cubicle area
situation: The Boss orders Alice to finish a six-phase project in one month, with his approval required at every phase. Alice points out that his vacation, travel, executive retreat and three-week calendar backlog make this impossible. The Boss zones out mid-conversation, and Alice eats his doughnuts; he later wonders where they went.
punchline: The Boss's unrealistic schedule is so self-defeating that he mentally checks out when told, and he is oblivious to what happened, including Alice taking his doughnuts.
summary: A manager's impossible deadline collides with his own unavailability, and when he tunes out the bad news his employee quietly helps herself to his snack.

file: 1997/1997-09-19_downsized_dinosaurs_spike things_safety hazrd_ate ficus tree_being professional.gif
title: Dinosaurs Argue Over Who Gets Downsized

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's not enough room for all of you dinosaurs. One of you must be downsized.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: If it helps, these spikey things are a safety hazard. And little Rex ate your ficus tree.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks for being professional about this, Bob.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: When you put him in good light, how cute is he really?

setting: Office conference room with a large table
situation: Dogbert, acting as a manager, tells three dinosaurs that there is only room for two and one must be downsized. Bob the dinosaur calmly lists reasons to cut the horned dinosaur and the baby dinosaur, including the spikes being a safety hazard and the baby eating the ficus. Dogbert thanks Bob for being professional, and Bob then undermines the cute baby dinosaur.
punchline: Bob's 'professional' behaviour in a layoff is really self-preservation: he throws his colleagues, including a helpless baby, under the bus to save himself.
summary: Faced with a layoff, a dinosaur coolly sabotages his coworkers by pointing out their flaws and even belittling the cutest one.

file: 1997/1997-02-01_more work_feeling unappreciated_hard working employee_hourly basis.gif
title: Hard Work Gets You More Work

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The more work I do, the more I'm given.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It doesn't pay to be a talented and hard-working employee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's it pay to be YOU?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Not bad on an hourly basis.

situation: A bald coworker pours coffee at the vending machine and complains to Dilbert that being talented and hard-working only earns him more work. Dilbert asks him how it pays to be him, and the coworker replies that it's not bad on an hourly basis.
punchline: The coworker's reply implies he is paid by the hour, so being given extra work, which he resents, does pay off in a way, and Dilbert's question exposes that his complaint is partly hollow.
summary: A grumbling employee insists diligence goes unrewarded, until a pointed question makes him admit the extra work comes with extra pay.

file: 1997/1997-08-09_open book management_debt_equity ratio_sweeping_broom_carpets.gif
title: Janitor Sweeps After Reading Financials

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Open Book Management

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: ...Then I sez, "Hey our debt to equity ratio is increasing."

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: I leapt into action and started sweeping like I've never swept before!

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Then I sez, "Hey, why am I using a broom on carpets?"

situation: A janitor holding a broom tells a seated, big-haired female employee about his reaction to seeing company financials under an open book management program. He says he noticed the rising debt to equity ratio and furiously swept in response, then realized he was using a broom on carpets. The employee listens with a pained expression.
punchline: Giving a janitor access to financial data doesn't make him able to act usefully on it, so open book management just leads to pointless, misguided effort.
summary: A custodian shares company financials-inspired frenzy of sweeping, only to realize he has been brooming a carpet.

file: 1997/1997-03-21_body rejected_payment technology_smart card_body rejected card.gif
title: Body Rejects the Smart Card

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's called a "smart card," and we should build our next product to handle this sort of payment technology.

transcript.speaker: Smart Card
transcript.text: Aaagh!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Foop

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never seen that happen.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: His body rejected the "smart card."

situation: Dilbert tells his coworkers that their next product should handle smart card payment technology while a short bespectacled colleague holds the card. The Boss appears to have swallowed or absorbed the card, and it is suddenly spat out from his mouth into the air. The coworker explains it as the Boss's body rejecting the smart card, as if it were an organ transplant.
punchline: The 'smart card' is ejected from the Boss's body like a rejected transplanted organ, a pun on medical rejection used to mock how dim the Boss is.
summary: A pitch for smart card payment technology is interrupted when the card pops out of a manager's mouth, treated as a medical rejection.

file: 1997/1997-06-29_ten percent raise_fifteen percent more_twenty percent_no budget_raises_give big raises_reward for leaving work_price sheet.gif
title: Rewarding Disloyalty With Big Raises

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want a ten-percent raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no budget for raises.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have an offer from another company that will pay fifteen percent more.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll give you twenty percent if you stay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you said there's no budget for raises.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... it's supposed to be a secret but...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our policy is to give big raises to people who spend their time interviewing for other jobs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good news! The secret company policy is to reward disloyalty!

transcript.speaker: Coworkers
transcript.text: Yippee! Yes! Woo-woo-woo

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What's the reward for leaving work early?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He wouldn't show me the price sheet.

setting: The Boss's office, then the office cubicle area
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for a ten-percent raise and is told there is no budget. When he mentions an outside offer, the Boss immediately offers twenty percent, then admits the secret policy is to give big raises to people who interview elsewhere. Dilbert shares the news with coworkers, who celebrate and ask what other disloyal behavior gets rewarded.
punchline: The company only pays raises to employees who threaten to leave, so the way to get ahead is to be disloyal, and Wally wonders what other bad behavior pays off.
summary: A manager pleads poverty until an employee flashes a rival job offer, revealing that the company quietly pays people for threatening to quit.

file: 1997/1997-11-21_catbert_evil hr director_no contact_employed_wally_total loyalty.gif
title: Catbert's One-Sided Loyalty Demand

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company has no implied contract to keep you employed, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But we expect total loyalty out of you.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I really, REALLY wish you wouldn't do your face-stretching exercises here every morning!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: (thinking) 1-2-3...

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, stands beside Wally's desk and tells him the company has no obligation to keep him employed. He then adds that the company still expects total loyalty from him. Wally silently grimaces and counts to himself while Catbert complains about his morning face-stretching exercises.
punchline: Wally is so exasperated by the company's one-sided demand for loyalty that he does face-stretching grimaces and counts to calm himself down, which Catbert finds annoying.
summary: An evil H.R. cat informs an employee that the firm owes him no job security yet demands complete devotion, and the employee tries to hold in his rage.

file: 1997/1997-10-18_money chetter_dogbert mutual fund_highest perfromer_read anything_tv show_financial reports.gif
title: Dogbert's Mutual Fund Hands Out Scripts

transcript.speaker: TV Host
transcript.text: My guest today on "Money Chatter" is the head of the "Dogbert Mutual Fund."

transcript.speaker: TV Host
transcript.text: It's reported that your fund is the highest performer of the decade. Tell us how you made that happen.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently, this guy will read anything you hand him.

setting: Television studio set for a financial talk show
situation: A TV host introduces Dogbert as the head of the top-performing mutual fund of the decade on a show called "Money Chatter." The host reads a question from a sheet of paper, and Dogbert replies by saying the host will read anything handed to him. It implies Dogbert supplied the host's script, including the glowing claim about his fund.
punchline: Dogbert's fund isn't really the top performer; he simply handed the gullible host a script claiming it was, and the host read it on air without checking.
summary: A canine fund manager on a finance show reveals his stellar reputation exists because the host dutifully reads whatever text he is given.

file: 1997/1997-04-04_training course_night_won't miss work_immortal abuse_mutual investment_fist of death_vending machines.gif
title: Night Training as Mutual Investment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sending you to a training course that runs at night so you won't miss any work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It might seem like an immoral abuse of my power, but I like to call it "a mutual investment in your career."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control... fist... of... death...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they have vending machines if you get hungry!

situation: The Boss tells Alice he is sending her to a training course held at night so she won't miss any work time. He admits it might look like an abuse of his power but spins it as a mutual investment in her career. Alice, seething, clenches her fist and thinks about restraining herself from violence while he cheerfully mentions the vending machines.
punchline: The Boss disguises forcing an employee to give up her evenings as a generous career investment, and his offer of vending machine snacks as compensation pushes Alice to the edge of violence.
summary: A manager cheerfully rebrands mandatory after-hours training as a perk, while his furious employee fights the urge to punch him.

file: 1997/1997-03-01_budget cuts_do more with less_first staff meeting_less planning_unnecessary work.gif
title: Doing More With Less Everything

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As you requested, I have learned to "do more with less."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm doing more unnecessary work, with less planning, less intelligence, and less guilt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate the first staff meeting after budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And less career aspiration, too!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: At the first staff meeting after budget cuts, Wally tells the boss he has obeyed the order to 'do more with less.' He explains that this means more pointless work with less planning, intelligence and guilt. Dilbert grumbles about these meetings, and Wally adds that he has less career ambition too.
punchline: Wally sarcastically interprets 'do more with less' as doing worse, more pointless work while caring less about everything, mocking management's empty slogan.
summary: A slacker employee gleefully reports that he has obeyed the cost-cutting slogan by cutting back on everything except pointless activity.

file: 1997/1997-02-07_stop watch_testing theory_people get dumber_emotional intelligence_twelve seconds.gif
title: Dogbert Times Dilbert's Dumbness

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't mind the stopwatch. I'm testing my theory that people get dumber every minute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not so simple, Dogbert. You also have to consider my "emotional intelligence," which is defined in a book I haven't read.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Twelve seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me that watch, you hog!

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert lying on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch holding a stopwatch and explains he is testing his theory that people get dumber every minute. Dilbert, reclining, objects that it isn't simple because of his 'emotional intelligence,' a concept from a book he hasn't read. Dogbert clicks the stopwatch and announces twelve seconds, and Dilbert angrily demands the watch.
punchline: Dilbert confidently cites a book he hasn't read and then gets ridiculously upset over the stopwatch, proving Dogbert's theory that he gets dumber almost immediately.
summary: A dog times how quickly his owner's intelligence collapses, and the owner confirms it within seconds by blathering about a book he never read and then throwing a tantrum.

file: 1997/1997-01-17_annual performance review_past two weeks_vacation_two weeks_spread motivation.gif
title: Review Based on Two Weeks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's your annual performance review, Tina.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I focused on your performance for the past two weeks because I don't remember anything farther back.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I was on vacation for the past two weeks!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No time to chat. I need to spread some motivation over here.

situation: The Boss hands Tina her annual performance review and admits he based it only on the last two weeks because his memory doesn't go back further. Tina angrily points out she was on vacation for that entire period. The Boss brushes her off, saying he has to go spread motivation elsewhere.
punchline: The Boss's annual review is based on a period when the employee wasn't even at work, and he dismisses her complaint while claiming to be motivating staff.
summary: A manager's yearly appraisal rests on a stretch of time when the employee was away, and he blithely walks off to inspire others.

file: 1997/1997-03-23_bug in software_alert_work many hours_buy stock in competition_industry halo effect_compensation plan.gif
title: Wally Profits From Software Bug

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa... I found a huge bug in our new software product.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I could alert the development team and work many hours of unpaid overtime to fix it...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or I could surf over to my online brokerage service and buy stock in our competition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you going to lunch?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I have to do an analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When Wally works through lunch... It's time to buy stock in our competition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally's working through lunch!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Quick! To the online brokerage service!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our competitor is up ten points on no news. We're up two, maybe from the industry halo effect.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...Or maybe our new compensation plan is motivating smarter behavior.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think you nailed it.

situation: Wally discovers a serious bug in the company's new software but decides to buy stock in the competitor instead of reporting it and working unpaid overtime. Dilbert and Alice notice Wally skipping lunch, deduce what it means, and also buy the competitor's stock. The Boss sees the stock movements and credits the new compensation plan for the 'smarter behavior'.
punchline: The compensation plan really is motivating smarter behavior, but it rewards employees for profiting from their own company's defects instead of fixing them, and the clueless Boss takes credit.
summary: Instead of fixing a major flaw in the company's product, employees quietly bet against their own firm while their manager congratulates himself on his incentive scheme.

file: 1997/1997-12-21_wally_training_big binder_training forgotten_binder last forever_living monument_temporary knowledge_cubcile_approve funding_free up funds_training budget.gif
title: Training Forgotten, Binder Lasts Forever

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm back from training.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got a big binder.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The training is already forgotten, but the binder will last forever.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A living monument to temporary knowledge!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll put it in my cubicle with the others.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Speaking of my cubicle, which direction is it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay, thanks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That information should be in a binder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did he approve funding for our project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not yet. Step one was to free up funds from the training budget.

situation: Wally returns from a training course carrying a big binder and cheerfully admits he has already forgotten everything he learned. He then has to ask The Boss which direction his own cubicle is, joking that the answer belongs in a binder. Finally he tells Dilbert that the funding request for their project is still pending because the first step was freeing up money from the training budget.
punchline: Wally's training budget is spent on courses that leave only a binder behind, and he has so completely forgotten everything that he can't even find his own cubicle, implying that the training was wasted money.
summary: A colleague returns from a course with nothing but a thick binder and a vanished memory, then gets lost on the way back to his desk.

file: 1997/1997-05-19_chair the fun commitee_improve morale_internet_personal reasons_technology.gif
title: Fun Committee Chair Caught Browsing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, two things...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Number one, I want you to chair the "Fun Committee" to improve employee morale.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Two, according to this report, you've been using the Internet for personal reasons.

situation: The Boss approaches Wally's cubicle and announces two items. First he appoints Wally to chair the 'Fun Committee' meant to boost employee morale. Then he reprimands Wally, citing a report showing he has used the Internet for personal reasons.
punchline: Management wants someone to promote workplace fun while simultaneously punishing the employee for having fun on the job, exposing the contradiction in its morale efforts.
summary: A manager puts an employee in charge of boosting office fun and then scolds him for personal web surfing in the same breath.

file: 1997/1997-05-05_calculated_total time_humans wait_web pages_information age_big plot_web is plot_normal society.gif
title: Web Waiting Cancels Productivity Gains

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I calculated the total time that humans have waited for web pages to load...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It cancels out all the productivity gains of the information age.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I think the web is a big plot to keep people like me away from normal society.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh, he's on to me.

setting: Dilbert's living room, at home on and near a couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch holding a handheld device and muses aloud about how much human time has been spent waiting for web pages to load. He concludes the delays wipe out the productivity gains of the information age, then suspects the web is a plot to isolate people like him. Dogbert, lying on the couch, thinks to himself that Dilbert has figured him out.
punchline: Dilbert's suspicion that the web is a plot to keep him from society is correct, as Dogbert's thought bubble reveals he is the one behind it.
summary: A man grumbling about slow internet speculates that the web is a conspiracy to isolate him, unaware his dog is secretly the mastermind.

file: 1997/1997-03-18_disguise arousal_jerk magnet_talk to death_turkey deceased_sandwhich.gif
title: Dilbert Clumsily Ignores Tina's Advances

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I always fall for the wrong guys. I'm a jerk magnet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tina, the turkey in your sandwich is already deceased. You don't have to talk it to death.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I must disguise my arousal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, look! We're eating exactly the same quantities for lunch!

situation: Tina sits across from Dilbert at lunch and remarks that she always falls for the wrong guys. Dilbert responds with a dry quip about her sandwich, then cheerfully points out that they are eating the same amounts of food, while Tina's thought bubble reveals she is trying to hide her attraction to him.
punchline: Tina's thought bubble shows she is attracted to the oblivious Dilbert, whose insulting and awkward remarks prove she really is a jerk magnet.
summary: A lunch companion pines for a socially clueless coworker who answers her romantic hints with sandwich trivia.

file: 1997/1997-10-19_catbert_evil director_human resources_randomly selected_drug test_unlucky at work_hair samples_one whole eyebrow_lost box_business.gif
title: Catbert's Cruel Hair Sample Drug Test

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: The Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're next.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, you've been randomly selected for an employee drug test.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Randomly? Why am I the only one who gets picked every week?!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're very unlucky at work. But I'm sure you compensate by being lucky at love.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Anyway... our new drug test uses hair samples...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: To be safe, give me six hairs... and one whole eyebrow.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll come back in an hour and say I lost the box. Purr purr purr

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, picks Wally from a list of victims for a drug test. When Wally complains that he is picked every week, Catbert mocks him and bursts into laughter. He then asks for hair samples, including a whole eyebrow, and plans to claim he lost the box so Wally must repeat the ordeal.
punchline: Catbert's drug test is just a sadistic excuse to pluck Wally's hair, and he plans to feign losing the samples so he can torment Wally again.
summary: A malicious HR cat repeatedly targets the same employee for a bogus drug test just to harvest his hair and eyebrow for fun.

file: 1997/1997-10-20_baseball_forgeries_low investment_moses_sports memorabilia_worth something_autographs_sports.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Forged Moses Baseball

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going into the sports memorabilia business.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've heard that most autographs are forgeries, so my initial investment will be low.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can I interest you in a baseball signed by Moses?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! That's going to be worth something.

situation: Dogbert announces he is entering the sports memorabilia business while Dilbert works on his laptop in an armchair. He explains that since most autographs are forgeries, his startup costs will be minimal. He then offers Dilbert a baseball supposedly signed by Moses, and Dilbert gullibly says it will be valuable.
punchline: Dogbert's forged memorabilia is absurdly implausible, since Moses lived thousands of years before baseball, yet Dilbert still believes the ball will be worth something.
summary: A scheming dog plans a cheap collectibles venture built on fakes and promptly tries to pawn off an impossibly ancient autograph on his gullible owner.

file: 1997/1997-08-12_catbert_evil director_clean desk policy_lick clean_spineless_stupid.gif
title: Clean Desk Policy Means Licking

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Here's the new "clean desk" policy, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Employees must lick their workplaces clean at the end of each business day."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do they seriously think we're this spineless and stupid?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ahm nah chanthing it.

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, hands Wally a new "clean desk" policy that requires employees to lick their workplaces clean every evening. Wally storms into the boss's office, outraged that the company thinks employees are so spineless and stupid. The boss replies with a lisp, his tongue evidently already busy licking his own desk.
punchline: The boss's garbled, lisping reply reveals he has already been licking his desk clean, proving the company's contempt for employees is justified.
summary: An absurd hygiene rule from H.R. is met with indignation until the boss's slurred speech shows he has obediently complied.

file: 1997/1997-08-04_abusing power_cucbicle_floors of luxury_gambling_housing_huge structure_office relocation_other reasons_shopping_wallyville.gif
title: Wally Builds Wallyville With Relocation Power

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm in charge of the office relocation. Where do you want your cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's this huge structure?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wallyville. It's two floors of luxury housing, shopping, and gambling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think you might be abusing your power?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What would be the other reasons to have power?

setting: Office during a relocation, at Wally's desk
situation: Dilbert, carrying a box of his belongings, is told by Wally that he is in charge of the office relocation and asks where Dilbert wants his cubicle. Dilbert notices a huge structure on the floor plan, which Wally reveals is Wallyville, a private complex of luxury housing, shopping and gambling. Dilbert suggests Wally might be abusing his power.
punchline: Wally sees nothing wrong with using his authority for personal gain, since he can't imagine any other reason to have power.
summary: Handed control of the office move, a lazy coworker designs himself a luxurious private city and shrugs off the idea that power should serve anything but his own benefit.

file: 1997/1997-12-14_beg food_carpet_cubicle_dog collar_invisible boundary_mark boundary_mild shock_new guy_new hire_offcie_high tech device.gif
title: New Hire Gets Invisible Fence Collar

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't have a cubicle available for you yet, Bruce.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'm declaring this part of the carpet to be your office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If someone goes to a meeting, you can sneak into his cubicle and use the phone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our computer budget is gone, but we have an old monitor that you can put on top of your briefcase.

transcript.speaker: Bruce
transcript.text: Can I put tape on the carpet to mark my boundary?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That won't be necessary, thanks to this hi-tech device.

transcript.speaker: Bruce
transcript.text: A dog collar?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It will give a mild shock if you cross your invisible boundary.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The new guy hasn't left that spot for a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally taught him to beg for food.

situation: The Boss tells a new hire named Bruce there is no cubicle for him, so he assigns a patch of carpet as his office, with a leftover monitor balanced on his briefcase. When Bruce asks to mark the boundary with tape, the Boss instead fastens a shock collar on him to enforce an invisible boundary. A week later, coworkers note he never leaves the spot and has been trained to beg for food.
punchline: The Boss treats a new employee like a pet, using an invisible-fence shock collar in place of a real workspace, and the employee ends up fully conditioned like a dog.
summary: With no desk to offer a new hire, a manager assigns him a patch of floor and shocks him into staying there.

file: 1997/1997-05-13_thermostat wars_warm for you_too hot_compromise_temprature_shirtless men.gif
title: Shirtless Thermostat Compromise Argument

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Thermostat Wars

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Be reasonable, Alice. When it's warm enough for you, it's too hot for normal humans.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Logically, you could wear a sweater. But there's nothing I can do to be less warm. Therefore, you must compromise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did she buy the argument?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. But I'm going to shave my back and take another run at it.

situation: Wally, stripped down to his boxer shorts and a necktie, argues with Alice that she should compromise on the office thermostat because she can add clothing while he cannot remove any more. Alice is unmoved. Afterward Dilbert asks if she bought it, and Wally says he will shave his back and try again.
punchline: Wally is so committed to his 'I can't get any cooler' argument that he thinks removing his back hair, rather than conceding, will finally persuade Alice.
summary: A half-dressed coworker lectures a colleague on thermostat logic, then plans to remove his back hair to bolster his case.

file: 1997/1997-06-11_hearty slap_practice swings_visiting the customer_smile_less follow thorugh_aim higher_trans suddenly.gif
title: Overenthusiastic Back Slap Practice Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Visiting the customer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I introduce you to the customer, smile and give him a hearty slap on the back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get ready. Here he comes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better take some practice swings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next time, less follow-through, aim higher, and if he turns around suddenly, hold off.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Ow ow ow ow ow

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry

setting: Office reception or hallway before a customer meeting
situation: Before meeting a customer, the Boss instructs Dilbert to smile and give the customer a hearty slap on the back. Dilbert practices his swings, then wallops the customer so hard he is knocked to the floor, with only his legs visible. The Boss calmly offers feedback on his technique.
punchline: The Boss's dry, clinical critique of the back slap, treating the customer being flattened as a mere technique problem, shows how oblivious and absurdly demanding management is.
summary: A manager's odd order to slap a client on the back ends with the client sprawled on the floor and the manager coolly critiquing the swing.

file: 1997/1997-01-31_asok the intern_installed calendar_software_schedule meetings easuer_cubicle justice_meeting until 3006_engineering.gif
title: Calendar Software Reveals Endless Meetings

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I installed calendar software on our network.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now you can see everyone's schedule and easily set up meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I say we grab him and apply some cubicle justice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Good idea, but I'm in meetings until the year 3006.

situation: Asok the intern proudly announces that he has installed calendar software so everyone can see each other's schedules and set up meetings easily. Dilbert suggests grabbing Asok and giving him some 'cubicle justice' as punishment. Alice agrees but says she is booked solid in meetings until the year 3006.
punchline: The software that makes scheduling meetings easier just makes it easier to fill everyone's time with meetings, so Alice has no free time for even a quick act of revenge for 1,000 years.
summary: An intern's helpful scheduling tool exposes how meeting-saturated everyone's calendar already is, leaving colleagues too booked to even retaliate against him.

file: 1997/1997-03-10_most absurd activity_timecard_no project code_staring at wall_fretting_reorganization_training_their or liar.gif
title: Timecard Fibbing About Reorganization Worry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And now for the most absurd activity of the week: the timecard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no project code for "staring at the wall and fretting about the reorganization." I'll call it "training."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Before I worked here I wasn't a thief or a liar.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't get that kind of training in school.

situation: Dilbert sits in his cubicle filling out his weekly timecard and realizes there is no project code for the time he spent worrying about a reorganization. He decides to log the hours as "training." A coworker overhears his remark about becoming dishonest at work and quips that school doesn't teach that.
punchline: Dishonest timecard padding is described as workplace "training," with the coworker sarcastically noting that you can't learn lying and stealing in school, only on the job.
summary: Forced to account for hours spent anxiously idling, an engineer invents a bogus timecard entry and a coworker wryly notes the corrupting education offered by corporate life.

file: 1997/1997-03-24_spelled wrong_technical recommendation_boss doubts dilbert_obver shoulder_computer_technology.gif
title: Boss Rejects Already-Working Solution

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I studied your technical recommendation and decided it's impossible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already did it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It will never work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's working perfectly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You spelled this word wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a number.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has reviewed his technical recommendation and concluded it is impossible, but Dilbert, typing at his computer, says he has already implemented it. The Boss insists it will never work even as Dilbert says it is working perfectly. Desperate to find a flaw, the Boss points out a misspelled word, which turns out to be a number.
punchline: The Boss ignores clear evidence that the solution works and clings to a nitpick, which exposes his own incompetence when the supposed misspelling is actually a numeral.
summary: A manager declares a proposal impossible after Dilbert has already built it, then fumbles to find fault with a typo that isn't one.

file: 1997/1997-02-21_appliances_lewd condcut_plea bargain_plead guilty_stealing computer_mr coffee.gif
title: Lewd Conduct With Appliances Plea Deal

transcript.speaker: Prosecutor
transcript.text: You're accused of stealing a computer. We'll reduce the charge to "lewd conduct with appliances" if you'll plead guilty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds fair. People will understand it's just a plea bargain.

transcript.speaker: Prosecutor
transcript.text: Would you like a minute alone with "Mr. Coffee"?

setting: A conference room or courtroom-style meeting room, then a kitchen with a coffee maker
situation: Dilbert, handcuffed and seated beside Dogbert, is told by a prosecutor that his computer theft charge will be reduced to "lewd conduct with appliances" if he pleads guilty. Dilbert naively accepts, assuming people will understand it is just a plea bargain. The prosecutor then cheerfully offers him a minute alone with a Mr. Coffee machine, as if the plea made the accusation true.
punchline: Dilbert accepts a plea deal assuming the embarrassing charge will be seen as meaningless, but the prosecutor treats it as real and offers him private time with the coffee maker.
summary: A defendant trades a theft charge for a humiliating appliance-related offense and promptly discovers that everyone is willing to take the new accusation literally.

file: 1997/1997-06-30_need to know_basis_complete list_run for it_volcano erupting.gif
title: Dilbert's Need-to-Know List

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm putting you on a "need to know" basis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's a complete list of the things I need to know. If it's not on the list, I probably don't need to hear it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Number one: "Run for it, Dogbert! The volcano is erupting!"

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Plurals will also be allowed.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is being put on a "need to know" basis, then hands him a complete list of the only things he wants to be told. Dogbert reads the first item aloud, a warning that a volcano is erupting, and adds that plurals will also be allowed.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to restrict information to a short list is absurdly narrow, and Dogbert's sarcastic reading of the first item implies the list is so ridiculous that only an emergency would qualify, with 'plurals' as a deadpan loophole.
summary: After limiting his dog to a short list of permitted messages, a man finds the very first entry is a volcano warning.

file: 1997/1997-10-22_autographed by jesus_footbal_stitches_healed_oink.gif
title: Jesus-Autographed Football Scam

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You say this football was autographed by Jesus...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'm no fool. This isn't a football. It has no stitches.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They healed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I think I heard it oink.

setting: Dogbert's sports memorabilia counter or shop
situation: Dilbert examines a football that Dogbert, acting as a memorabilia dealer, claims was autographed by Jesus. Dilbert points out the ball has no stitches, and Dogbert glibly says they healed, which Dilbert accepts. Dogbert then adds that he thinks the ball oinked, hinting it is really a pig product.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd excuse that the stitches 'healed' fools the gullible Dilbert, and the oink reveals the 'football' is really a pigskin, underscoring that Dilbert is being conned.
summary: A swindling dealer talks a credulous customer into believing a smooth, seamless ball is a miraculously healed holy relic, then lets slip that it may be something far more porcine.

file: 1997/1997-04-03_loud conversation_cubicle_goaway_pound head_strange noise_alice threatens.gif
title: Alice Threatens Loud Cubicle Neighbors

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hate to interrupt your loud conversation outside my cubicle...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But if you don't go away, I'll pound your inconsiderate head so far into your torso that you have to drop your pants to say hello.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you just hear a strange noise?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It sounded like, "Melp! Melp!"

situation: Alice, with her big hair, politely interrupts two coworkers chatting loudly outside her cubicle and then threatens to pound one of them into the ground if they don't leave. In the last panel Wally and Dilbert wonder about a strange noise, and a tiny pair of arms waves from a heap on the floor where the coworker has been flattened.
punchline: Alice carries out her violent threat so thoroughly that the noisy coworker is flattened into the floor, and all that remains is a muffled "Melp!"
summary: A woman fed up with hallway chatter makes an outrageous threat and promptly makes good on it, leaving her victim squashed and squeaking.

file: 1997/1997-03-17_linch time_sandwich_cafetria_borrow five dollars_keep professional_girl like dilbert_untamed beast.gif
title: Untamed Beast Needs Five Dollars

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: It's noon. Let's grab a sandwich at the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but make sure that's all you grab. I'd like to keep this on a professional basis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I'll need to borrow five dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: He's like a beautiful, untamed beast. Sigh.

situation: A female coworker with big brown hair invites Dilbert to lunch at the cafeteria. Dilbert agrees but warns her to keep things professional, then casually asks to borrow five dollars from her. She is not put off and swoons, thinking of him as a beautiful, untamed beast.
punchline: Dilbert lectures her about professionalism while mooching money off her, yet his rudeness only makes her more infatuated with him.
summary: A smitten coworker is charmed rather than offended when the man she invited to lunch sets ground rules and then asks her for cash.

file: 1997/1997-12-07_weekly_wally status report_process pride_impact on earnings_pride in results_high level_morale_pride in process.gif
title: Wally's Pride in Pointless Process

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It is my pleasure to present the weekly "Wally status report."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I developed what I call "process pride."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It all started when I realized I have no impact on earnings.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Obviously I can't take pride in the results of my work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Obviously.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I need pride. Otherwise, how could I maintain my high level of morale?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I learned to take pride in my processes instead of my results.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Everything I do is still pointless, but I'm very proud of the way I do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that all you did this week?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, I'm only one person.

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: Wally presents his weekly status report to the boss, Dilbert and Alice. He explains that since he has no effect on earnings, he has taught himself to take pride in his processes rather than his results, admitting his work is still pointless. The boss responds by asking if that's all he did this week.
punchline: Wally dresses up doing nothing useful as a morale-boosting achievement, and the boss, instead of questioning the pointlessness, merely wants more output, to which Wally lamely replies he's only one person.
summary: A lazy employee reports that he has found a way to feel proud of how he works despite accomplishing nothing of value.

file: 1997/1997-11-02_marketing dept_engineering dept_other engineers_careless mistake_need nets_rope_tranquilizer darts_askengineering.gif
title: Engineers Hunt the Marketing Magazine

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Marketing department

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: Hey! It's a magazine!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Engineering department

transcript.speaker: Engineer Alarm
transcript.text: Danger! A magazine has been discovered in Marketing!

transcript.speaker: Engineer (Alice)
transcript.text: Marketing has a magazine!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gasp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gather the other engineers. We must get that magazine.

transcript.speaker: Engineer (Alice)
transcript.text: Check

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We think it was a careless mistake by someone in the mail department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you know, there is nothing more dangerous than a marketing person with a little bit of knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We know where the magazine will be read. We need nets, rope and tranquilizer darts.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: I'll have to ask Engineering to build one of these space stations...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Phoot

setting: Marketing and engineering departments of an office, with a war room and a men's restroom
situation: A marketing employee finds a magazine, and the engineers treat it like a dangerous wild-animal sighting. Dilbert organizes a war room strategy to capture the magazine and its reader with nets, rope and tranquilizer darts. The marketing man, reading about space stations in the restroom, gets hit by a dart.
punchline: Engineers treat a marketing person reading a magazine as a threat to be hunted and tranquilized, because they believe marketing people with a little knowledge will start demanding impossible engineering projects.
summary: Engineers mount a military-style operation to stop a marketing colleague from learning something from a magazine before he can demand absurd products.

file: 1997/1997-08-31_make copy_secretary_more cost effective_highly paid_document_high level plnning_secretary takes lunch_never makes copy.gif
title: Too Important to Photocopy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll make a quick copy, then we can discuss it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no, I'll have my secretary do that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That will take longer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's more cost-effective.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're highly paid professionals. Carol is ... well... I don't know if we pay her at all.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now we're free to do high-level planning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... we kinda need that document.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ooh, time for lunch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... do you fish?

setting: The Boss's office, plus Carol's cubicle
situation: Dilbert offers to quickly photocopy a document so they can discuss it, but the Boss insists his secretary Carol should do it because highly paid professionals shouldn't make copies. Carol, with an urgent pile on her desk, simply leaves for lunch, so the copy never gets made. Dilbert is left idly making small talk with the Boss.
punchline: The Boss's claim of cost-effectiveness backfires, since delegating a thirty-second task to an overloaded secretary means the document never arrives and the two highly paid professionals end up with nothing to do.
summary: A manager refuses to let his employee do a trivial task because it is beneath their pay grade, and the delegated job simply vanishes into the secretary's lunch break.

file: 1997/1997-02-08_work smarter_not harder_pay more work less_frightened idiot.gif
title: New Slogan: Work Like Frightened Idiot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My old slogan was, "Work smarter not harder."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But people kept leaving for companies that pay more for less work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Work like a frightened idiot!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Catchy.

situation: The Boss, in thought bubbles, recalls his old slogan about working smarter, not harder, and admits employees kept quitting for companies that pay more for less work. He then announces his new slogan aloud to Alice, urging employees to work like frightened idiots. Alice sarcastically remarks that it's catchy.
punchline: Rather than fixing pay or conditions that drive people away, the Boss replaces the slogan with an insulting one that demands fearful, mindless labor, and Alice sarcastically calls it catchy.
summary: After his motivational motto fails to stop staff from leaving for better pay, the boss swaps it for one that openly demands fearful, thoughtless effort.

file: 1997/1997-08-14_rumor_south dakota_ceo_grew up_near parents_baby sitting_most cycnical_blushing.gif
title: Cynical Theory About CEO Relocation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a rumor that my company will move to South Dakota. But I don't believe it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: South Dakota... isn't that where your CEO grew up? Maybe he wants to be near his parents to get free baby-sitting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is the most cynical thought I have ever heard in my life.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks. I'm blushing under my fur.

setting: Outdoors on a neighborhood walk, at a mailbox
situation: Dilbert walks home with Dogbert and mentions a rumor that his company will relocate to South Dakota, though he doesn't believe it. Dogbert suggests the CEO, who grew up there, may be moving the company just to get free baby-sitting from his parents. Dilbert is appalled, and Dogbert takes it as a compliment.
punchline: Dogbert proposes that a major corporate relocation is driven by the CEO's personal convenience, and happily accepts being called cynical as praise.
summary: A pet dog explains a rumored corporate move by imagining the boss wants his parents to watch his kids, and is flattered when his owner calls the idea shockingly cynical.

file: 1997/1997-05-22_catbert_evil_executed_hr driector_ill be fired_internet_non buiness_personal thoughts_sadistic policies_senseless_warning_mass email_technology.gif
title: Catbert's Senseless Sadistic Policies Memo

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Any employee who uses the Internet for non-business purposes will be fired.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And any employee who sits in a company chair while having a personal thought will be executed by security.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The great thing about senseless, sadistic policies is that they don't require a lot of explanation.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, seated at a computer
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, sits at his computer composing a company-wide policy announcement. He first threatens to fire anyone using the Internet for non-business purposes, then escalates to threatening execution for having a personal thought in a company chair. In the last panel he smugly reflects on how convenient cruel, arbitrary rules are.
punchline: Catbert gleefully admits that absurd, cruel policies are easy to issue because they need no justification, satirizing arbitrary corporate rules.
summary: A malicious personnel chief fires off increasingly ridiculous workplace edicts and then congratulates himself on how little effort it takes to justify cruelty.

file: 1997/1997-12-08_compliments_compliments list_everything you say_lower opinion_analyze identity.gif
title: Dating Advice From Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you're with a woman, everything you say will lower her opinion of you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I can give her compliments, right?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: No! That's the worst thing!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Women keep a log of all compliments. They analyze the pattern to identify negative trends.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I use my real name?

setting: Outdoors on a sidewalk, then beside a window of a building
situation: Ratbert gives Dilbert dating advice, claiming that anything he says to a woman will lower her opinion of him. When Dilbert asks about compliments, Ratbert says women log every compliment and analyze the pattern for negative trends. A paranoid Dilbert asks whether he should use his real name.
punchline: Ratbert's absurd claim that women data-mine compliments makes Dilbert so paranoid that he considers giving a false name to avoid being tracked.
summary: A tiny lab-rat advisor convinces an anxious engineer that romance is a surveillance operation where even kind words get statistically audited.

file: 1997/1997-02-05_benefit of doubt_haven't bothered_laziness_low performance rating_many issues_difficult.gif
title: Low Ranking for Not Bothering Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I gave you a low performance ranking because you haven't bothered me all year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Logically, if your job were difficult and important, you would have brought me many issues to resolve.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you think of ANY other reason I might not bring you issues?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, laziness. But I gave you the benefit of a doubt.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Alice he gave her a low performance ranking because she never brought him any issues, reasoning that a difficult and important job would generate many problems for him to resolve. Alice asks if he can think of any other reason she might not bother him, and he says laziness, claiming he was generous to doubt that.
punchline: The Boss assumes Alice is lazy rather than competent enough to solve her own problems, and he thinks that assumption is generous, so his logic punishes self-sufficiency.
summary: A manager downgrades an employee's review because she never troubled him with problems, never considering that she might simply be good at her job.

file: 1997/1997-11-04_cobol programmer_millenium problem_dinosaur.gif
title: Hiring a Dinosaur for COBOL

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need COBOL programmers for our mainframe millenium problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you see anyone who looks like a COBOL programmer, let me know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Turn around.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you a COBOL programmer?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: No, but I'm often told I look like one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert the company needs COBOL programmers to fix its mainframe millennium problem and asks him to point out anyone who looks like one. Dilbert tells him to turn around, revealing a green dinosaur standing behind him. The Boss asks the dinosaur if he is a COBOL programmer, and after a non-answer, hires him anyway.
punchline: COBOL is such an ancient language that its programmers are stereotyped as dinosaurs, and the Boss is so clueless that he hires a literal dinosaur based on appearance alone rather than any actual skills.
summary: Told to flag anyone resembling an old-school mainframe coder, the Boss finds a literal dinosaur behind him and immediately offers him a job.

file: 1997/1997-10-25_seeing beautiful woman_curtains_venetian blinds_lawn chair in yard.gif
title: Wally's Neighbor Blocked By Blinds

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've been seeing a beautiful woman. But something came between us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Her curtains?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Venetian blinds. Totally unforgiving.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe she got spooked when you put the lawn chair in her yard.

situation: Wally tells Dilbert he has been 'seeing' a beautiful woman but something came between them. Dilbert guesses it was her curtains, and Wally confirms it was her venetian blinds. Dilbert then suggests she may have been spooked when Wally put a lawn chair in her yard.
punchline: Wally's 'relationship' is actually him spying on a woman through her window, and Dilbert deadpans that the lawn chair in her yard probably tipped her off.
summary: A coworker's romantic boast turns out to be window-peeping on a neighbor, who has shut him out with blinds after he camped out on her lawn.

file: 1997/1997-02-09_cafeteria_heimlich maneuver_insecure_job interview_low self esteem_pretend to choke_special kind of employee_work here_working unpaid overtime_overqualified.gif
title: Interviewing for Low Self-Esteem Employees

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: We're looking for a special kind of employee, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Specifically, we like people with low self-esteem.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: That way we can bully them into working unpaid overtime.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you're insecure enough to work here?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me put it this way.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sometimes I pretend to choke in the cafeteria ...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then when someone performs the Heimlich maneuver on me I spin around suddenly ...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Just to get a hug.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did he really say you're over-qualified?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aak! Mmph!

setting: A job interview in an office, then a cafeteria table
situation: An interviewer tells Wally the company wants employees with low self-esteem so they can be bullied into unpaid overtime. Asked if he's insecure enough, Wally describes faking choking in the cafeteria so someone will give him the Heimlich maneuver, just to get a hug. In the last panel, Alice and Dilbert ask Wally if the interviewer really called him over-qualified while Wally chokes on his food.
punchline: Wally's pathetic hug-seeking confession makes him over-qualified for a job that demands deep insecurity, and he ends up actually choking.
summary: A hiring manager seeks needy, insecure staff to exploit, and Wally wins him over by admitting he fakes choking just to be embraced.

file: 1997/1997-10-15_monkeys_pick stocks_dogbert mutual fund_better professional_employee only monkeys_high fees_hiring the best_paid commercial.gif
title: Dogbert's Monkey-Run Mutual Fund

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (TV)
transcript.text: Studies have shown that monkeys can pick stocks better than most professionals.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (TV)
transcript.text: That's why the Dogbert Mutual Fund employs only monkeys.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (TV)
transcript.text: Yes, our fees are high, but I don't apologize for hiring the best.

setting: A living room with a TV showing a paid commercial, then a TV studio set
situation: A man relaxes in an armchair watching a paid commercial in which Dogbert pitches his mutual fund. Dogbert cites studies showing monkeys pick stocks better than professionals and says his fund employs only monkeys. In the last panel, monkeys crowd around him as he defends the fund's high fees.
punchline: Dogbert admits his fees are high but justifies them as the cost of hiring the best, even though the 'best' are monkeys, mocking overpriced investment funds and their cheap, random stock-picking.
summary: A TV pitch for a mutual fund staffed entirely by monkeys ends with the host proudly defending his steep fees.

file: 1997/1997-03-11_young and inexperinced_naive question_doing email_after tax earnings_alice_stuffed body_shirt sleeve.gif
title: Asok Questions Alice's Email Habit

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am young and inexperienced, so please excuse this naive question, Alice...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You spend hours every day "doing e-mail." How does this contribute to net after-tax earnings?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Today I learned that Alice can stuff my entire body into one shirt sleeve.

situation: Asok, the young intern, politely apologizes for his inexperience and then asks Alice how her hours of daily e-mail contribute to the company's net after-tax earnings. Alice reacts violently off-panel. In the last panel Asok's whole body is stuffed into a shirt sleeve while Dilbert sits calmly at his computer.
punchline: Asok's earnest but impertinent question about the value of e-mail provokes Alice's wrath, and he ends up crammed into his own shirt sleeve, learning the painful lesson that you don't challenge Alice.
summary: A naive intern challenges a coworker's productivity and gets physically punished in an absurd cartoon way.

file: 1997/1997-12-05_write resume_large fee_dogbert_having trouble_invented coffee_patent.gif
title: Dogbert's Resume Has Impossible Credentials

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Can you help me write a résumé?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, for a large fee.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: How do I know you're qualified?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Check my résumé.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: I'm having trouble believing that you invented coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Check my patent.

setting: Dogbert's office, with a desk and purple chair
situation: A red devil in a costume, holding a large wooden spoon, asks Dogbert to help write a résumé. Dogbert quotes a large fee and, when asked about his qualifications, hands over his own résumé. The devil doubts the claim that Dogbert invented coffee, and Dogbert points to a patent as proof.
punchline: Dogbert's credentials are absurdly inflated, and he offers self-produced documents like a résumé and a patent as proof of his claims, implying such paperwork can be manufactured or is worthless as verification.
summary: A devil seeking résumé help gets skeptical when the consultant's own paperwork claims he invented a famous beverage, and the consultant just points to more paperwork.

file: 1997/1997-10-14_dogbert_mutual fund_past performance_no indication_future perfromance_strategy_entire investment_personal expenses_talking to wall.gif
title: Dogbert Spends Your Investment Personally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Dogbert Mutual Fund

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As you know, past performance is no indication of future performance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So my strategy is to use your entire investment for my personal expenses and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Has that strategy ever worked before?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Geez, it's like I'm talking to a wall here.

setting: Dogbert's office at the Dogbert Mutual Fund
situation: Dogbert, running his own mutual fund, sits behind a large desk and tells a prospective investor that past performance doesn't predict the future. He then reveals his strategy is to spend the client's entire investment on his own personal expenses. When the client reasonably asks if this has ever worked, Dogbert complains that the client is not listening.
punchline: Dogbert twists the standard investment disclaimer into a blatant excuse to embezzle client funds, then deflects the client's sensible question by accusing him of being unresponsive.
summary: A crooked canine fund manager turns a routine financial disclaimer into a license to blow his customer's savings on himself.

file: 1997/1997-11-03_starting business_masseur_cubicle dwellers_touch my back_chair massage.gif
title: Chair Massage Business Misunderstanding

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I'm starting my own business as a masseur.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: My specialty will be in-office chair massages for cubicle dwellers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Were you planning to touch my back at any point?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: It's a chair massage, pervert.

situation: A green dinosaur holding a towel and a bottle of oil announces to a colleague that he is starting a business as a masseur. He explains his specialty will be in-office chair massages for cubicle workers. A bespectacled coworker at a desk nervously asks whether he plans to touch his back, and the dinosaur indignantly calls him a pervert while massaging the chair.
punchline: The dinosaur literally massages the chair rather than the person, so the coworker's reasonable assumption that a massage involves touching is met with an accusation of perversion.
summary: A dinosaur launching a massage service for office workers turns out to be rubbing the furniture instead of the customers.

file: 1997/1997-09-10_control_during takeouff_laptop computer_plane control_takeoff_plane descent_excel_pilot communication.gif
title: Laptop Controls the Plane

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Have a nice flight. Remember to turn on your laptop computer during takeoff.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought they tell you to turn it OFF.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Off?!! How would they transfer control to you if they had trouble?

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Turn off that !*#% laptop!!

transcript.speaker: Boss (in plane)
transcript.text: No way! I have to land this baby! ...Can I do that in "Excel"?

setting: Office cubicle, then a plummeting airplane
situation: The Boss is leaving on a flight when Alice tells him to keep his laptop on during takeoff, claiming the airline might need to hand control of the plane over to him in an emergency. In the last panel the plane is nose-diving, someone screams at him to turn off the laptop, and he refuses because he is trying to land the plane, wondering if he can do it in Excel.
punchline: Alice sends the gullible Boss off with absurd advice, and he ends up trying to fly a crashing plane from a spreadsheet.
summary: A traveling manager is fed nonsense about airline procedures by a coworker and ends up attempting to pilot a falling jet with office software.

file: 1997/1997-01-10_pig with wig_paid for bride_send back_mail order bride.gif
title: Mail-Order Bride Was a Pig

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: ...So my Elbonian mail-order bride turns out to be a pig with a wig.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What a rip-off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're taking this well. I'd be mad if I paid for a bride and then I had to pay to send her back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You did send her back...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: B.L.T.?

situation: Wally tells Dilbert that his Elbonian mail-order bride turned out to be a pig wearing a wig. Dilbert sympathizes, noting that returning her would add insult to injury, and wonders if Wally did send her back. Wally replies by holding up a bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich.
punchline: Wally did not send the pig back; he ate it, as shown by the B.L.T. sandwich in his hand.
summary: A coworker's disappointing foreign bride turns out to have been dealt with in a very delicious way.

file: 1997/1997-07-21_agenda_ubr_first job_crash dummies_spent a fortune_unfocused boss rambling.gif
title: Unfocused Boss Rambling Meeting Agenda

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the agenda. The first hour will be U.B.R., as usual.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This reminds me of my first job, before crash dummies were popular. Man, I spent a fortune on aspirin.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What exactly is U.B.R.?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unfocused boss rambling. Only 58 minutes to go.

situation: The Boss opens a meeting by announcing that the first hour is reserved for 'U.B.R.' He then launches into a rambling, irrelevant story about his first job and buying aspirin. Alice asks what U.B.R. means, and Dilbert, reading a booklet with his feet up on the table, explains it and counts down the minutes remaining.
punchline: U.B.R. stands for unfocused boss rambling, a regular scheduled hour that the boss himself unwittingly demonstrates, leaving the staff to simply endure it.
summary: A manager's standing agenda item turns out to be an hour of aimless chatter, which his bored team quietly waits out.

file: 1997/1997-04-22_family freindly_policy_childless people_tax_child care_lower profit sharing_time off_pick up slack_victim.gif
title: Family-Friendly Policy Taxes Childless Workers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This so-called "family friendly" policy is like a tax on childless people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You get child-care; I get lower profit-sharing. You get time off for family; I get to pick up your slack...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a victim, but in some strange way I'm enjoying it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then you'll love this.

situation: Dilbert walks beside Alice, holding a memo, and complains that the company's family-friendly policy unfairly burdens childless employees through lower profit-sharing and extra work. Alice listens silently as he vents. When he admits he's weirdly enjoying his victimhood, she cracks her knuckles and tells him he'll love what comes next.
punchline: Alice responds to Dilbert's self-pitying complaint by threatening to punch him, offering him more victimhood to enjoy.
summary: After a coworker grumbles about being penalized for having no kids, Alice offers to give him something genuinely worth complaining about.

file: 1997/1997-03-08_rather the consulatant_sit on head_play bulldozer_too much power.gif
title: Consultant Ratbert Plays Bulldozer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Now that you're under my spell, I'd like to sit on your head and play bulldozer.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Make some engine noises with your lips!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Brbrbr brbrbr

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you think our consultant has too much power?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nah. He's barely moving that file cabinet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Brbr brbr brbr

situation: Ratbert, working as a consultant, hypnotizes the Pointy-Haired Boss, climbs onto his head and makes him make engine noises while pretending to be a bulldozer. Alice asks Dilbert whether the consultant has too much power, and Dilbert shrugs it off.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses the concern because the consultant, who has the boss under his spell, is only using his power to move a file cabinet, when it is the boss himself who is the one being used as the bulldozer.
summary: A tiny rat hypnotizes the boss into serving as his personal toy bulldozer, while a coworker idly wonders whether the consultant has gained too much influence.

file: 1997/1997-11-23_revenue figures_no revenue_upgradimg_project revenues_spread hseet_fist of death.gif
title: Boss Demands Fake Revenue Figures

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you show this to our VP, put in some revenue figures.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's no revenue. All we're doing is upgrading our network.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I might have told him the project has revenues.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's not confuse him by changing the story now.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yi-yi-yi

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: O-o-o-okay. How much revenue do you want? A million dollars?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I might have told him it was more.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Just tell me what lie to use!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can't you calculate it on the spreadsheet?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control... fist... of... death...

situation: The Boss tells Alice to add revenue figures to a presentation for the VP, even though the project is only a network upgrade with no revenue. He admits he already told the VP it had revenues and doesn't want to change the story. Alice, increasingly furious, asks him which lie to use, and he suggests she just calculate it on the spreadsheet while she struggles to restrain her violent rage.
punchline: The Boss expects Alice to manufacture legitimate-looking revenue numbers for a lie he already told, treating fabricated figures as a simple spreadsheet calculation, which drives Alice to the brink of violence.
summary: A manager who fibbed to his superior about a project's earnings pressures his furious employee to invent numbers that make the fib look true.

file: 1997/1997-12-29_photo_densely packed universe_first rat_win nobel prize_stranger things_have happened.gif
title: Ratbert's Photon Universe Nobel Dream

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So, I'm thinking: What if every photon is just a densely packed universe, and to them, our universe looks like a photon?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: If I'm right, I might be the first rat to win a Nobel Prize.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stranger things have happened.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Name one.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, at his desk
situation: Ratbert stands on Dilbert's desk and presents a speculative physics theory that every photon is a densely packed universe. He then muses that he could be the first rat to win a Nobel Prize. Dilbert offers a mildly encouraging 'stranger things have happened,' which prompts a challenge to name one.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at reassurance backfires, because the challenge to name something stranger than a rat winning a Nobel Prize exposes how absurd the idea really is.
summary: A small yellow rat floats a grand cosmic theory and dreams of scientific glory, only to have a casual platitude turned against the hopeful dreamer.

file: 1997/1997-03-12_telecommute_manage_preventing from working_your point_just beyond grasp.gif
title: Managing Prevents Working, Not Telecommuting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't let you telecommute because then I wouldn't be able to manage you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're managing me right now, and all it's doing is preventing me from working.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And your point would be...?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just beyond your grasp.

situation: Dilbert asks to telecommute, but the Boss refuses because he would no longer be able to manage him. Dilbert points out that the Boss's management is currently just keeping him from getting work done. When the Boss asks what his point is, Dilbert says it is beyond the Boss's understanding.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss by saying the point, that management obstructs work, is too complex for the Boss to comprehend.
