summary: A worker's request to work from home is denied for the sake of supervision, which he says is the very thing hindering his productivity.

file: 1997/1997-09-01_ignorant employees_controls information_board of directors_appointed emperor_escape key.gif
title: Dogbert Seizes Power Through Network Control

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (computer)
transcript.text: This is Dogbert the network systems administrator, to all ignorant employees.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He who controls your information controls you. I control your information.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (computer)
transcript.text: The board of directors has appointed me Emperor for life. Bring the Pointy-Haired Boss to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh! The escape key isn't working!

situation: Dogbert, now the network systems administrator, broadcasts messages to employees through their computer screens. He declares that controlling information means controlling people, then announces he has been made Emperor for life and summons the boss. The boss, reading it at his desk, tries to escape the message and finds the escape key doesn't work.
punchline: Whoever controls the network controls the company, and the boss's futile attempt to dismiss the message shows he is powerless against Dogbert's takeover.
summary: A scheming dog uses his IT admin access to broadcast his own coronation to every computer in the company.

file: 1997/1997-08-06_capital budget_ceo_motivation_open book mangement_read financial statement.gif
title: Open Book Management Is Demotivating

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to try something called "open book management."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll teach you to read the financial statements of this company. It's all very motivating.

transcript.speaker: Finance Employee
transcript.text: ...and our CEO got paid more than the entire capital budget...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is this what motivation feels like?

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces a new 'open book management' program and promises that learning to read the company's financial statements will motivate everyone. A finance employee then reads out that the CEO was paid more than the entire capital budget. Alice, her hair puffed up in anger, asks if this is what motivation feels like.
punchline: Revealing the company's finances shows employees how much the CEO takes home, which fuels anger and resentment rather than the motivation management promised.
summary: A manager's transparency initiative backfires when the staff learns their chief executive out-earned the whole investment budget.

file: 1997/1997-01-19_coaching session_never returned call_obstacle course_unpleasant coworker_blissful_productivity.gif
title: Dilbert's Office Obstacle Course Ends

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Office obstacle course

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh, it's Phil. I never returned his call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Walk faster.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh, it's an unpleasant co-worker who wants to be my friend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The crafty engineer blends with the herd to avoid detection.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh, I owe Alice some information.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's only one more obstacle between me and blissful productivity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aagh!!! My whole day is ruined!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looks like you need a one-on-one coaching session.

situation: Dilbert treats his walk through the office as an obstacle course, ducking Phil, an elevator-chasing coworker, a group of people he hides among, and Alice. Having dodged all of them and nearly reached his cubicle, he finds one last obstacle waiting: his boss.
punchline: Dilbert successfully evades every annoying coworker only to be cornered by the boss, who announces a one-on-one coaching session that ruins his day.
summary: After cleverly dodging every pest in the building, an engineer is undone by his manager's surprise mentoring session.

file: 1997/1997-11-16_urgent_doing work_more urgent.gif
title: Urgent Task Versus Mystery Workload

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is urgent. Stop what you're doing and work on it right now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it more urgent than what I was doing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what you were doing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Exactly. So how could you know if this is more urgent?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could work late and do both.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Work late? Is this more important than my health?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Forget it! I'll have Alice do it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Just out of curiosity, what are you doing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Playing "Quake."

situation: The Boss drops an urgent task on Dilbert and demands he stop his current work. Dilbert uses logic to point out the Boss can't judge urgency without knowing his workload, then refuses to work late, so the Boss gives the task to Alice. In the last panel Alice asks what Dilbert was actually doing, and he admits he was playing the video game Quake.
punchline: Dilbert's principled stand about priorities and his health was just a way to protect his time for playing a video game, so the 'more urgent' work he was defending was not work at all.
summary: A manager's rush job gets rebuffed with airtight reasoning, only for the real reason to emerge: the employee was gaming.

file: 1997/1997-09-08_ballon with sand_breaks_little ballon_requests new keyboard_sand in keyboard_stressful day_reduce stress.gif
title: Stress Balloon Ruins Dilbert's Keyboard

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's been a stressful day. Luckily I have this little balloon full of sand to squeeze to reduce my stress.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Piff

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need a new kybard? What's a kybard?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just sign the stupid thing!!!

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert squeezes a sand-filled stress balloon at his desk, and it bursts, spilling sand over his keyboard. He then goes to the Boss to request a replacement keyboard. The Boss, reading the request form, doesn't know what a 'kybard' is, so Dilbert angrily demands he just sign the form.
punchline: Dilbert's stress-relief toy ends up causing more stress by destroying his keyboard, and then he has to deal with a boss too clueless to approve a simple equipment request.
summary: A stress-relieving sand balloon pops over Dilbert's keyboard, leaving him to fight an uncomprehending boss for a replacement.

file: 1997/1997-01-25_employee survey_tabulated_under paid_management is incompetent_bizarre_unworldly response_travel alarm clock_company logo.gif
title: Survey Results, Logo Alarm Clock Response

transcript.speaker: Pointy-haired manager
transcript.text: The results of the employee survey have been tabulated.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-haired manager
transcript.text: As always, employees say they are underpaid, blah, blah, blah, and management is incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And your bizarre, unworldly response will be?

transcript.speaker: Pointy-haired manager
transcript.text: Everyone gets a travel alarm clock with the company logo!

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: Managers sit around a conference table reviewing the results of an employee survey. The manager reading the results summarizes the usual complaints about low pay and incompetent management. When Alice asks what the company will do about it, he proposes giving everyone a logo-branded travel alarm clock.
punchline: Management answers serious complaints about pay and competence with a cheap, irrelevant corporate trinket, proving the employees' point about incompetence.
summary: After a survey shows staff feel underpaid and badly managed, the managers decide the fix is a branded gadget handed out to everyone.

file: 1997/1997-12-18_military secrets_north elconia_signed agreements.gif
title: North Elbonians Mock Secrecy Agreements

transcript.speaker: North Elbonian
transcript.text: Don't worry that we'll take any military technology secrets back to North Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: North Elbonian
transcript.text: We signed these little agreements that say we won't.

transcript.speaker: North Elbonians
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Moving on ...

situation: Two bearded North Elbonian visitors in tall white hats meet with Dilbert and assure him they won't take military technology secrets home. They explain that they signed agreements promising not to, then burst into laughter and high-five each other. Dilbert, realizing the paperwork is worthless, awkwardly changes the subject.
punchline: The visitors openly treat the non-disclosure agreements as meaningless and laugh at the idea that a signature would stop them, leaving Dilbert to ignore the obvious security hole.
summary: Foreign guests dismiss the paperwork meant to protect sensitive technology as a joke, and their host simply pretends not to notice.

file: 1997/1997-08-13_south dakota_tax reasons_save money on taxes_disrupt lives_kill in sleep_sell organs.gif
title: Company Would Harvest Organs for ROI

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a rumor the company is moving to South Dakota for tax reasons.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you seriously think they would disrupt the lives of thousands of employees just to save money on taxes?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think they'd kill us in our sleep and sell our organs if the return on investment was good.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stop it. I'll be afraid to sleep in my cubicle now.

situation: Dilbert peers over a cubicle wall and tells a bald, bespectacled coworker about a rumor that the company is relocating to South Dakota for tax reasons. The coworker doubts the company would upend thousands of lives merely to save on taxes. Dilbert replies that the company would murder employees for their organs if the profit were good enough.
punchline: Dilbert's dark cynicism reveals that he believes the company values return on investment so much that it would literally kill its employees, and his coworker's response shows he finds the idea alarmingly plausible.
summary: A worker's hopeful faith in his employer is shattered when a colleague describes the grisly lengths the firm would go to for a decent profit.

file: 1997/1997-07-16_babbled_boss_meeting_appointment_office_blah blah_can't shut up_business.gif
title: Telepathic Pleas for Boss's Silence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only have thirty minutes and he's babbled for twenty-eight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Blah blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took three weeks to get on his calendar. My only hope is to send ESP messages for him to shut up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up shut up shut up shut up.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: Nice try, but it's time for his next filibuster.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Blah blah blah.

situation: Dilbert finally gets a thirty-minute appointment with a senior manager, who spends nearly all of it rambling. Dilbert tries to telepathically will him to be quiet, but the manager's assistant arrives to end the meeting and announce his next long-winded session.
punchline: Dilbert's desperate telepathy fails because the time is up, and the assistant knowingly describes the boss's rambling as a scheduled 'filibuster'.
summary: A man waiting weeks for a meeting with an endlessly talkative executive runs out his allotted time without ever getting a word in.

file: 1997/1997-12-02_analogy police_boss compared_mink coat_importance.gif
title: Analogy Police Mink Coat Complaint

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Analogy Police

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss said I was as important as a mink is to a mink coat.

transcript.speaker: Analogy Police Officer
transcript.text: That sounds fine to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But the mink dies.

transcript.speaker: Analogy Police Officer
transcript.text: I guess you won't be leaving a full fifteen percent tip.

situation: Dilbert walks into the Analogy Police station to report a bad analogy his boss used. He explains that his boss compared his importance to that of a mink to a mink coat. The red-costumed officer sees nothing wrong with it until Dilbert points out that the mink dies.
punchline: The boss's analogy unintentionally implies Dilbert is expendable, since a mink is killed to make a coat, and the officer's tip remark mocks the idea that Dilbert would leave a generous tip, as if the officer were a waiter.
summary: A worker files a complaint about a boss's flattering comparison that turns out to say something grim about how expendable he is.

file: 1997/1997-05-26_project_boss_information_being followed_cloud of doom.gif
title: Boss Knows Less Than He Shared

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd feel a lot more comfortable on this project if you'd tell me everything you know about it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've already told you more than I know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel like I'm being followed.

transcript.speaker: Doom
transcript.text: Doom

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to share everything he knows about a new project so he can feel more comfortable. The boss admits he has already told Dilbert more than he actually knows. Dilbert walks away uneasy, a small cloud labeled 'Doom' trailing him.
punchline: The boss has no real knowledge of the project, so Dilbert is being sent into it blind, and doom literally follows him out of the office.
summary: A worker hoping for reassurance learns his manager has nothing left to tell him, and a looming sense of disaster tails him as he leaves.

file: 1997/1997-09-25_pass inspection_pays inspector_dogbert inspector.gif
title: Paid Inspector Fails Everyone Again

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I understand it's your job to make sure your company can pass an ISO 14000 inspection.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I understand that your company pays the inspector for each inspection.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: ISO 14000 Inspector

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You fail again. That's $10,000 please.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Next time, could you actually walk around and look at stuff?

situation: Dogbert, posing as an ISO 14000 inspector, tells Dilbert that it is his job to make the company pass the inspection. He points out that the company pays the inspector for each inspection. Dogbert then fails the company, collects $10,000, and Dilbert asks him to at least walk around and look at things next time.
punchline: The inspector profits from every failed inspection, so he has a financial incentive to fail the company repeatedly without even bothering to inspect anything.
summary: A fee-collecting inspector gets rich by failing a company over and over without doing any actual inspecting.

file: 1997/1997-05-30_cloud of doom_transfer_new host body_starts tim down_dogbert_director special projects_doom.gif
title: Transferring the Cloud of Doom

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The only way to get rid of your cloud of doom is to transfer it to a new host body.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will accomplish this with the help of your pointy-haired boss and a clueless co-worker named Tim.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're secure. Begin transfer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tim, your new job will be director of special projects.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert, who is under a cloud of doom, that the curse can only be removed by moving it to someone else. He recruits the Boss and a clueless co-worker named Tim to help. Tim is strapped to a table and the Boss announces a promotion to director of special projects, at which point the cloud of doom moves over Tim.
punchline: The Boss's cheerful promotion of Tim is the act that transfers the doom, implying that being promoted to a vague management job is a curse in itself.
summary: A cursed man gets rid of his gloom by having a hapless colleague strapped down and handed a grand-sounding promotion that carries the curse over.

file: 1997/1997-09-09_growing beard_hide no chin_loose sweaters_no waist_sherlock holmes outfir_no clue_mannnequins_friends.gif
title: Disguising Your Flaws at Lunch

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm thinking of growing a beard to disguise the fact that I have no chin.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then I'll get some loose sweaters to disguise the fact that I have no waist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should get a Sherlock Holmes outfit to disguise the fact that you have no clue.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe some mannequins as friends...

situation: Dilbert, Wally and Alice sit together at a cafeteria table at lunch. Wally muses about growing a beard to hide his lack of a chin, Alice replies that she'll wear loose sweaters to hide her missing waist, and Dilbert joins in by suggesting a Sherlock Holmes outfit to hide Wally's cluelessness.
punchline: The group trades insults by pairing disguises with flaws, and Dilbert's jab that Wally is clueless prompts the final retort that Dilbert needs mannequins as friends because he has none.
summary: Lunchtime banter turns into a chain of cutting remarks as each coworker proposes a costume to cover another's shortcoming.

file: 1997/1997-07-13_bad advice show_married_divorce_radio show_dogbert_explain_dead woodchuck_household tips_black paint_stain remover_all cheese diet.gif
title: Dogbert's Terrible Radio Advice Show

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're on the radio with Dogbert's "Bad Advice Show." How may I hurt you?

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: My boss asked me for a date. We're both married. What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Divorce your husband. He sounds like a loser to me.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Yes, yes, it all makes sense when you explain it that way.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then mail a dead woodchuck to your boss with a note that says...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Unlike this woodchuck, my love for you will never die."

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Thanks. I love your show.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Moving on to household tips, did you know that black paint is an excellent stain remover?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we talk?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...and those are just some of the benefits of an all-cheese diet.

setting: Dogbert's radio studio, with a caller at her desk on the phone
situation: Dogbert hosts a radio call-in show where he deliberately gives awful advice. A married woman asks how to handle her married boss asking her out, and he tells her to divorce her husband and mail the boss a dead woodchuck with a romantic note. She gratefully accepts. Dogbert then moves on to nonsense household tips while Dilbert, with a black paint stain on his shirt, tries to talk to him.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is absurdly harmful, yet the caller gratefully accepts it, and his household tip about black paint as a stain remover has evidently already ruined Dilbert's shirt.
summary: A radio-host dog dispenses ruinous romantic counsel to a trusting caller, then turns his equally bad wisdom on stain removal and diet.

file: 1997/1997-07-11_petting_break up_roxanne_humans_kind_intelligent creatures_freaks out_until intimate.gif
title: Dogbert Dumps Roxanne After Getting Closer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As much as I like the petting, I still have to break up with you, Roxanne.

transcript.speaker: Roxanne
transcript.text: Why?!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Humans are kind, intelligent, well-adjusted creatures.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Until you get to know them.

transcript.speaker: Roxanne
transcript.text: May the horned demons of Ixpah smite you like the last six!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is what I'm talking about.

situation: Dogbert sits on the couch with Roxanne, who has been petting him, and announces he is breaking up with her. When she asks why, he explains that humans seem kind and well-adjusted until you get to know them. Roxanne then flies into a rage and curses him with horned demons, proving his point.
punchline: Roxanne's furious, bizarre curse immediately demonstrates Dogbert's claim that people seem normal until you know them better.
summary: A dog ends a relationship by explaining that people only seem sane at a distance, and his girlfriend's outburst instantly backs him up.

file: 1997/1997-11-08_cluelessness_indecisiveness_micromange_over analysis_risks_risk analysis.gif
title: Risk Analysis Lists the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll need a risk analysis on this project before I can approve it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Risk 1: Indecisiveness. Risk 2: Overanalysis. Risk 3: Cluelessness. Risk 4: Micromanagement...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click click click

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand these risks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's number thirty-six.

situation: The Boss demands a risk analysis from Dilbert before he will approve a project. Dilbert types up a list of risks that are really the Boss's own management flaws, such as indecisiveness and micromanagement. The Boss reads the list and says he doesn't understand the risks, and Dilbert replies that this is risk number thirty-six.
punchline: The biggest project risks are the Boss's own shortcomings, and his confusion at the list is itself one more of them, which Dilbert points out deadpan.
summary: An engineer answers a manager's request for project risks by listing the manager's own failings, and the manager's bewilderment proves the point.

file: 1997/1997-12-10_grunt grunt_excellent conversationalist_too perfect_you've been coached.gif
title: Too Perfect Date Is Suspicious

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grunt grunt. You're right. Grunt.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: All you do is grunt and agree with me.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I'd be lying if I said I didn't like it. You're an excellent conversationalist...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a trap.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aw, shucks. I'm not excellent at anything.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: You're too perfect. You've been coached!

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date and keeps grunting and agreeing with everything his date says. She admits she likes it and calls him an excellent conversationalist. Dilbert privately suspects a trap, so he feigns modesty, and she accuses him of being too perfect and having been coached.
punchline: Dilbert's strategy of agreeing with everything is so flawless that his date sees through it, and even his attempt at modesty reads as rehearsed.
summary: A man who mindlessly agrees with his dinner companion is praised, then accused of having been coached when his act seems too flawless.

file: 1997/1997-10-16_intelligent investor_lifes saving_name and address_steer clear_track record_dogbert mutaul fund.gif
title: Dogbert's Fund Avoids Intelligent Investors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Mutual Fund

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I don't understand why any intelligent investor would put money in a fund that has no track record.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I try to steer clear of intelligent investors.

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: Here's my life's savings.

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: Do you want my name and address?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, I trust you.

setting: Dogbert's mutual fund office, with Dogbert sitting on a filing cabinet
situation: A purple dinosaur wonders aloud why any intelligent investor would put money in a fund with no track record. Dogbert, who runs the fund, says he deliberately avoids intelligent investors, and a gullible customer immediately hands over his life savings. When the customer offers his name and address, Dogbert declines, saying he trusts him.
punchline: Dogbert's fund survives by attracting only foolish investors, and his refusal to take the man's name and address hints that he has no intention of ever being traceable or accountable.
summary: A con-artist dog running a brand-new fund gleefully collects an unwary customer's entire nest egg without even asking who he is.

file: 1997/1997-06-12_brought dilbert_competitors product_cover cost_cup of coffee_makes product special_visiting the customer_deceptive advertising.gif
title: Dilbert Honestly Explains Product Difference

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Visiting the customer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I brought Dilbert to explain what makes our product special.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's exactly like our competitor's product except we charge more to cover the cost of our deceptive advertising.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: While you're up, could you get me a cup of coffee?

situation: During a sales visit, the Boss introduces Dilbert to explain what makes their product special. Dilbert candidly says it is identical to the competitor's product but costs more to pay for misleading advertising. The angry customer responds by treating Dilbert like a servant and asking him to fetch coffee.
punchline: Dilbert's brutally honest sales pitch gets him demoted in the customer's eyes to a coffee-fetcher, showing that honesty is not rewarded in sales.
summary: A candid engineer sabotages a sales call by admitting the product is just a pricier copy of a rival's, and the irritated client reacts by ordering him around like a gofer.

file: 1997/1997-11-27_installation successful_second digital_access internet_tradition requires_victory dance_engineers_kill him_justified.gif
title: Engineer's Victory Dance Gets Filmed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The installation is successful. I have 128 kilobits per second of digital access to the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As tradition requires, I do the engineer's victory dance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...So if I ever have to kill him, the jury will realize it was justified.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Could you hurry?

setting: Dilbert's home, at his computer desk and living room
situation: Dilbert finishes installing a 128-kilobit digital internet connection at home and celebrates with a goofy engineer's victory dance. Dogbert secretly films the dance with a camcorder while Ratbert waits impatiently on the couch.
punchline: Dogbert is recording Dilbert's embarrassing victory dance as evidence so that a jury would find it justifiable if he ever had to kill him.
summary: A triumphant techie's celebratory jig is secretly videotaped by his dog as courtroom evidence for a future homicide.

file: 1997/1997-04-06_bitter secreatry_brain creates idea._business idea_creates words_delivered_life cycle_proactive synergy_words on paper.gif
title: Life Cycle of a Business Idea

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert presents: The life cycle of a business idea.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The brain creates an idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mmm.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The mouth - operating independently of the brain - creates words.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's form proactive synergy restructuring teams.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The words are written on large paper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Idiot.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The large paper is delivered to a bitter secretary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please?

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Grrrr.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The secretary types it.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: "Let's...form...protein...symphony reactionary...teens."

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Close enough.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The typed notes are delivered to the staff.

transcript.speaker: Staff Member
transcript.text: Drop it in the "To Do basket."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Repeat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mmm.

situation: Dogbert narrates how a business idea travels through a company. The boss's brain forms a vague thought, his mouth blurts out buzzword nonsense, Dilbert writes it on a flip chart, and a bitter secretary garbles it when typing. The notes end up in a staff member's to-do basket, and the boss starts the cycle again.
punchline: Business ideas are meaningless buzzword babble that gets further corrupted at each step and ultimately ignored, yet management keeps generating more of them.
summary: A boss's empty buzzword utterance gets scribbled, mistyped into gibberish, and filed away unread before he cheerfully produces the next one.

file: 1997/1997-11-25_installing line_phone line_connected_network_yank wire_central offcie.gif
title: Yanking Wire at the Central Office

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Installing an ISDN line

transcript.speaker: Telephone Technician
transcript.text: First we need to make sure your phone line is connected to our network.

transcript.speaker: Telephone Technician
transcript.text: I'll yank the wire while you listen for a "whump" sound at the central office.

transcript.speaker: Central Office Worker
transcript.text: I heard something.

setting: Dilbert's home, with a cutaway to a telephone company central office full of giant pipes and cables
situation: A telephone technician visits Dilbert to install an ISDN line and says he must first confirm the phone line connects to the network. He holds a mobile phone and says he will yank the wire while Dilbert listens for a whump at the central office. The final panel shows a worker at the central office, amid huge cables, hearing something as the wire is pulled.
punchline: The technician's connectivity test amounts to physically tearing out a cable and hoping someone at the other end hears it, a crude and absurdly low-tech check for an advanced digital service.
summary: A phone installer tests a new digital line by ripping out a wire and counting on a distant colleague to hear the result.

file: 1997/1997-12-20_military technology_huge laser_create user manual_sing helen reddy song.gif
title: Sabotaging Enemy Laser With Manual

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...The North Elbonians stole our military technology. We think they're building a huge laser to use against us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ask Tina the tech writer to create a user manual for them. Remind Tina how the North Elbonians treat women.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later in North Elbonia

transcript.speaker: North Elbonian
transcript.text: Okay... the timer is set... we're lined up in single file... now we sing a Helen Reddy song.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that the North Elbonians stole military technology and are building a huge laser. Dogbert suggests having Tina the tech writer write the enemy's user manual, reminding her how North Elbonians treat women. In North Elbonia, soldiers follow the manual's absurd instructions, lining up in single file to sing a Helen Reddy song beside the laser's timer.
punchline: Tina's revenge manual contains ridiculous steps, such as singing the feminist anthem 'I Am Woman', which the enemy soldiers obediently follow while operating the weapon.
summary: A spiteful technical writer's deliberately silly instruction manual leads enemy soldiers to perform a feminist anthem as part of operating their stolen superweapon.

file: 1997/1997-05-29_cloud of doom_zaps everyone_once a minute_past behavior_indication of future_won't happen again.gif
title: Dilbert's Cloud of Doom Dating Ad

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a cloud of doom that zaps everyone near me once a minute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm looking for a woman who doesn't think that past behavior is an indication of the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... a woman with absolutely no sense of pattern recognition.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Ouch. I'm glad that won't happen again.

setting: A bench or railing, apparently on a date
situation: Dilbert sits beside a woman and explains that he carries a cloud of doom that zaps everyone near him once a minute. He says he wants a woman who doesn't believe past behavior predicts the future, and she gets zapped repeatedly, ending up singed with frizzy hair. She cheerfully says she's glad it won't happen again, proving she fits his description.
punchline: The woman keeps getting zapped yet optimistically insists it won't happen again, showing she truly has no pattern recognition, which is exactly what Dilbert said he needed.
summary: A man with a zapping storm cloud over his head seeks a partner too oblivious to learn from repeated shocks, and finds one immediately.

file: 1997/1997-07-06_brilliant advice_few points_iq points_not harder_people_pillow gone_smarter_speak latin_wally dream_wanting to_working in dump_work smarter.gif
title: Wally Dreams of Wanting to Be Smarter

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, Pointy-Hair!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thanks for your brilliant advice that I should, "Work smarter not harder."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't realize people could become smarter just by wanting to.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Watch me add a few IQ points right now!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Grrr grrr

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow! Suddenly I can speak Latin!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's crank it up a few more points.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Grrr grrr

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why am I working in this dump? I should be a consultant.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When I woke up, my pillow was gone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, wow. You woke up in the wrong joke.

setting: Wally's dream in bed, then the office cubicle area
situation: Wally dreams that he thanks the Boss for the advice to 'work smarter not harder' and strains to raise his own IQ, suddenly speaking Latin and deciding he should be a consultant. He then wakes up at the office and mentions his pillow is gone, and Dilbert says he woke up in the wrong joke.
punchline: Wally's dream of effortlessly boosting his intelligence is a fantasy, and his waking comment about a missing pillow suggests a different, unrelated joke, which Dilbert points out.
summary: A sleeping Wally imagines he can simply will himself into genius and consultant status before a morning remark reveals the dream's absurdity.

file: 1997/1997-05-28_cloud of doom_dangerous and sexy_lighting strikes_woman_flirting with dilbert.gif
title: Cloud of Doom Zaps Flirting Woman

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's cloud
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I notice you have a cloud of doom. I must admit it makes you seem dangerous and sexy.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's cloud
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry. That happens to everyone who gets near me.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: No problem. I'm one of those women who never learn.

setting: A crowded party or social gathering
situation: At a party, a woman approaches Dilbert and says his personal cloud of doom makes him seem dangerous and sexy. A lightning bolt from the cloud immediately zaps her, leaving her singed and frizzled with her glass flying. Dilbert apologizes, and she cheerfully admits she is the type who never learns.
punchline: The woman's attraction to a man who literally electrocutes anyone near him reveals that she habitually falls for dangerous, bad-for-her men.
summary: A woman finds Dilbert's ominous storm cloud alluring until it blasts her with lightning, yet she shrugs it off as her usual romantic folly.

file: 1997/1997-08-01_more office space_share cubicle_arrange usual accident_got box.gif
title: Cubicle Sharing Accident Sabotage

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: I hope we get more office space soon. Otherwise, I'll have to share my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: If they send someone here, I'll arrange the usual "accident."

transcript.speaker: New coworker
transcript.text: Hi!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sproing!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. She got the box too.

situation: A coworker with enormous hair complains over her cubicle wall that she may have to share her space. When a cheerful new employee arrives to share it, her chair is rigged with a spring that launches him and his belongings into the air. Dilbert and Wally watch from the aisle and remark on how thorough the stunt was.
punchline: The woman has a habit of ejecting unwanted cubicle mates with a booby-trapped spring chair, and it works so well that even the new guy's box of belongings goes flying.
summary: A territorial worker keeps her cubicle to herself by catapulting any newly assigned roommate out of it with a spring-loaded trap.

file: 1997/1997-10-29_catbert_evil hr director_java coding_raise salary_spinning head_10 years experience.gif
title: Ten Years of Java Experience

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can't raise your salary level because you don't have ten years experience with "Java" coding.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Nobody has ten years experience with new technology! You're just being evil. Admit it.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And could you please shake your head back and forth instead of spinning it around?

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, refuses an employee a salary increase because he lacks ten years of experience with Java, a brand-new technology. The employee points out the requirement is impossible and accuses Catbert of being evil. Catbert responds by spinning his head around, and the employee asks him to shake it instead.
punchline: Catbert's spinning head is a nod to the possessed-demon trope, so the employee is both accusing him of being evil and asking him to stop acting like a demon, while the impossible experience requirement shows the absurdity of H.R. job criteria.
summary: An H.R. cat denies a raise over an impossible years-of-experience requirement for a brand-new programming language, then reacts to the accusation of evil with a demonic head spin.

file: 1997/1997-04-28_wally report_weekly stats upadte_industry average_income_supply cabinet unlocked.gif
title: The Wally Report Status Update

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time now for the Wally Report, a weekly status update.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My income is 80% of industry average, enthusiasm is at 63% of capacity and my ego shield is holding at 15%.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your enthusiasm is up from last week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Someone left the supply cabinet unlocked!

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by announcing a weekly status report on Wally. Wally recites statistics about his own pay relative to industry average, his enthusiasm and his ego shield. When the Boss notes that his enthusiasm has risen, Wally explains that someone left the supply cabinet unlocked.
punchline: Wally's only source of enthusiasm is the chance to steal free office supplies, which shows how low morale and pay have sunk.
summary: A manager's weekly report on an employee's morale gets a cheerfully pathetic explanation for why his mood has improved.

file: 1997/1997-09-05_box of electronics_breadwinner_jennifer_dogbert manor_major bread winner_shut up.gif
title: Dogbert Names Dilbert's Gadget Jennifer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Since I'm the major breadwinner here, I decided to name the house "Dogbert Manor."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I've decided to name you Jennifer because I like the name.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know why I bought this. It's just a box full of electronics that you can look at.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Shut up, Jennifer.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and holding a gold scepter, declares himself the major breadwinner and renames the house "Dogbert Manor." He then announces he is naming Dilbert "Jennifer," while Dilbert fiddles with a gadget he bought. Dilbert muses that the purchase is pointless, and Dogbert tells him to shut up, calling him Jennifer.
punchline: Dogbert arbitrarily renames Dilbert and then dismisses his complaint by addressing him as "Jennifer," showing his absurd, self-appointed authority.
summary: A crowned Dogbert claims ownership of the household and hands Dilbert a new name, then silences his grumbling about a useless gadget purchase.

file: 1997/1997-04-02_reduce expenses_essentail jobs_business cards_borrow some.gif
title: Business Cards Reveal Who's Essential

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In order to reduce expenses, only the employees in essential jobs may have business cards.

transcript.speaker: Thought bubble (employees at the meeting)
transcript.text: I'd better order some business cards to find out if I'm "essential."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, order some new business cards for me.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ooh. No can do. But you can borrow some of mine.

setting: Conference room and the Boss's office area
situation: At a meeting the Boss announces that only employees in essential jobs may have business cards to cut costs. The employees privately think they should order cards to test whether they count as essential. Later the Boss asks his assistant Carol to order cards for him, and she refuses and offers to lend him hers.
punchline: The Boss is told he isn't essential enough for business cards, and his assistant Carol is, so he has to borrow hers.
summary: A cost-cutting rule about who gets business cards turns into a quiet test of worth, and the manager himself fails it.

file: 1997/1997-11-09_engineering conference_most valuable asset_decline_overtime_assets decline_fine art_every year_louve_certification of depreciation_earned your air.gif
title: Employees Are Depreciating Assets

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: The theme of our engineering conference is...

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: "Employees are our most valuable asset."

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: And like most assets, you decline in value over time.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: I know what you're thinking: not all assets decline in value.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: For example, fine art is worth more every year.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: But I don't think the Louvre will be asking for one of these anytime soon.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: On your way out, Mister Catbert will give each of you a certificate of depreciation.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: It's still better than last year's theme, "Have you earned your air today?"

setting: Auditorium at a company engineering conference
situation: A horned, pointy-haired conference speaker at a podium announces that the theme is "Employees are our most valuable asset," then explains that employees, like most assets, decline in value over time. He shows a slide of Dilbert and has Catbert hand out certificates of depreciation. Afterward, a bald audience member comments that it is still better than last year's theme.
punchline: The speaker twists the cliché that employees are valuable assets into a cynical reminder that assets depreciate, and the audience is relieved only because last year's theme was even more demeaning.
summary: A conference speaker turns a motivational slogan about valued staff into a grim lesson in depreciation, complete with parting certificates handed out by Catbert.
keywords: employees are our most valuable asset

file: 1997/1997-02-17_ask for one_juggle mushrooms_project review meeting_trained bats_five year budget forecast.gif
title: Bats Juggling Mushrooms Instead of Budgets

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't give me your five-year budget forecast.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't ask for one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was discussed at the project review meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't invite me to that meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you accomplish anything this week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I trained the bats who live in my cubicle to juggle mushrooms.

situation: The Boss accuses Dilbert of failing to deliver a five-year budget forecast. Dilbert points out that he was never asked for one and was never invited to the meeting where it was discussed. When the Boss then asks what he accomplished this week, Dilbert answers with an absurd claim about training bats.
punchline: Since the Boss's own communication failures leave Dilbert with nothing real to work on, Dilbert dryly reports an absurd achievement, trusting the Boss won't question it.
summary: A manager blames an employee for a deliverable nobody requested, so the employee offers a ridiculous claim about his week.

file: 1997/1997-05-06_invented first web browser_garbage man_flashback_computer_waiting fro nothing_out of hand_blame on college kid_technology.gif
title: Dogbert and Garbage Man Invented Browser

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you telling me that you invented the first web browser?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not alone. I worked with our garbage man.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flashback

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wonder how long people would sit in front of a computer waiting for nothing.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Let's find out!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: What if this thing gets out of hand?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll blame it on some drunken college kid.

setting: Outdoor path, then a flashback to a trash can area and a desk with a computer
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert whether he really invented the first web browser, and Dogbert says he did it with the garbage man. In a flashback, the two wonder how long people will sit at a computer waiting for nothing, then set up the browser and plan to blame any fallout on a drunken college kid.
punchline: The web browser is portrayed as a cynical experiment in wasting people's time, built by a dog and a garbage man who plan to pin any trouble on a random college student.
summary: A flashback reveals the web browser began as a prank by Dogbert and a garbage man to see how long people would stare at a screen doing nothing.

file: 1997/1997-04-24_catbert_evil hr director_discriminated against_family emergencies_ratted out boss_family friendly policy_love family.gif
title: Family Friendly Means Not Loving Family

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm being discriminated against because I take time off for family emergencies.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll handle this by telling your boss that you ratted him out to the Director of Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I thought we had a "family friendly" policy.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The key word is friendly. You've been acting as if you love your family.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, with Carol seated across from him as he lounges on a green couch
situation: Carol complains to Catbert, the evil H.R. director, that she is being discriminated against for taking time off for family emergencies. Catbert responds by threatening to tell her boss that she ratted him out to H.R. When Carol points to the company's family friendly policy, Catbert twists its wording to blame her.
punchline: Catbert reinterprets "family friendly" to mean being merely friendly toward family, so that actually loving your family and needing time off for them counts as a violation.
summary: An H.R. cat answers a worker's complaint about family leave with a threat and a twisted reading of the company's own policy wording.

file: 1997/1997-09-16_information technology dept_jordan the preventer_request for service_resource shortages_reverse psychology.gif
title: Denying Services Nobody Requested

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac the Preventer, your liason from the Information Technology Department.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I come with tales of resource shortages. Your request for our services is denied.

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: I didn't request any of your services.

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: Don't try your reverse psychology on me.

situation: Mordac, the IT department's Preventer, visits an employee at her desk and announces that her request for IT services is denied because of resource shortages. The employee, a woman with large hair, replies that she never requested any services. She accuses him of trying reverse psychology on her.
punchline: Mordac denies a request that was never made, showing that IT's reflex to refuse is so automatic it does not even need a request, and the employee suspects a manipulation tactic instead.
summary: An IT gatekeeper rejects a service request that a puzzled employee insists she never made, and she suspects a trick.

file: 1997/1997-01-04_policies_use prodcuts_will to live_new corporate policy_not intended to punish.gif
title: Mandatory Use of Company Products

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new corporate policy is that all employees must use the products we sell.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Aaargh!!!! What have we done to deserve this??!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So you're saying that many of these policies are NOT intended to be punishments?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You get used to it after you lose your will to live.

setting: A conference room, then a hallway or office
situation: At a meeting, the boss announces that all employees must use the products the company sells. One employee screams in horror, asking what they did to deserve this. Afterward Dilbert asks whether such policies aren't meant as punishment, and Wally says you get used to the products once you lose your will to live.
punchline: The company's products are so bad that being forced to use them feels like punishment, and the only way to cope is to give up all hope.
summary: Staff are horrified to learn they must use their own employer's terrible products, and a jaded coworker explains that resignation is the only cure.

file: 1997/1997-07-22_perfromance review_meeting over_stood up_boss_talked about himself_self centered_egotistical_unprofessional.gif
title: Employee Hijacks His Own Performance Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...And that's your performance review. Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: One.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You talked about yourself for the full hour. Can we talk about me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. You don't seem to know that your meeting is over when you see me stand up.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ooh.

situation: The Boss finishes delivering a performance review and asks if there are any questions. The employee points out that the boss spent the entire hour talking about himself and asks to discuss his own performance instead. The boss gets up from his desk and tells the employee that standing up signals the meeting is over, leaving the employee to realize he has been dismissed.
punchline: The boss responds to a fair complaint about his self-absorbed review by abusing his authority and ending the meeting, so the employee never gets his turn.
summary: A worker calls out his boss for monopolizing his own evaluation, and the boss shuts the conversation down by simply standing up.

file: 1997/1997-05-31_conversation_boss approval_mixed messages_staus report.gif
title: Honest Status Report Causes Mixed Messages

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I understand you had a conversation with my boss without my approval.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't want to give mixed messages. It would be very bad if she got any mixed messages.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I just gave her an honest status report.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aaargh!!! Mixed messages!

situation: The Boss scolds Alice for talking to his own boss without his approval, insisting that upper management must never receive mixed messages. Alice calmly replies that she simply gave the boss's boss an honest status report, which sends him into a panic.
punchline: The Boss considers an honest status report to be the 'mixed message' because it contradicts the rosy picture he has been feeding upper management.
summary: A manager frets about conflicting information reaching his superior, only to realize his employee's candor has exposed the gap between truth and his spin.

file: 1997/1997-10-24_accident_ask questions_bury survivors_dont embarrass boss_highly visible_meetings_put them in trunk_promoted.gif
title: Easy Questions Get You Promoted

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you want to be promoted, you have to be highly visible.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ask questions at meetings. But make them easy so you don't embarrass your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So if there's an accident in a company car, where should we bury the survivors?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I usually put them in the trunk.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then a conference room during a meeting
situation: Dogbert coaches Dilbert on getting promoted by being visible and asking questions at meetings, but only easy ones that won't embarrass the boss. Dilbert then attends a meeting and asks a ridiculously phrased question about burying accident survivors, and a coworker answers it in a deadpan, gruesome way.
punchline: Dilbert's 'easy' question is absurdly morbid, and a colleague's calm reply that he puts survivors in the trunk shows how little anyone in the meeting is actually listening or thinking.
summary: After getting advice to ask softball questions in meetings for visibility, Dilbert poses a grotesque query about burying crash survivors and gets an equally grim answer.

file: 1997/1997-09-27_internet community_sarcastic suggestion_email campaign_improve image_mass unsolicited_tell people_how nice we are.gif
title: Sarcastic Spam Campaign Backfires on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have to improve our image in the Internet community.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's do a mass unsolicited e-mail campaign to tell people how nice we are.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have the look of a man who was just put in charge of implementing his own sarcastic suggestion.

situation: The Boss says the company needs to improve its image in the Internet community. Dilbert sarcastically suggests a mass unsolicited e-mail campaign telling people how nice the company is. The Boss takes the idea seriously, and Dogbert observes that Dilbert now looks like he has been put in charge of carrying it out.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic suggestion, spamming people to prove how nice the company is, is accepted as a real plan and he is assigned to implement it.
summary: A manager wants a better online reputation, and an offhand joke about spamming everyone gets taken literally, landing the joker with the job.

file: 1997/1997-09-14_address envelope_death penalty_helpless_master plan_one way trip_solve small problems_speaking engilsh_training_south korea.gif
title: Carol's Plan to Make Boss Helpless

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I forget... how do I address an envelope?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm training him to be helpless.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's part of my master plan to eliminate him.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I do everything for him. Soon he'll lose his ability to solve small problems alone.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Then I'll "accidentally" book him on a one-way trip to South Korea.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Before he goes, I'll tell him they have a death penalty for speaking English.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We'll never see him again. Buwahaha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's worth a shot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, what do I dial for an outside line?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll do it.

situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol how to address an envelope, and she eagerly does it for him. She explains to Dilbert that she is deliberately making the Boss helpless so she can trick him into a one-way trip to South Korea, where she'll tell him English is punishable by death. Dilbert muses that it's worth a shot, and the Boss then asks how to dial an outside line, proving her plan is working.
punchline: Carol's sinister plan to eliminate the Boss by making him dependent on her is already succeeding, since he can't even figure out how to dial a phone.
summary: A scheming assistant reveals she is deliberately turning her clueless manager into a helpless dependent so she can ship him off for good.

file: 1997/1997-01-20_bad news_perfromance review_bell curve_make up flaws_does not wash hands_after restroom.gif
title: Invented Flaws for Bell Curve

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bad news on your performance review, Wally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone performed the same. But I'm required to rank the group on a bell curve.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had to make up some flaws to move you down the curve. Here's a pen. Sign it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Employee does not wash hands after using the restroom".

situation: The Boss tells Wally he has bad news about his performance review. Although everyone performed equally, the Boss must rank his staff on a bell curve, so he has invented flaws to justify marking Wally down. Wally is handed a pen and told to sign a review accusing him of not washing his hands after using the restroom.
punchline: Forced ranking policies make managers fabricate fake faults for employees who did nothing wrong, and then require the employee to sign off on the lie.
summary: A manager admits he has invented a embarrassing defect for an employee so that a mandatory ranking system produces the required spread of scores.

file: 1997/1997-04-23_home early_sick kid_family freindly_test for drugs.gif
title: Family Friendly Policy Drug Test

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm going home early because my kid is sick.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, we have a new "family friendly" policy.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that why my family seems so friendly?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'd test 'em for drugs.

situation: Carol tells the Boss she is leaving early because her child is sick. The Boss reminds her of the company's new "family friendly" policy, and Carol is surprised it exists. When the Boss wonders if the policy explains why his own family seems so friendly, Carol suggests they should be tested for drugs.
punchline: Carol sarcastically implies that the Boss's family is only 'friendly' because they are on drugs, since a genuinely family-friendly workplace would not have made her feel she had to ask to care for a sick child.
summary: A mother leaving work for her ill child gets a lecture about company policy and then a sarcastic jab about the boss's suspiciously friendly family.

file: 1997/1997-12-03_misuse of analogies_dressed odd_casual day_frightening outifit_bicycle pants.gif
title: Devil's Casual Day Outfit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure this is where I report the misuse of analogies? You're dressed very odd.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: It's casual day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the most frightening outfit I've ever seen.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: You haven't seen me in bicycle pants.

setting: The devil's office, a desk and chair in a plain room
situation: Dilbert goes to an office to report the misuse of analogies and finds a man in a red devil costume with horns and a tail behind the desk. The devil explains that it is casual day. Dilbert calls the outfit the most frightening he has ever seen, and the devil replies that he has not seen him in bicycle pants.
punchline: Even the devil's red horned costume is merely his casual-day wear, and his formal look is apparently less scary than his bicycle pants, a jab at both casual day and bad analogies.
summary: Dilbert seeks out the right office to complain about sloppy analogies and meets a devil whose casual-day attire is surprisingly mild compared to what he could wear.

file: 1997/1997-04-19_success at work_coffee cup_document_whats in hands_binder_cigarette_good or bad.gif
title: Wally's Fast Track to the Restroom

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your success at work depends on what you have in your hands when you walk around.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A coffee cup is bad. A document is good. A cigarette is bad. A binder is good. But the very worst thing...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It doesn't look like you're heading for the fast track, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Actually, I am, unless it's occupied.

setting: Office, Dilbert's cubicle or office area
situation: Dogbert lectures Dilbert on how career success depends on what you carry while walking around the office, ranking coffee cups and cigarettes as bad and documents and binders as good. Wally then appears holding a coffee cup and a newspaper, and Dilbert remarks that he isn't on the fast track.
punchline: Wally twists 'fast track' into a literal reference to the express route to the restroom, where he's headed with his newspaper and coffee, rather than a career advancement path.
summary: After a lecture on how carrying the right props signals ambition, the newspaper-toting office slacker claims he's on the fast track to the bathroom.

file: 1997/1997-12-13_presentation_brilliant_ineffciency_procrastination.gif
title: Procrastination Disguised as Martyrdom

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We'll probably have to work all night on this presentation, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's brilliant! You plan to use your inefficiency to make your procrastination look like martyrdom!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now I have to kill you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please do. Reincarnation is my only hope.

situation: Alice tells Asok they will probably have to work all night on a presentation. Asok cheerfully points out that she is deliberately being inefficient and putting off the work so that her procrastination looks like heroic self-sacrifice. Alice threatens to kill him, and Asok welcomes it as his only chance of escaping his life.
punchline: Asok exposes Alice's all-nighter as staged martyrdom, and when she threatens him, he happily accepts death because his workplace existence is so miserable that reincarnation is his only hope.
summary: A junior employee sees through a colleague's late-night work excuse and gets a death threat that he gladly welcomes.

file: 1997/1997-04-29_compensation lan_good news_stock options_updated agreement_mugging.gif
title: Good News Feels Like Mugging

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news about your compensation plan...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate good news about my compensation plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Twenty percent of your pay will now be in the form of stock options instead of cash!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To get your stock options, simply sign this updated employment agreement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does good news feel like a mugging?

situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert with what he calls good news about his compensation plan. He explains that 20 percent of Dilbert's pay will be replaced by stock options instead of cash, and asks him to sign an updated employment agreement to receive them. Dilbert is wary from the start and ends up comparing the whole exchange to being mugged.
punchline: Replacing part of an employee's cash salary with speculative stock options is a pay cut dressed up as a benefit, so the supposed good news feels like being robbed.
summary: A manager cheerfully announces a pay restructuring that swaps some of an employee's cash for stock options, and the employee sees it as theft.

file: 1997/1997-04-17_boredom_conference room_dead emplyee_employee of the week_headcount down.gif
title: Dead Employee Boosts Headcount Savings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found another dead employee in the conference room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what got him - the boredom or the hard work. But headcount is down one and the company has life insurance on him!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looks like I found my "Employee of the Week."

setting: Office hallway near the conference room
situation: The Boss carries a dead employee's body and tells Dilbert he found another one in the conference room. He speculates the cause was boredom or hard work, but is mainly pleased that headcount is down and the company holds life insurance on the man. In the last panel, still hauling the body, he muses that he has found his "Employee of the Week."
punchline: The Boss values a dead employee more than a living one because he cuts headcount and triggers a life insurance payout, making him the perfect "Employee of the Week."
summary: A callous manager hauls away a worker who died in a meeting room and cheerfully counts the cost savings instead of mourning him.

file: 1997/1997-02-11_how big bonus_work on project_digits.gif
title: Bonus Digits: One Per Hand

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Today I'll find out how big my bonus will be.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: After all the work I did on that project, I'm thinking four digits, maybe five.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many digits?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I used one on each hand.

situation: Alice excitedly anticipates a large year-end bonus, predicting it will be four or even five digits because of her hard work on a project. Later, Dilbert asks how many digits her bonus had. Alice, clearly angry, answers that she used one digit on each hand, meaning she raised two middle fingers.
punchline: Alice's bonus turned out to be so insulting that she answers Dilbert's question about 'digits' by saying she used one finger on each hand, i.e., she gave the company a rude gesture with both hands.
summary: After boasting about her expected bonus, an employee reveals her disappointment with a double-fingered rude gesture instead of a dollar figure.

file: 1997/1997-09-06_earnings_handle investments_maxed out_money_relax_retire_risk_strangers.gif
title: Risk Tolerance Maxed Out

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: We can handle your investments so you can retire and live off the earnings.

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: Just sign this incomprehensible contract, hand all your money to total strangers and relax!

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: We'll need to know what your tolerance to risk is.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I just maxed out.

situation: A financial advisor pitches Dogbert on letting his firm manage his investments so he can retire on the earnings. The advisor cheerfully asks him to sign a huge, incomprehensible contract and hand his money to total strangers. When the advisor asks about his risk tolerance, Dogbert says he has already reached his limit.
punchline: Handing all your money to strangers under a contract you can't understand is already the maximum amount of risk, so the advisor's question comes too late.
summary: A sales-minded money manager asks a prospective client how much risk he can stomach after already requesting blind trust and a signature on an unreadable document.

file: 1997/1997-08-23_digital pager_phone has pager_built in_dinosaur.gif
title: Pager Envy and Vibrating Ear Cleaning

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Envy me, Bob. I have a digital pager and you don't.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I don't need one. My digital PCS phone has a built-in pager function.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Oh, wow.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But the worst part is that he only uses it to clean his ears.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I taught him that. The vibrating action is excellent.

setting: Office (a desk and a computer workstation)
situation: Ratbert brags to Bob the dinosaur that he owns a digital pager, but Bob replies that his digital PCS phone already has a pager built in, deflating Ratbert. Ratbert then complains about Bob, saying he only uses the gadget to clean his ears, and Dilbert at his computer proudly admits he taught Bob that trick.
punchline: A modern communication gadget gets put to a ridiculous, unintended use, with the vibration feature repurposed as an ear cleaner.
summary: A boastful tech purchase is outdone by a rival's phone, then the gadget's vibrating motor ends up being used for personal grooming.

file: 1997/1997-06-13_no on fired_occasional beating_statistical clustering_suicides_voting the customer_buying product.gif
title: Product Safety Includes Occasional Suicides

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Visiting the customer

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: No one has ever been fired for buying our product!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is the occasional savage beating... and more than our share of suicides...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that has "statistical clustering" written all over it.

setting: Customer's office during a sales visit
situation: Dilbert accompanies a salesman to meet a customer. After the salesman boasts that no one has been fired for buying their product, Dilbert agrees, then cheerfully admits that buyers sometimes suffer savage beatings and an above-average number of suicides. He dismisses it as mere statistical clustering while the customer looks increasingly alarmed.
punchline: Dilbert's honest 'technically true' defense of the product reveals that its customers meet far worse fates than being fired, and he waves it away with statistics jargon.
summary: A sales pitch collapses when a candid engineer concedes that buyers of the product face violence and suicide, which he dismisses as a statistical quirk.

file: 1997/1997-07-24_demeaning insulting_director_human resources_learned helplessness_managerial influence_new job title_new card_business.gif
title: Director of Learned Helplessness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new job titles from Human Resources are demeaning and insulting!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've got to use your managerial influence to do something!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new card...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How'd it go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't expect much help from the "Director of Learned Helplessness."

setting: Office, Boss's desk and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Dilbert angrily complains that the new job titles issued by Human Resources are demeaning, and begs the Boss to use his managerial influence to fix it. The Boss simply holds up his new business card in response. Dilbert then tells Wally he can expect no help, because the Boss's new title is "Director of Learned Helplessness."
punchline: The Boss's new title literally labels him as an expert in helplessness, so it's obvious he won't do anything about the problem.
summary: A manager whose assigned title announces his own passivity is the last person who could rescue employees from humiliating HR job titles.

file: 1997/1997-06-03_bearer_bead news_tragic_find humor_husband_village people_coming back_relationships.gif
title: Dogbert Delivers Bad News With Jokes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going into business as a professional bearer of bad news.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll try to find the humor that is inherent in every tragic situation.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I give up. What is the difference between my husband and the seventies pop group "Village People"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're coming back.

situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he is starting a business as a professional bearer of bad news, promising to find humor in tragedy. A woman then appears at the doorway and asks a riddle about her husband and the Village People. Dogbert delivers the bad news as the punchline: the Village People are coming back.
punchline: The riddle's answer reveals that the woman's husband is not coming back, either because he has left her or died, while the Village People are, which is both a dark joke and a delivery of bad news.
summary: A dog starts a service that breaks terrible tidings with a gag, and his first customer gets a darkly funny answer about her missing spouse.

file: 1997/1997-04-18_catbert_evil hr dierctor_life insurance policy_raise blood pressure_dangerous levels_fifty time salary_ceo.gif
title: Catbert Plots Wally's Blood Pressure

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, the company bought a life insurance policy on you.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our plan is to raise your blood pressure to dangerous levels.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did you know that our CEO makes fifty times your salary even though our stock is down?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, peers over Wally's cubicle wall and tells him the company has taken out a life insurance policy on him. He explains the plan is to drive up Wally's blood pressure to dangerous levels. He does it by pointing out the CEO earns fifty times Wally's salary despite falling stock, and Wally clutches his head in pain.
punchline: The company stands to profit if Wally dies, so Catbert tries to kill him by stressing him with the truth about executive pay inequity.
summary: An evil personnel cat tries to cash in on an employee's life policy by enraging him with facts about his boss's lavish pay.

file: 1997/1997-02-02_cake_engineers_patent celebration_patents_schedule celebration.gif
title: Patent Party Without the Engineers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, could you check our Pointy-Haired Boss's calendar?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Grumble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'd like to schedule a celebration for the engineers who got patents.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Grumble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're all available on the sixth, ninth, twentieth and the twenty-first.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll schedule it for the tenth. That's the only day he can do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... none of the engineers can make it on the tenth.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's not a perfect world.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When's the patent celebration?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: On the tenth

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We should do this more often.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Yeah, I like cake.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the Boss's assistant, to schedule a celebration for engineers who earned patents. Despite the engineers being free on four dates, Carol books the one day only the Boss is available, when no engineers can attend. On the day, only the Boss and Carol are there eating the cake.
punchline: The celebration honoring the engineers is scheduled around the Boss's convenience, so the engineers are absent and the management and assistant simply enjoy the cake themselves.
summary: A party meant to honor patent-winning engineers gets booked for the one day none of them can come, leaving the boss and his assistant to eat the cake.

file: 1997/1997-08-10_project sparkle_desk policy_company wide effoert_tiny question_curious_top executives_competitive threat_panic_lone voice of reason_paper towles_laminated card_mission statement.gif
title: Clean Desk Policy Mocks Executives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Announcing Project "Sparkle," the clean desk policy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is a company-wide effort to keep our work spaces clean.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Tiny question. I'm curious about one thing.
