transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm picturing our top executives in the "war room."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They talk about the competitive threat and our lack of resources. Suddenly, panic sets in!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A lone voice of reason penetrates the confusion. Two words: "Paper towels."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is that pretty much how it went?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Moving along, you each get a laminated card with our mission statement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me do this one.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces a company-wide clean desk policy called Project Sparkle. Alice asks a pointed question, imagining the top executives panicking in their war room over competition and scarce resources until someone offers the brilliant idea of paper towels. The Boss ignores her and moves on to handing out laminated mission statement cards.
punchline: Alice sarcastically suggests the executives responded to a serious competitive crisis by coming up with a trivial cleanliness initiative, and the Boss's dodge confirms she's right.
summary: A sarcastic employee deduces that panicked executives faced with real business threats settled on a tidy-desk campaign, and her boss refuses to deny it.

file: 1997/1997-08-29_dogbert_network systems_software manual_manuals_mean spirirted_meet half way_door_window.gif
title: Dogbert Locks Away Software Manuals

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the network systems administrator

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The software manuals are locked in this room.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't let users have manuals, for reasons that could only be described as mean-spirited.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is there any way we can meet half-way on this?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, that door didn't always have a window.

situation: Dogbert, working as the network systems administrator, tells an employee that the software manuals are locked in a room and that users are not allowed to have them. When the frustrated employee tries to negotiate a compromise, he smashes through the door, leaving a window-shaped hole, and Dogbert comments on the damage.
punchline: Dogbert openly admits his manual hoarding is just meanness, and the employee's attempt to compromise ends with him breaking through the door, which Dogbert dryly notes.
summary: A gleefully spiteful IT administrator keeps the documentation under lock and key, and a desperate user literally breaks in to bargain with him.

file: 1997/1997-03-16_assignment_electrical engineer_redesign brochures_highly skilled engineer_not graphic designer_ugly brochure.gif
title: Engineer Assigned Brochure Design Duty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll love your new assignment, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're going to redesign all of our brochures!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm an electrical engineer, not a graphic artist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can discuss your huge inadequacies during your annual review.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not inadequate. I'm a highly skilled engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And yet you can't make brochures.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay, let me try to explain this in the simplest possible way...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You... are... an... idiot.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The simplest possible explanation isn't always the best.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, it looks like a brochure, only uglier!

setting: Office, in a hallway and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Alice she is being reassigned to redesign all the company brochures. Alice protests that she is an electrical engineer, and the Boss retorts that her refusal proves her inadequacy. Alice tries to insult him in the simplest terms, then realizes the blunt approach was a mistake as a coworker mocks her work.
punchline: Alice's blunt 'simplest possible' insult backfires, leaving her to concede that simple isn't always best, while a coworker gets in a dig at her ugly brochure.
summary: A specialist engineer is dumped with an unrelated design task and pays for pushing back against a boss who twists her objection into a performance problem.

file: 1997/1997-07-20_cancelled meeting_dilmom_effort_glass half full_made extra money_no over time pay_not funded_not important work_optimitic_power point slides worse_wast of time_waste of enery_worked till midnight_dilberts mother.gif
title: Dilbert's Mom Seeks Silver Linings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As usual, I worked until midnight last night, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Well, at least you made some extra money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't get paid for overtime.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Well, at least it was important work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not really.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss made me change my "PowerPoint" slides, but the changes make them worse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Well, at least you're prepared for your meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was canceled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that's okay, because the project isn't funded anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: So... you worked for free to worsen a presentation for a meeting that won't happen for a project that doesn't exist?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Well... at least you could travel back in time without having any impact on history.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, my glass is half full.

setting: Dilbert's mother's home, then a walk outdoors on a grassy hillside
situation: Dilbert tells his mother about working until midnight, and she keeps offering optimistic 'at least' comments. Each one is undercut: no overtime pay, unimportant work, worsened slides, a canceled meeting, and an unfunded project. She finally sums up the pointlessness and offers a last bright side.
punchline: Even when the mother summarizes that he did unpaid work on a worse presentation for a canceled meeting on a nonexistent project, Dilbert cheerfully concludes his glass is half full, because the futility at least changes nothing.
summary: A son's string of wasted late-night effort gets met with one cheery consolation after another until nothing positive is left to say.

file: 1997/1997-01-16_answer this quiz_bill gates_towel boy_humans are primates_three monkeys_stupid trick question.gif
title: Bill Gates Towel Boy Quiz

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: You have been chosen as Bill Gates' towel boy. But first you must answer this quiz.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: You're in a room with three monkeys. One has a banana, one has a stick, one has nothing. Which primate is the smartest?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: I guess the successful towel boys know that humans are primates too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stupid trick question.

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of a talking computer screen, then on the living room couch
situation: A talking computer announces that Dilbert has been chosen as Bill Gates' towel boy, but he must first pass a quiz. It asks which of three monkeys is the smartest. Dilbert hesitates, and the computer reveals that the answer is the human, since humans are primates too.
punchline: The towel boy quiz hinges on a trick question whose answer is the person answering, so Dilbert fails by overlooking himself, and he resents the question's unfairness.
summary: A computer gives Dilbert an absurd job-screening riddle about monkeys and the answer turns out to be himself.

file: 1997/1997-03-05_rather the consultant_strategy optuons_matrix_four boxes_something_phase two_concentric circles_labels and arrows.gif
title: Ratbert's Meaningless Strategy Matrix

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Your strategy options can be shown in this matrix.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The four boxes are "something... something... some other thing and whatever."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: In phase two I hope to turn this matrix into concentric circles with labels and arrows.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm under the consultant's spell.

situation: Ratbert, posing as a consultant, presents a four-box strategy matrix on a chalkboard to the Boss and Dilbert. He labels the boxes with meaningless filler words, then promises to turn it into circles with labels and arrows in phase two. The Boss is completely captivated by the nonsense.
punchline: The Boss is so impressed by a consultant's empty diagrams and vague jargon that he admits he is under a spell, mocking how easily management is dazzled by consulting buzzwords.
summary: A small rodent consultant wins over a gullible manager with a chalkboard grid whose boxes contain nothing but filler words.

file: 1997/1997-07-02_everyone talks funny_not morons_incapable_clear communication_think outside box_watch ego_before ego dies_rebel_do it.gif
title: Rebels Who Talk in Jargon

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finally figured out why everyone talks so funny in this company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're not morons who are incapable of clear communication. We're rebels who like to "think outside the box."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's always fascinating to watch an ego just before it dies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a rebel! Task me with a "do it."

situation: Dilbert stands before the Boss's desk and announces a theory about why employees speak in strange corporate jargon: they see themselves as rebels thinking outside the box rather than people who can't communicate clearly. The Boss coolly remarks on watching an ego about to die, and Dilbert, still playing the rebel, asks to be given a task using buzzword-style phrasing.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to prove he is a nonconformist rebel ends with him requesting a "do it" task in the same empty corporate-speak he claimed to be rising above, so his ego collapses and he conforms.
summary: An employee insists that office buzzword-speak is an act of rebellion, then immediately undermines himself by begging for work in the same jargon.

file: 1997/1997-10-03_mob_stupid people_attack dogbert_drink hose water_isn't working_grass_attack_ruin our lawn_spraying water_hose fight.gif
title: Mob Attacks Dogbert With Hose Water

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A mob of stupid people attack Dogbert's house

transcript.speaker: Protester
transcript.text: Our plan to drink all of his hose water isn't working.

transcript.speaker: Protester
transcript.text: Hey, careful! You're getting water all over the grass...

transcript.speaker: Man in cap
transcript.text: Wait, that gives me an idea!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's the attack going?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They tried to ruin our lawn by spraying water on it. But now it's turned into a hose fight.

setting: Outside Dogbert's house, then inside the living room
situation: A mob of protesters with 'Down with Dogbert' signs tries to attack Dogbert's house by drinking all of his hose water. When the plan fails, one protester starts spraying water instead, and the attack degenerates into a hose fight. Dilbert, reading the newspaper, asks Dogbert how the attack is going.
punchline: The mob's absurdly feeble 'attack' on Dogbert, first trying to drink his water and then spraying his lawn, ends up as a harmless playful hose fight.
summary: Dim-witted protesters besieging Dogbert's home fumble their water-based assault until it turns into a silly game of squirting each other.

file: 1997/1997-01-14_shrink wrap license_new software_bill gates_new mansion_towel boy.gif
title: Shrink-Wrap License Makes Dilbert Bill's Towel Boy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't read all of the shrink-wrap license agreement on my new software until after I opened it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently I agreed to spend the rest of my life as a towel boy in Bill Gates' new mansion.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Call your lawyer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too late. He opened software yesterday. Now he's Bill's laundry boy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It must be dangerous for lawyers to iron pants. They'd always have one hand in a pocket.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert lounging nearby
situation: Dilbert explains that he opened new software before reading its shrink-wrap license and has apparently signed himself into servitude as a towel boy in Bill Gates' mansion. Dogbert suggests calling a lawyer, but Dilbert says his lawyer also opened software yesterday and is now Bill's laundry boy. Dogbert wraps up with a joke about lawyers ironing pants.
punchline: Even the lawyer who would defend you has fallen victim to the same absurd software license, and Dogbert caps it off with a pun about lawyers always keeping a hand in their pockets.
summary: Opening a software package accidentally commits Dilbert to servitude for Bill Gates, and his lawyer has suffered the same fate.

file: 1997/1997-02-28_speak about project_plan_created input_arrogant baboon_slap you_flashbacks_honeymoon.gif
title: Dogbert Insults Boss, Slap Offered

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dilbert asked me to speak to you about the project plan you created without his input.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's impossible, you arrogant baboon!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lean over here so I can slap you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm having flashbacks to my honeymoon.

situation: Dogbert, standing on the Boss's desk, says he has been asked by Dilbert to confront him about a project plan the Boss created without engineering input. He angrily calls the plan impossible and the Boss an arrogant baboon, then tells the Boss to lean over so he can slap him. The Boss responds that this reminds him of his honeymoon.
punchline: The Boss's weirdly wistful remark implies his marriage involved abuse or hostility, turning Dogbert's threat into an unintentionally sad joke.
summary: A dog scolds a manager for planning a project without consulting the engineer, threatens to slap him, and the manager wistfully compares it to his marital past.

file: 1997/1997-02-27_primitive cultures_no concept of zero_zero time left_additional work_conversation_downhill_zorro.gif
title: Boss Has Zero Concept of Zero

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've heard that some primitive cultures had no mathematical concept of "zero."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I think you're like that when I tell you I have zero time left for additional work.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The conversation went downhill from there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, that's "Zorro." You're NOT like Zorro!!

situation: Dilbert tries to make small talk by mentioning that some primitive cultures had no concept of zero. The Boss takes it as a dig and says Dilbert is like that whenever the Boss says there is zero time left for more work. Dilbert, now flustered, mistakenly says the Boss is not like "Zorro" and the conversation falls apart.
punchline: The Boss misreads Dilbert's remark as an insult about workload and blunders it further, so Dilbert garbles the word and ends up shouting "You're NOT like Zorro!!" in a failed attempt to correct him.
summary: A casual remark about ancient number systems is twisted into a workload complaint, and the argument degenerates into a confused mix-up over a masked swordsman.

file: 1997/1997-05-17_agenda_project meeting_two hours_temporaily sane_repeat mission statement.gif
title: Two-Hour Meeting, Ten Minutes of Work

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Alice, here's the agenda for the next project meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Two hours?!! Aaagh!!! There's only ten minutes' worth of tasks!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I think I'm temporarily sane.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Try breathing into a paper bag and repeating our mission statement.

situation: Carol hands Alice the agenda for the next project meeting. Alice sees that the meeting is scheduled for two hours when there are only ten minutes of actual tasks, and she screams in frustration. She then realizes her reaction means she is thinking rationally, and Carol advises her to calm down with a paper bag and the company mission statement.
punchline: Being upset about an absurdly padded meeting is treated as a lapse into sanity, and the cure is to recite corporate jargon until the rational reaction goes away.
summary: An engineer who is outraged at a bloated meeting agenda is told that her sensible reaction is a problem to be treated with breathing exercises and corporate slogans.

file: 1997/1997-02-06_catbert_evil hr dircetor_boss didn't see struggle_low performance_alice_human resources binder_downsize.gif
title: Catbert's Downsize Binders

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was so good at my job that I never needed to bother my boss. But he gave me a low rating because he didn't see me struggling.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I must refer to my human resources binders to see how to deal with this.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Catbert faces a bookshelf of binders labeled "Downsize" and "Hire Losers" - no dialogue)

situation: Alice complains to Catbert, the evil H.R. director, that her boss gave her a low rating because she was too competent to ever need help. Catbert says he must consult his human resources binders for guidance. The shelves turn out to be filled almost entirely with binders labeled 'Downsize', plus a couple labeled 'Hire Losers'.
punchline: Catbert's H.R. manuals offer only one answer to every problem, downsizing, so Alice's legitimate complaint is headed for a layoff rather than a fair review.
summary: A complaining employee learns that the only guidance in the H.R. director's reference library is how to get rid of people.

file: 1997/1997-05-14_human stupidity_simple interface_point at people.gif
title: Stupidity Detector Needs No Features

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My invention can detect human stupidity.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It has a very simple interface. All I do is point it at people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then what does it do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why would it need to do anything else?

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert, standing on the sofa, shows Dilbert his new invention, a wand-like device that detects human stupidity. He explains that its interface consists only of pointing it at people. When Dilbert asks what the device actually does, Dogbert replies that nothing more is needed.
punchline: The device does nothing except point at people, implying that merely pointing at people is enough to indicate stupidity, since everyone qualifies.
summary: Dogbert unveils a gadget that finds foolishness in people simply by being aimed at them, and sees no reason for it to have any other function.

file: 1997/1997-10-17_dogbert mutual fund_earnings report_steal investors money_compare perfromance_common assumptions.gif
title: Dogbert's Creative Earnings Report

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Dogbert Mutual Fund

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it hard to write an earnings report after you steal the investors' money?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nah.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll just compare my fund's performance to the S&P 500 under a common set of assumptions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How did our Dogbert fund do?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: "Ten percent better than the S&P 500 if it were also managed by an unscrupulous dog!"

setting: Dogbert's office at the Dogbert Mutual Fund, then a hallway or office with two investors
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, who runs a mutual fund, whether writing an earnings report is difficult after stealing investors' money. Dogbert explains he will simply benchmark his fund against the S&P 500 under a contrived set of assumptions. Two investors then read the report and see the result: the fund beat the index only if the index were run by an unscrupulous dog.
punchline: Dogbert's report technically claims outperformance by comparing his fund to a hypothetical benchmark that assumes the same fraud, making the 'good' result meaningless and exposing how financial reports can be spun.
summary: A dog who embezzled his fund's money dresses up the results by comparing them against an imaginary, equally crooked version of the stock market.

file: 1997/1997-02-12_need secreatry_six months now ork_too busy_secretary needs secreatry.gif
title: Secretary Demands Her Own Secretary

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: I need my own secretary. I'm too busy to help you unless I get some support.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Too busy? You haven't done any work for me in six months.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Oh, suddenly this is about you?

situation: The boss's secretary tells him she needs her own secretary because she is too busy to help him. The boss points out that she hasn't done any work for him in six months. She responds indignantly, as if he is being selfish for bringing up his own needs.
punchline: The secretary, who has done nothing for her boss in months, acts offended that he is making the conversation about himself, showing absurd entitlement and deflection.
summary: An idle secretary asks for an assistant of her own, then scolds her boss for being self-centered when he calls out her months of doing nothing.

file: 1997/1997-05-25_discouraged_pointy haired boss_pep talk_dead end job_grinding away_high blood pressure_stock options_doctor kevorkian.gif
title: Pep Talk From Equally Miserable Boss

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Lately I've been feeling discouraged about my job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You should talk to our Pointy-Haired Boss.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That'll cheer you up.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Maybe you're right. All I need is a little pep talk from our leader.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ha ha ha! Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You think you're discouraged...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been stuck in this dead-end job for years, grinding away, day after day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And all I have to show for it is high blood pressure and worthless stock options.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's so gratifying to watch them grow up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need the number for Doctor Kevorkian.

setting: Conference room and the Boss's office, with a cubicle at the end
situation: Asok complains of feeling discouraged at work, and his coworkers in a meeting tell him to get a pep talk from the Pointy-Haired Boss, then laugh at him. Asok visits the Boss expecting encouragement, but the Boss turns out to be even more miserable, complaining about his dead-end job, high blood pressure and worthless stock options. The Boss ends up asking for the number of Dr. Kevorkian while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: Asking the Boss for a pep talk backfires because he is more demoralized than the employee, ending with him seeking the assisted-suicide doctor's phone number.
summary: A young employee seeks cheering up from his manager, only to find the manager is far more despondent than he is.

file: 1997/1997-06-19_dogbert_invited to worthless meetings_say no_sense of self_can't be bothered.gif
title: Dogbert Refuses to Teach Saying No

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, I need your help. I keep getting invited to worthless meetings and I can't say no.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can say no to anything. You have such a clearly defined sense of self-interest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you teach me to be like you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nope... can't be bothered.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert sitting on a blue chair
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for help because he keeps getting invited to worthless meetings and cannot decline them. He praises Dogbert's ability to refuse anything thanks to his strong self-interest, then asks to be taught. Dogbert simply declines.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates the very skill Dilbert wants to learn by saying no to the request to teach him how to say no.
summary: A meeting-weary engineer begs his dog for lessons in refusing things, and the dog turns him down on the spot.

file: 1997/1997-12-28_making soup_highly trained engineer_sea salt_regular salt_marhoram_parmigiano cheese_eggs_hot soup.gif
title: Engineer Improvises Terrible Soup Recipe

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Making soup is easy for a highly trained engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't seem to have any "coarse sea salt."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just mix regular salt with water.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Corn starch...hmm... That's basically flour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Marjoram... I think that's French for butter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Five inches of Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese rind."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eggs are basically cheese that comes from chickens.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is this supposed to be served hot?

transcript.speaker: Guest
transcript.text: You're thinking of gazpacho.

situation: Dilbert, wearing a chef's hat and following a cookbook, confidently decides making soup is easy for an engineer. He keeps substituting wrong ingredients, such as plain salt water for sea salt, flour for corn starch, butter for marjoram and eggs for cheese. At dinner, a guest and Dogbert are served a strange dish, and Dogbert asks if it's supposed to be served hot.
punchline: Dilbert's engineering confidence masks total ignorance of cooking, and the guest's reply implies the soup is so bad that it is not even recognizable as hot soup.
summary: An overconfident engineer ruins a recipe through a string of absurd ingredient swaps and serves a baffling dish to his dinner guests.

file: 1997/1997-10-10_alice_around house_cubicle_dang_house covered_telecommuting_giant cubicle_im free.gif
title: Alice Hides From Cubicle Police

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Come out of there, Alice! We know you're telecommuting!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Never! I'm free! You can't make me go back to a cubicle!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dang

setting: Alice's suburban home, seen from the front door, the living room, and the street
situation: The Boss stands at Alice's front door with a megaphone, demanding that she come out because he knows she is working from home. Alice, with her hair standing on end, cowers behind her couch and refuses to return to a cubicle. In the last panel, the Boss has surrounded her entire house with giant cubicle walls, thinking 'Dang' as if the problem is solved.
punchline: Since Alice refuses to return to a cubicle, the Boss simply builds cubicle walls around her house, so her telecommuting freedom is defeated anyway.
summary: A manager hunts down a remote-working employee and responds to her defiance by boxing in her whole house with oversized partitions.

file: 1997/1997-01-11_perfromance review_napping_key board face_qwertytis_working hard.gif
title: Qwertytis Excuse at Performance Review

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wish me luck. I'm off to get my performance review.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you been napping? You've got a bad case of keyboard face.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's wrong with your face?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have qwertytis. It's from working too hard.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's meeting table
situation: Wally tells Dilbert he is heading to his performance review. Dilbert notices Wally's face is covered in key-shaped impressions, suggesting he has been napping on his keyboard. In the review, the Boss asks about Wally's face and Wally invents a made-up condition caused by overwork.
punchline: Wally disguises the evidence of sleeping at his desk by claiming the keyboard marks on his face are a medical condition from working too hard.
summary: A slacking employee spins the telltale marks of a desk nap into proof of his diligence during his evaluation.

file: 1997/1997-12-30_each photo_universe_tiny skull_going to explode_tarpaulin_rat talks  garbageman.gif
title: Ratbert's Brain Overload from Garbage Man

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So... each photon is a universe... then mass is just a probability cluster?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: That's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Wow! I think my tiny skull is so full it's going to explode.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Let me get a tarpaulin.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you been talking to our garbage man again?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't get too close.

setting: Outdoors by a garbage can, then a grassy hillside
situation: Ratbert sits on a trash can discussing physics with the garbage man, who casually confirms his theory about photons and mass. Ratbert says his tiny skull is so full it might explode, and the garbage man offers to fetch a tarpaulin to contain the mess. Dogbert then asks if he has been talking to the garbage man again, and Ratbert warns him not to get too close.
punchline: The garbage man's profound physics insights are so mind-blowing that Ratbert's head is about to literally explode, and he warns others to keep their distance.
summary: A small yellow rodent's mind is stretched to bursting by cosmic ideas from a surprisingly brilliant sanitation worker.

file: 1997/1997-11-15_hugged your date_snagged in blouse_hilarious_free your arm_ripped top off_engineer_diamond cutter_engineering.gif
title: Ratbert Recounts Dilbert's Disastrous Date

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I loved it when you hugged your date and your arm got snagged on her blouse...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And it was hilarious when you tried to free your arm and accidentally ripped her top off.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But the best part was when you yelled, "I'm an engineer, not a diamond cutter, dang it!"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on his blue couch
situation: Ratbert, perched on the couch next to a sulking Dilbert, cheerfully recalls the highlights of Dilbert's recent bad date. He describes how Dilbert's arm got snagged on his date's blouse and he accidentally ripped her top off while trying to free himself. Dilbert sits with his arms crossed and finally tells Ratbert to shut up.
punchline: Ratbert gleefully relishes Dilbert's humiliating date, and Dilbert's awkward outburst that he's an engineer and not a diamond cutter shows how his technical identity gets mixed into even his most embarrassing social failures.
summary: A gleeful little pet replays every cringeworthy moment of his owner's wardrobe-malfunction date until the owner snaps at him to stop.

file: 1997/1997-08-17_uncertainty_anxiety_wally_no strength_reorganzie_downsize_merger_sarcasm_cynicism.gif
title: Uncertainty Weighs Down Wally's Briefcase

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have a vague feeling of uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It gets stronger at the office.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The uncertainty saps my strength. My briefcase is getting heavier.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Must... get... to... cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The uncertainty feels like a piano upon my chest.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to reorganize. Or maybe downsize. Unless there's a merger.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mmph mmph

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I summon the unholy demons of apathy, sarcasm and cynicism!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good thinking! Reorganizations always increase profits!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. Third time today.

setting: Wally's car, the office hallway, and his cubicle
situation: Wally narrates his growing feeling of uncertainty as he drives to work and then crawls to his cubicle under the weight of his briefcase. The Boss appears and rambles about reorganizing, downsizing, or merging, flattening Wally further. Wally summons demons of apathy, sarcasm and cynicism, who sit on him and sarcastically praise the boss's idea.
punchline: Wally's dread about management indecision is so strong that he literally conjures demons, who sarcastically endorse reorganization as a profit booster while the Boss notes it's his third such plan today.
summary: A worker buckles under dread about his boss's shifting restructuring plans until he summons cynical demons to cheer them on.

file: 1997/1997-07-31_claustrophobic in here_copy machine_new roomate_share cubicles_space constraints.gif
title: Copy Machine Becomes Cubicle Roommate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Due to space constraints, some people will have to share cubicles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to the list, your new roommate will be ... the copy machine.

transcript.speaker: Other Employee
transcript.text: Is it claustrophobic in here or is it just me?

situation: The Boss tells a bald, bespectacled employee that space constraints will force cubicle sharing. He then reads from a list and announces that the employee's new roommate is the copy machine. In the final panel the employee sits at his desk while a coworker leans over him to operate the copy machine crammed into his cubicle.
punchline: The 'cubicle sharing' turns out to mean sharing with office equipment, and the coworker using the copier right over the employee's head shows how absurdly cramped it is.
summary: A manager's space-saving plan literally puts a photocopier in an employee's workspace, leaving colleagues crowding in to use it.

file: 1997/1997-11-13_dogcarts dating service_advice_accomplishments;lishments_hate men_designated bragger_humble_potential problem_makeup.gif
title: Dogbert's Designated Bragger Dating Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Dating Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Women like men who have accomplishments. But they hate men who boast.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will be your designated bragger, allowing you to appear humble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One potential problem with this plan is that I have no accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If she isn't wearing makeup, we'll be honest too.

situation: Dilbert combs his hair as Dogbert gives him dating advice and offers to act as his designated bragger so he can seem humble. Dilbert points out that he has no accomplishments for Dogbert to brag about. Dogbert replies that they will only be honest if the woman isn't wearing makeup.
punchline: Dogbert's plan relies on lying about Dilbert's achievements, and he casually admits that honesty will only be used when the date is also being honest by wearing no makeup.
summary: A scheming dog offers to boast on a man's behalf for dating purposes, but the plan hinges on fabricating the achievements he lacks.

file: 1997/1997-10-08_gauge glug_keep discipline_tendency snack_zesty italian dressing_telecommunting.gif
title: Telecommuting Alice Drinks Salad Dressing

transcript.speaker: Phone voice
transcript.text: How do you like telecommuting, Alice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's good, except I've developed a tendency to snack.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Glug glug glug glug glug glug glug glug glug

transcript.speaker: Phone voice
transcript.text: I'm sure you'll keep your discipline.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I love "zesty Italian" dressing.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Burp

setting: Alice's home office, at a desk with a phone
situation: Someone phones Alice to ask how she likes telecommuting. She admits she has started snacking at home, then is shown chugging a bottle of salad dressing. When the caller says he trusts her discipline, she burps and says she loves zesty Italian dressing.
punchline: Alice's lack of self-discipline while working from home has sunk to drinking salad dressing straight from the bottle, which makes the caller's confidence in her discipline absurd.
summary: A telecommuting worker's snacking habit turns out to mean guzzling bottled dressing while her caller praises her self-control.

file: 1997/1997-03-14_negotiate_telecommuting_ratbert illogical things_drains will_unproductive things_will to argue.gif
title: Ratbert Drains Boss's Will to Argue

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm here to negotiate for more telecommuting days.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My negotiating strategy is to have Ratbert say such illogical things that it drains your will to argue.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You can't work at home because you might do unproductive things there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've lost my will to argue.

situation: Dilbert walks into the Boss's office to negotiate for more telecommuting days, with Ratbert perched on his head. He explains that his strategy is to have Ratbert say such illogical things that the Boss gives up arguing. Ratbert offers a nonsensical objection, and the Boss immediately concedes that he has lost his will to argue.
punchline: Ratbert's absurd reasoning (you can't work at home because you might do unproductive things there) is so illogical that the Boss is worn down at once, which shows how flawed the arguments against telecommuting are. The line is also ironic because unproductive things happen in offices all the time.
summary: Dilbert pushes for more work-from-home days by bringing Ratbert along to wear his manager down with nonsense until the manager simply gives in.

file: 1997/1997-05-16_catbert_evil hr director_new policy_official company font_obscure_impractical font_elbonia_elbonian font.gif
title: Catbert Mandates Elbonian Company Font

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: New policy: All company documents must use the official company font...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Let's see... What would be the most obscure and impractical font imaginable?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purr Purr Purr

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Somewhere in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I understand I can get the Elbonian font software from you.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Yep. Unless you need consonants for some reason.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, then a muddy village in Elbonia
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces a new policy requiring all company documents to use the official company font. He purrs while deciding which font would be the most obscure and impractical possible. Dilbert then travels to Elbonia to get the Elbonian font software from a local, who warns it lacks consonants.
punchline: The official company font turns out to be Elbonian, a typeface so impractical it has no consonants, making documents unreadable.
summary: An H.R. cat picks the most useless typeface he can think of, and it turns out to be a consonant-free font from a backward foreign land.

file: 1997/1997-04-21_family friendly policies_higher profits_high profits_true costs_camouflage_five minute break.gif
title: Family-Friendly Policies Question Gets Slapped

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: My study shows that the companies with "family friendly" policies have higher profits.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Do family policies cause high profits or do high profits simply camouflage the true costs of the policies?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: We'll take a five-minute break so the married people can slap you for asking that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch!

situation: A presenter at a projector shows a chart claiming that companies with family-friendly policies earn higher profits. Dilbert, sitting among his coworkers, asks whether the policies cause the profits or the profits merely hide what the policies really cost. The presenter calls a break so married people can slap him for the question.
punchline: Dilbert's question implies that family-friendly policies are a hidden burden on single employees, and the presenter's reply suggests the married coworkers will physically punish him for saying so.
summary: A skeptical question about the real cost of family benefits earns the questioner a literal beating from offended colleagues.

file: 1997/1997-07-18_statement of core values_change behavior_planning to poiosn_sarcasm_necessary.gif
title: Core Values Won't Stop Poisoning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you explain how the company's new "statement of core values" will change my behavior?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was planning to poison the town's water supply.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But wait! It's against our core values!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is your sarcasm absolutely necessary?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me check. Hmm... it's not addressed.

situation: Dilbert holds the company's new statement of core values and asks the Boss how it could possibly change anyone's behavior. He sarcastically pretends he was about to poison the town's water supply until the values stopped him. When the Boss asks if the sarcasm is necessary, Dilbert consults the document and reports that sarcasm isn't covered.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the useless corporate values statement by showing it would never actually stop bad behavior, then uses its silence on sarcasm to justify continuing to be sarcastic.
summary: An employee ridicules a vague corporate values document with deadpan sarcasm and then cites its gaps to excuse himself.

file: 1997/1997-01-30_glass half empty_half in another glass_lips on glass_optimist half full_redundant glass.gif
title: Engineer's Redundant Glass of Water

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: A pessimist says the glass is half empty. An optimist says it's half full.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you put your lips on my glass again?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And the engineer says...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a good thing I put half of my water in a redundant glass.

situation: Ratbert stands on Dilbert's desk and begins the classic joke about a glass being half empty or half full. Dilbert, annoyed that Ratbert has been drinking from his glass, interrupts. He delivers the engineer's version of the punchline, claiming he poured half his water into a second glass as a backup.
punchline: The engineer's answer to the half-full joke is that the glass is redundant by design, which also lets Dilbert pointedly keep Ratbert's lips away from his water.
summary: A tiny pet's riddle about a half-filled glass gets answered with an engineer's backup-system solution that doubles as a hygiene precaution.

file: 1997/1997-07-14_alice_boss_give presentation_technology_trade show_wiggle room_for or against.gif
title: Boss Delegates Vague Trade Show Talk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been asked to give a presentation at the trade show.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to put that together for me, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's your topic?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Technology. They didn't say if I'm for it or against it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll leave some wiggle room.

situation: The Boss tells Alice he has been asked to give a trade show presentation and wants her to write it for him. When she asks about the topic, he can only say 'technology' and admits he doesn't know whether he is supposed to be for or against it. He then tells her to leave some wiggle room.
punchline: The Boss hands off a presentation with no real topic or position, expecting Alice to produce something vague enough to cover any stance.
summary: A manager pawns off a conference talk on his subordinate, with a subject so broad and undefined that she has to hedge on everything.

file: 1997/1997-03-15_let me telecommute_called in sick_total days off_working for nothing_ahead in principle_stupidity is principle.gif
title: Telecommuting by Calling in Sick

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I convinced my boss to let me telecommute.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, technically, I called in sick, which comes out of my time bank for total days off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, technically, I'm working for nothing, but I'm ahead in principle.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Way ahead, now that stupidity is a principle.

setting: Dilbert's home, in his bathrobe at a home computer
situation: Dilbert, wearing a bathrobe, tells Dogbert he got his boss to let him telecommute. He admits he actually called in sick, so the day is deducted from his time off, and he is working unpaid from home. Dogbert sarcastically agrees that he is way ahead.
punchline: Dilbert's convoluted reasoning that working for free while burning his own vacation days puts him 'ahead in principle' is mocked by Dogbert, who says he is way ahead now that stupidity counts as a principle.
summary: A man brags about working from home, only to reveal he is secretly burning his own sick time to do his employer's work for free.

file: 1997/1997-11-17_changing_job titles_non technical_sec group_second class citizens.gif
title: S.C.C. Group Stands For Insult

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, we're changing the job titles of all non-technical people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Collectively, you'll be known as our S.C.C. group.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I like the sound of it - very dignified. We were beginning to feel like second-class citizens. What's S.C.C. stand for?

situation: The Boss tells Tina that all non-technical employees are getting new job titles and will be grouped under the name S.C.C. Tina likes how dignified it sounds and says her group had been feeling like second-class citizens, then asks what the letters stand for. The Boss looks uneasy, hinting the answer will not be flattering.
punchline: S.C.C. almost certainly stands for 'second-class citizens', so the dignified-sounding new title simply confirms exactly what Tina's group feared.
summary: A rebranding of non-technical staff turns out to be an acronym that quietly names the very slight they were hoping to escape.

file: 1997/1997-10-05_dilbert mother_promoted_executive engineer_same pay_responsibility_throw party_no gifts_no music_no food_no guests_business cards.gif
title: Hollow Promotion, Lonely Celebration

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom, guess what... I got promoted!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're talking to the new "Executive Engineer."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No... Nobody reports to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No... it's the same pay as before.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I do get a lot more responsibility!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's going to throw a party for me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: No... No gifts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: No... No music.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: No... No food.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: No... No guests.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess it's just you and me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I'm busy that day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to get new business cards, but I can write my new title on the old ones!

transcript.speaker: Dog
transcript.text: Zzzz

setting: Dilbert's home, on the phone and on the couch, then at a table for a party
situation: Dilbert phones his mother to announce a promotion to "Executive Engineer", but each of her questions reveals the job has no direct reports, no raise, and only extra responsibility. His mother offers a party with no gifts, music, food or guests, and then begs off attending herself. Dilbert ends up celebrating alone with his sleeping dog, cheerfully writing the new title on his old business cards.
punchline: The promotion is a title-only change that adds responsibility without pay or authority, and the pitiful party shows even his own mother sees through it.
summary: A proud son's fancy new job title unravels into extra work for no reward and a party attended only by a snoozing pet.

file: 1997/1997-11-14_dilbert_dogbert_hugger_first date_watch snagged_bra strap.gif
title: Awkward First Date Hug Mishap

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Hi, Dilbert! Hi, Dogbert!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's a hugger on the first date. I never know where my arms should go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope this doesn't seem awkward, but my watch is snagged on your bra strap.

setting: Outside Dilbert's front door, at the start of a date
situation: Dilbert's date arrives at his door with her arms open, greeting him and Dogbert. Dilbert privately worries about what to do with his arms during a first-date hug, and then fumbles the embrace so that his watch gets caught on her bra strap.
punchline: Dilbert's anxiety over where to put his arms leads to the worst possible outcome: he ends up stuck to his date's bra strap and has to awkwardly announce it.
summary: A nervous man dreads the customary hug from his date and then ends up literally tangled in her clothing.

file: 1997/1997-06-04_dogbert_professional_bearer of bad news_offer position_qualified_six billion_earth_resume.gif
title: Dogbert's Rejection Letter Service

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Professional bearer of bad news

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: We cannot offer you a position at this time, but you are obviously qualified.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Unfortunately, the other six billion people on Earth are more qualified.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: We'll keep your résumé on file.

setting: Dogbert's office, at a desk with a computer
situation: Dogbert works as a professional bearer of bad news and composes a job rejection message at his computer. The message begins politely, then reveals that every other person on the planet is more qualified. In the last panel he tosses the applicant's résumé over his shoulder into the trash while the message says it will be kept on file.
punchline: The polite promise to keep the résumé on file is a lie, since Dogbert is literally throwing it away, and the rejection insults the applicant by saying everyone else on Earth is better.
summary: A canine rejection specialist delivers a brutally honest hiring letter and then bins the applicant's paperwork while promising to hold onto it.

file: 1997/1997-08-20_recruiting on campus_company_not first choice_business.gif
title: Campus Recruiter Crushes Dilbert's Hand

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Recruiting on campus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice to meet you...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crush

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaeeii!

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: I have to be honest; your company isn't my first choice.

setting: A campus recruiting event at a table
situation: Dilbert, acting as a company recruiter, goes to shake hands with a student at a campus recruiting event. The student crushes his hand in a painful grip and screams. The student then hauls Dilbert off the floor by his tie and says the company isn't his first choice.
punchline: The student's violent handshake and tie-grabbing show he is hostile and aggressive toward the recruiter, which clashes with his polite remark that the company is not his first choice.
summary: A job candidate answers a recruiter's friendly handshake by wrecking his hand and dangling him by the necktie while admitting he'd rather work elsewhere.

file: 1997/1997-05-07_flashback_first web browser_prank_people waiting aorund_nothing happening.gif
title: The Web Browser Prank Origin

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flashback to the invention of the first web browser

transcript.speaker: Man in cap
transcript.text: What should we call our prank, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, it's designed to make millions of people sit around waiting for nothing to happen...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A few years later

transcript.speaker: Skeletal user
transcript.text: Hey, I can almost see a recognizable blotch! This is awesome!

transcript.speaker: Note
transcript.text: Note

setting: A computer desk during the invention of the web browser, then years later in front of a monitor
situation: In a flashback, a man in a cap and Dogbert plan a prank and Dogbert explains it is meant to make millions of people wait for nothing to happen. Years later, a skeletal-looking user who has waited so long that he has wasted away gleefully watches an image slowly load on his monitor.
punchline: Early web browsers were so slow that users waited endlessly, so the web was effectively a prank on the public, and the user's delight at barely seeing a blotch shows how low expectations had fallen.
summary: Dogbert reveals that the first web browser was a joke on humanity, and years later a withered user cheers a barely loaded image.

file: 1997/1997-04-01_going on vacation_compile our inputs_highest human potential.gif
title: Family Circus Kid Invades Dilbert Office

transcript.speaker: Billy
transcript.text: Hey, Dilbert! You'll never be hungry as long as you're workin' in this strip...

transcript.speaker: Billy
transcript.text: ...'cause you're sure of three squares every day!

transcript.speaker: Billy
transcript.text: Some of us hafta keep goin' around in circles!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: -Security?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with a computer on the desk
situation: Billy from The Family Circus, drawn in that strip's style, appears in Dilbert's office and points out that Dilbert's strip uses square panels, so he will never go hungry. Billy complains that Family Circus characters have to keep going around in circles, a reference to its round panels and Billy's looping dotted-line paths. Dilbert calmly picks up the phone and calls security on the intruder.
punchline: The crossover jokes about comic panel shapes ('three squares' a day versus 'going around in circles'), and Dilbert's deadpan reaction is to treat the cartoon kid as a trespasser and call security.
summary: A cartoon child from a rival comic wanders into Dilbert's office to gloat about square panels versus circular ones, and gets reported to building security.

file: 1997/1997-12-23_illogical scientist_idea won't work_religious nuts.gif
title: The Illogical Scientist Rejects Ideas

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Hi. I'm Dan, the illogical scientist.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: That idea won't work. I know because I've read many reports about ideas that didn't work.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You haven't even looked at my idea.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Oh, I get it; you're one of those religious nuts.

situation: A scientist introduces himself as Dan, the illogical scientist, to a woman with enormous hair who is taking notes. He dismisses her idea without looking at it, claiming that past reports about failed ideas prove it won't work. When she objects that he hasn't examined her idea, he accuses her of being a religious nut.
punchline: The self-declared illogical scientist rejects ideas on flawed reasoning and then labels anyone who objects a religious fanatic, proving he is exactly as illogical as advertised.
summary: A self-proclaimed illogical scientist waves away a colleague's proposal by citing other failures, then insults her when she protests his refusal to even consider it.

file: 1997/1997-10-04_glorious day_telecommuting_district me_talking refrigerator_jar of pickles.gif
title: Telecommuting With a Taunting Refrigerator

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ahhh... it's going to be a glorious day of telecommuting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's nothing here to distract me. It's just me...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ...and my talking refrigerator.

transcript.speaker: Refrigerator
transcript.text: I'll bet you can't eat a whole jar of pickles.

situation: Alice wakes up in her bathrobe, delighted at the prospect of working from home with no distractions. She walks toward the kitchen, confident she will be productive. Her refrigerator then speaks up and dares her to eat an entire jar of pickles, proving that home has plenty of distractions.
punchline: Alice's confidence that working from home will be distraction-free is undercut by a talking refrigerator that goads her into silly snacking challenges.
summary: A cheerful telecommuter expects a peaceful day of focused work until her kitchen appliance starts tempting her into mischief.

file: 1997/1997-11-06_problems_waiting it out_standing motionless_reorganization.gif
title: Waiting for Problems to Disappear

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Most problems go away if you wait long enough, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: It might look like I'm standing motionless, but I'm actively waiting for our problems to go away.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: There's been a reorganization...

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I don't know why this works, but it does.

situation: A green dinosaur co-worker explains to Asok that most problems vanish if you simply wait long enough, describing his inaction as active waiting. A manager then appears to announce that a reorganization has occurred, apparently making the dinosaur's problems disappear. The dinosaur admits he doesn't understand why his strategy works, but it does.
punchline: The dinosaur's do-nothing strategy is vindicated when a corporate reorganization conveniently eliminates his problems, suggesting that inaction succeeds because companies constantly reshuffle responsibilities.
summary: A passive dinosaur preaches the virtue of waiting out problems and is proven right when a company shake-up makes them vanish.

file: 1997/1997-11-18_losers_bad ideas_test a new idea_research_science.gif
title: Testing Ideas on Known Losers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All great ideas look like bad ideas to people who are losers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's always good to test a new idea with known losers to make sure they don't like it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Research Co.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: What a coincidence. We both lost three homes in flood zones.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's begin.

setting: A grassy park, then Dogbert's research company office
situation: Dilbert walks through a park with a frisbee, explaining to Dogbert that great ideas look bad to losers, so new ideas should be tested on known losers to confirm they dislike them. He throws the frisbee. In the final panel, Dogbert runs a research session with two test subjects who bond over both having lost three homes in flood zones.
punchline: Dogbert's research company recruits people who are visibly hapless, such as those who repeatedly buy homes in flood zones, as its test panel of 'known losers', so their rejection of an idea is treated as proof the idea is great.
summary: A research firm deliberately picks chronically unlucky people as its focus group, reasoning that their disapproval is a sign an idea is brilliant.

file: 1997/1997-05-27_cloud of doom_overlook_lighting strikes_meeting_business.gif
title: Cloud of Doom Strikes Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll need everyone's help on this project. I hope you can overlook the cloud of doom that hovers nearby.

transcript.speaker: Cloud
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Boom!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crack

transcript.speaker: Cloud
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. It's lucky that wasn't someone we like.

transcript.speaker: Cloud
transcript.text: Doom

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: Dilbert asks his coworkers for help on a project and warns them to ignore a small cloud of doom hovering nearby. The cloud zaps a bald, glasses-wearing coworker with lightning, leaving smoking shoes behind. Dilbert then remarks how fortunate it is that the victim wasn't someone they like.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan remark reveals he considers the lightning victim an unliked colleague, treating a coworker's zapping as a mere stroke of luck.
summary: A personal storm cloud follows a project leader to a meeting and fries a disliked colleague, to everyone's relief.

file: 1997/1997-09-04_plundered_downsized_equity_massive stock options_victory seems hollow_meaningful contribition_book deal_trophy wife.gif
title: Hollow Victory After Plundering Company

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've downsized this company and plundered its equity by exercising my massive stock options.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yet my victory seems hollow. Something is missing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you're missing a sense of meaningful contribution to society.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe... but I'm thinking book deal and trophy wife.

setting: Outside a limousine, then Dilbert's living room couch
situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and carrying a scepter, boasts that he has downsized a company and cashed in huge stock options. As a chauffeur holds his limo door, he muses that his victory feels hollow, and Dilbert suggests he lacks a meaningful contribution to society. Dogbert dismisses this and says he wants a book deal and a trophy wife instead.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of what is missing from his life is more status symbols rather than any real purpose, mocking executives who get rich by gutting companies.
summary: A crowned Dogbert gloats over wrecking a company for personal gain, then waves off a chance at moral reflection in favor of more perks.

file: 1997/1997-11-30_interesting presentation_spies_slides_new prodcut_kills mold_mildew_software_placebo effect_stunned silence_engineering.gif
title: Software That Kills Mold and Mildew

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ken, may we have a word with you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We heard that you gave an interesting presentation at the sales staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our spies gave us copies of your slides.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told them that our new product kills mold and mildew.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Won't it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We make software!

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: So? Haven't you ever heard of the placebo effect?!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stunned silence

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: ... In company news, our entire sales force shriveled up and died for no apparent reason.

situation: Dilbert and a fellow engineer confront Ken, a salesman, about his sales meeting slides, which claim the company's new software product kills mold and mildew. Ken defends the claim by invoking the placebo effect. After a stunned silence, the Boss announces that the entire sales force has mysteriously died.
punchline: Ken's absurd defense of lying about the product leads to the implication that the engineers, tired of such nonsense, somehow caused the whole sales force to die, which the Boss deadpans as a mystery.
summary: A salesman gets called out for promising that a software product eliminates household mold, then shrugs it off as a placebo, and soon afterward his whole department is mysteriously wiped out.

file: 1997/1997-04-14_asap_a stupid acting person_deadlines_embarrasing.gif
title: ASAP Means Stupid Acting Person

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I need this ASAP.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ASAP? Does that stand for A Stupid-Acting Person, i.e., someone who ignores tasks until the deadline?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was embarrassing. I hope the other things I say don't mean anything.

situation: The Boss hands Alice a document and tells her he needs it ASAP. Alice responds by reinterpreting the acronym as 'A Stupid-Acting Person,' accusing him of ignoring tasks until the deadline. Walking away, the Boss thinks to himself that he hopes his other phrases aren't similarly meaningless.
punchline: The Boss is so embarrassed by being called out on his deadline procrastination that he realizes much of his managerial jargon might be equally empty or meaningless.
summary: A manager's rush request gets turned into an insult by his sharp-tongued employee, leaving him doubting the substance of everything he says.

file: 1997/1997-07-27_albert einstein_marketing_idea_never work_don't fully understand_albert_quite an ego_experienced managers_work smarter_not harder_business.gif
title: Einstein Pitches Idea to Dismissive Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: What if... Albert Einstein had been in marketing?

transcript.speaker: Einstein
transcript.text: I have a great idea for increasing sales.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nope. This will never work.

transcript.speaker: Einstein
transcript.text: Um... Is it possible that you don't fully understand the idea?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's quite an ego you have there, Allan.

transcript.speaker: Einstein
transcript.text: Albert.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experienced managers know how to identify bad ideas...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bad ideas come from other people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now go work smarter, not harder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I worry that a guy like that will go off and build a huge bomb.

situation: A marketing employee who looks like Albert Einstein pitches an idea for boosting sales, and the boss rejects it outright without hearing it. When Einstein suggests the boss may not understand it, the boss accuses him of having an ego, gets his name wrong, and says bad ideas always come from other people. After sending him off to work smarter, the boss privately worries he'll build a bomb.
punchline: The boss is so arrogantly dismissive and clueless that he fears the greatest scientific mind in history will turn vengeful, while never recognizing that his own attitude wastes brilliant ideas.
summary: A genius in a marketing job gets brushed off by a boss who treats every idea but his own as worthless and then frets about the employee's resentment.

file: 1997/1997-01-08_wally ordered_laughter_elbonia_mail order bride_local girls.gif
title: Wally's Elbonian Mail-Order Bride

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, Wally. I hear you're getting an Elbonian mail-order bride!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's so sad and pathetic, yet so funny! I feel sorry for her already!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hu-hahaha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And people ask why I gave up on local girls.

situation: Alice approaches Wally's cubicle and mocks him for getting a mail-order bride from Elbonia, saying it is both sad and funny and that she already pities the bride. She doubles over laughing while Wally calmly replies.
punchline: Wally says that Alice's cruel, mocking reaction is exactly why he gave up on dating local women and turned to a mail-order bride.
summary: A coworker howls with laughter over a colleague's plan to import a bride, and her rudeness proves his reason for avoiding local women.

file: 1997/1997-06-24_be specific_bounus_congratulations_expect bonus_good work_act randomly.gif
title: Unexplained Bonus Motivates Random Behavior

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, here's a bonus for your good work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: On what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't be specific, because then you might do it again and expect another bonus.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Congratulations; you've motivated me to act randomly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going over here and I don't know why.

situation: The Boss hands Alice a bonus for unspecified good work. When she asks what it was for, he refuses to say, fearing she will repeat it and expect more money. Alice tells him he has motivated her to act randomly, and he promptly wanders off without knowing why.
punchline: A reward given with no explanation reinforces no particular behavior, so the only thing it motivates is random action, which the boss immediately demonstrates himself.
summary: A manager withholds the reason for a reward and gets exactly the aimless results that such vagueness deserves.

file: 1997/1997-01-24_alice_application_compliment_executive review commitee_must be approved_compliments are entitlement.gif
title: Compliments Require Committee Approval

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I put you in for a compliment, Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not automatic. The application must be approved by the Executive Review Committee.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Executive Review Committee

transcript.speaker: Committee Member
transcript.text: I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: Committee Member
transcript.text: We don't want them to think compliments are an entitlement.

setting: Office cubicle, then a conference room
situation: The Boss tells Alice he has nominated her to receive a compliment, but explains that it must be approved by the Executive Review Committee. In the boardroom, a committee member rejects the application, saying employees shouldn't come to expect compliments.
punchline: Management has turned even a simple compliment into a bureaucratic approval process, and then denies it so employees won't feel entitled to praise.
summary: Praise for a hard-working employee gets stuck in red tape and is turned down by executives who are stingy with recognition.

file: 1997/1997-11-29_masters degress_top colleges_new hires.gif
title: Hiring Policy Excludes Short Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, we'll only hire people with masters degrees from the top colleges.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't have a masters degree from a top college. I'm insulted by this new policy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And new hires must be this tall to work here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey!!

situation: The Boss announces a new hiring policy requiring masters degrees from top colleges. Wally objects that he doesn't qualify and is insulted. The Boss responds by adding a height requirement and holds up a height chart that shows Wally is too short.
punchline: The Boss adds an arbitrary height requirement that conveniently excludes Wally, mocking him for complaining and showing how absurd and capricious his hiring criteria are.
summary: A manager's elitist hiring rule draws a complaint from an employee, so he piles on a pointless height rule that targets that very employee.

file: 1997/1997-05-18_restaurant_tipping waitress_14 % tip_service was excellent_cheap_lying_unscrupulous weasel_bad sevice.gif
title: Lunch Bill Tip Shortfall Mystery

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: Thank you. Please come again.

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: After I'm dead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we each put in twelve dollars, that will give her a healthy fourteen percent tip.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The service was excellent. I'll put in a little extra.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That gives us...um... only thirty-four dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One of us is a cheap, lying, unscrupulous weasel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe the service was bad.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: She didn't smile enough.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Same as last week.

situation: After a waitress thanks them and privately wishes they would never return, Dilbert proposes that each of the three put in twelve dollars for a 14 percent tip. Everyone claims to add a little extra because the service was excellent, yet the pile totals only thirty-four dollars. Dilbert accuses one of them of being a cheap liar, then the group suddenly pivots to claiming the service was bad.
punchline: The coworkers, caught shortchanging the tip, collectively abandon their claim of excellent service and retroactively blame the waitress, revealing they are all cheapskates who do this every week.
summary: Three lunch companions who swore they were tipping extra come up short on cash and instantly decide the waitress deserved less anyway.

file: 1997/1997-01-28_figure of speech_lost work_server crashed_unplanned outages_advance notice.gif
title: Advance Notice of Server Outages

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The network went down and I lost my work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The server crashed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I want advanced notice of any unplanned outages.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I need it yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I used to think that was just a figure of speech.

situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that the network went down and he lost his work, and Dilbert explains the server crashed. The Boss then demands advance notice of any unplanned outages, adding that he needs it yesterday. Dilbert silently thinks he used to believe that phrase was just a figure of speech.
punchline: The Boss's demand for advance warning of unplanned outages is impossible by definition, and his 'I need it yesterday' makes literal a cliché that Dilbert had assumed was only an expression.
summary: A manager who lost his files insists on being warned about surprise crashes before they happen, even asking for the warning in the past.

file: 1997/1997-04-13_project plan requested_working day and night_wold chipmunks_clip art_never mic sarcasm_good clip art.gif
title: Sarcastic Project Plan, Dead Chipmunks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my project plan as you requested.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our team is already working day and night on other projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assumed we'd give up eating, sleeping and bathing to fit this in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By the second week we'll be starving, delirious and stinking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll be like wild, unpredictable animals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Specifically, we'd be like wild chipmunks. None of us are very aggressive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This clip-art represents us in week three as a pile of dead chipmunks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now he wants it in two weeks?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never mix sarcasm with good clip-art.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway outside
situation: Dilbert hands his boss a project plan and sarcastically explains that his overworked team will be starving, delirious and stinking by week two, and a pile of dead chipmunks by week three, illustrated with clip-art. The Boss listens without reacting. Afterward Wally asks if the boss now wants it in two weeks, showing the sarcasm was taken literally.
punchline: The boss ignores the sarcasm and treats the plan's two-week mention as a deadline, so Dilbert's ironic warning backfires, and he blames the effective-looking clip-art for making the sarcasm convincing.
summary: A worker's mocking presentation about his exhausted team's grim fate is taken at face value by his boss, who shortens the schedule.

file: 1997/1997-06-17_four hour meeting_surrogate social life_bring chips_wish_had a spine.gif
title: Meetings as Surrogate Social Life

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You're invited to a four-hour meeting, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Tina, it would seem that all of your meetings have no purpose other than to provide you with a surrogate social life.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Can you bring chips?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I wish, I wish, I wish I had a spine.

situation: Tina hands Asok an invitation to a four-hour meeting. Asok boldly tells her that her meetings exist only to give her a social life, but she cheerfully ignores the criticism and asks him to bring chips. Asok, defeated, laments that he lacks the courage to refuse.
punchline: Asok correctly calls out the meeting's pointlessness, but Tina's breezy request for snacks shows she doesn't care, and he is too spineless to actually decline.
summary: A junior engineer accuses a coworker of holding meetings just to socialize, then meekly agrees to supply snacks anyway.
