file: 1997/1997-08-11_blowing off idiots_information_web page_misunderstood.gif
title: Deflecting Questions With Web Page

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I have a new method for blowing off the idiots who ask questions.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I say, "That information is on my web page. Shoo, shoo."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happens when they find out it isn't?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll say, "You must have misunderstood your question."

situation: Ratbert tells Dilbert, who is working at his computer, about his new technique for getting rid of people who ask him questions: claim the answer is on his web page. Dilbert asks what happens when people discover it isn't there, and Ratbert says he will blame them for misunderstanding their own question.
punchline: Ratbert's brush-off strategy relies on lying about a web page and then shifting blame to the questioner, who is absurdly told they misunderstood their own question.
summary: A smug little pet describes his foolproof scheme for dodging questions by pointing people to a website that has nothing useful on it.

file: 1997/1997-09-18_joined late_dinosaur_hiding behind furniture_space.gif
title: Dinosaurs Hiding Behind Office Furniture

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For those who joined us late, this is Bob the Dinosaur. He lives with Dilbert and me.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Hi

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Dinosaurs aren't extinct. They're just hiding behind furniture.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: This is Dawn, my mate, and little Rex.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: You'll notice that they use a lot of space and they aren't very relevant.

transcript.speaker: Dawn
transcript.text: I think Rex has my eyes.

setting: A desk or lectern in front of a purple wall, as if during a presentation
situation: Dogbert introduces Bob the Dinosaur, who lives with him and Dilbert, to a late-arriving audience. Bob claims dinosaurs never went extinct and introduces his mate Dawn and their baby Rex, then describes them as space-hogging and irrelevant while Dawn remarks on the baby's eyes.
punchline: Bob's description of dinosaurs as space-consuming and irrelevant is a thinly veiled jab at obsolete employees or technologies that linger in organizations long after they are useful.
summary: A pet dinosaur presents his family as outdated relics that survive by lurking out of sight and taking up room.

file: 1997/1997-06-21_ego_pointy haired boss_standing in offcie_thimble sized morale_tic tac container_protect.gif
title: Morale Stored in a Thimble

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... So our Pointy-Haired Boss put me in charge of your project...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... Because I was standing in his office when he thought about the project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it makes you feel better, you can keep your morale in this thimble with mine.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I keep mine in a "Tic Tac" container with my ego.

situation: Dilbert tells a bald, bespectacled coworker that he has been put in charge of the coworker's project, only because he happened to be standing in the Boss's office when the Boss thought of it. He then offers to let the coworker store his morale in a thimble alongside his own. The coworker replies that he keeps his morale in a Tic Tac container along with his ego.
punchline: Both men's morale is so depleted that it fits in a thimble or a Tic Tac container, showing how randomly and thoughtlessly the Boss hands out responsibility.
summary: A man given a colleague's project by sheer chance of location offers a tiny shared vessel for their shrunken morale, and gets an equally tiny container in reply.

file: 1997/1997-03-04_business startegy_example_good strategy_learn_panty hose_ratbert the consultant_walmarts.gif
title: Ratbert's Wal-Mart Strategy Lesson

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: "Wal-Mart's" business strategy was very successful. You can learn from their example.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Does their strategy involve sitting around and making irrelevant comparisons to other companies?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: All I know for sure is that they don't let rats try on all the pantyhose in the store.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good strategy.

setting: Conference room during a consulting presentation
situation: Ratbert, acting as a consultant, tells Alice and Dilbert that they should learn from Wal-Mart's successful business strategy. Alice sarcastically asks if the strategy is just making irrelevant comparisons to other companies. Ratbert admits the only thing he knows is that Wal-Mart doesn't let rats try on all the pantyhose, and Dilbert approves.
punchline: The consultant has no real knowledge of Wal-Mart's strategy, so his only 'insight' is a ridiculous detail about rats and pantyhose, which the audience grudgingly accepts as sound strategy.
summary: A rat posing as a business consultant offers a vacuous comparison to a famous retailer and is called out by a skeptical colleague.

file: 1997/1997-03-27_come back_manager_moron_promotions_raises_leaving company.gif
title: Quit, Return, Get Promoted Manager

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: When I was your age, we had things called "promotions" and "raises."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: These days you can only get ahead by leaving the company for a year then coming back as a high-level manager.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So the theory must be that anyone who would return to this company is...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: A moron. Correct.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Tina, a veteran employee with big hair, tells young Asok that promotions and raises used to exist. She explains that now the only way to advance is to quit for a year and return as a high-level manager. Asok works out the implication, and Tina confirms it.
punchline: Because the company rewards people who leave and then come back, it effectively promotes only those foolish enough to return, so its managers are morons.
summary: An older coworker explains to a junior colleague that career advancement now requires quitting and being rehired as a boss, which implies that management is made up of fools.

file: 1997/1997-08-25_catbert_evil director_human resources_deadlines_embarrassing_fuzzy_laughed_embarrasing_business.gif
title: Catbert Taunts Alice About Vacation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Alice, you have to use your vacation time or you'll lose it.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But if you take time off, you'll miss your deadlines. Ha ha ha ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This is embarrassing. I laughed myself fuzzy.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, peeks over the wall of Alice's cubicle and tells her she must use her vacation time or lose it. He then points out that taking time off will make her miss her deadlines and bursts into laughter while she glares at him. Alone afterward, he thinks to himself that he laughed so hard his fur is fuzzy.
punchline: Catbert deliberately puts Alice in a no-win bind between losing vacation and missing deadlines, and he finds her predicament so funny that he is embarrassed by how hard he laughed.
summary: An evil personnel cat delights in trapping an employee between a use-it-or-lose-it leave policy and an unmanageable workload.

file: 1997/1997-11-22_new fog_rolling in_mean one thing_time to reorganize.gif
title: Fog Rolls In, Reorganization Follows

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: A new fog is rolling in.

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: This can only mean one thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, schedule a staff meeting. It's time to reorganize the department.

setting: Office cubicle area engulfed in a cloud of fog
situation: A bank of fog drifts through the office while Carol announces its arrival from her cubicle. The fog fills the workspace and hides everyone from view. The Boss, emerging from the fog, takes this as his cue to order a staff meeting to reorganize the department.
punchline: The Boss treats confusion and lack of visibility as the perfect moment to launch a reorganization, implying reorganizations are what managers do when they are in a fog.
summary: When a literal haze settles over the office, the Boss reads it as a sign to shake up the department's structure.

file: 1997/1997-06-23_catbert_evil_hr director_new policy_travel separate flights_dangerous hobbies.gif
title: Policy Naming Wally Is Bad News

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: New policy: Key employees must travel on separate flights to reduce risk.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Other employees, such as Wally, are encouraged to take up dangerous hobbies.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've noticed that when a new policy mentions me by name, it's never a good thing.

setting: Office cubicle and a conference room
situation: Catbert, perched on Wally's head and shoulders, announces a new HR policy requiring key employees to fly on separate flights to reduce risk. He then adds that less valuable employees, such as Wally, are encouraged to take up dangerous hobbies. In a meeting, Wally calmly observes that policies naming him are never good news.
punchline: The company treats Wally as so expendable that its risk-management policy actively encourages him to endanger himself, and Wally deadpans that he has noticed the pattern.
summary: An HR policy protects valuable staff from shared risk while cheerfully urging a named, disposable coworker to court danger.

file: 1997/1997-01-22_canceling life insurance_catbert_evil hr director_extend vacations_family freindly_no longer allow_remove incentives_time off for death_kill relatives.gif
title: Catbert's Family Friendly Policy Kills Incentives

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Effective immediately, the company will no longer allow time off for the death of a family member.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This "family friendly" policy will remove your incentive to extend vacations by killing relatives.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And more good news: We're canceling your life insurance so your family won't try to snuff you out either.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, at his desk and computer
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces over his computer that employees will no longer get time off when a family member dies. He claims this removes any incentive for workers to kill relatives to get extra vacation. He then adds that life insurance is canceled so employees' families won't be tempted to kill them either.
punchline: Catbert presents deeply callous cost-cutting measures as "family friendly" benefits, with dark logic that employees and their families would murder each other over perks.
summary: A malicious cat in human resources dresses up the removal of bereavement leave and life insurance as a kindness that prevents people from murdering relatives.

file: 1997/1997-05-03_designing a brochure_emphasize things_product unique_higher prices_stale technology_fewer feature.gif
title: Brochure Highlights: Everything Wrong With Product

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Designing a brochure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll want to emphasize the things that make our product unique.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Good good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see... We have higher prices... stale technology... fewer features... and it's hard to use.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you work with that?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Suddenly I don't feel so bad that we won't be using 100% recycled paper.

situation: Dilbert meets with a marketing colleague to plan a product brochure and says they should emphasize what makes the product unique. He then lists only the product's flaws: higher prices, stale technology, fewer features and poor usability. The marketer, unfazed, remarks that the list makes him feel better about not printing on recycled paper.
punchline: The product's only distinguishing traits are its drawbacks, so the marketer concludes the brochure is so hopeless that skimping on environmentally friendly paper hardly matters.
summary: Asked to spotlight what sets a product apart, an engineer can only name its shortcomings, and the marketer shrugs it off with a joke about paper.

file: 1997/1997-03-02_new ceo_tall caucasian male_no experince_necktie_resume_bizarre logic_never worked in industry.gif
title: CEO Chosen For Total Inexperience

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new CEO will be announced today, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rumor has it that they picked a tall Caucasian male with no experience in our industry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't wait to hear the bizarre logic behind this choice.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like your necktie. Is it new?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

transcript.speaker: New CEO
transcript.text: Our new CEO has never worked in our industry, but that's exactly what we were looking for...

transcript.speaker: New CEO
transcript.text: ...because we wanted a CEO who doesn't know what can't be done!

transcript.speaker: New CEO
transcript.text: Other hand... other hand.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He looks a bit overqualified.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I really took the wrong approach on my résumé.

setting: Dilbert's home in the morning, then a company meeting hall with a podium
situation: Dilbert gets dressed at home, predicting that the new CEO will be a tall white man with no industry experience, and he looks forward to hearing the absurd reasoning. At the announcement, the CEO's lack of experience is cheerfully spun as a virtue, and he awkwardly fumbles through a balanced speech. Dilbert and coworkers watch from the audience, impressed by how little it took to land the job.
punchline: The company treats total ignorance as a qualification, so Dilbert and his coworkers realize that real expertise and a strong résumé were the wrong way to get the top job.
summary: A clueless outsider is hired to run the company because he is too uninformed to know which goals are impossible, leaving the staff feeling that their own qualifications were a mistake.
keywords: doesn't know what can't be done

file: 1997/1997-04-10_box lower_intern is boss_new boss_new org chart_graphics.gif
title: Org Chart Reveals New Boss

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I notice that the new org chart has your box lower than before.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It means nothing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Perhaps. But your box seems smallish. And your reporting line brushes against my box.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It means nothing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, I'm sure this means I'm your new boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if I killed someone in a previous life.

situation: A coworker holding a printout of the new org chart points out that Dilbert's box has moved lower, looks smaller, and has a reporting line touching the coworker's own box. Dilbert twice insists it means nothing, but the coworker concludes he is now Dilbert's new boss. Dilbert privately wonders whether he is being punished for something from a past life.
punchline: Dilbert's denial collapses as the org chart makes it plain he now reports to this coworker, which he can only explain as cosmic punishment for a past-life crime.
summary: A colleague deciphers the reorganization chart and gleefully announces he now outranks a reluctant Dilbert, who blames karma.

file: 1997/1997-08-18_task force_recruit_smartest college seniors_lie often_real life experince_meetings_parties.gif
title: Recruiting Seniors With Orgy Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be on the task force to recruit the smartest college seniors to work here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember to lie often. And don't mock them for their lack of real life experience.

transcript.speaker: College Senior
transcript.text: So you're saying meetings are just like parties?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I'm not allowed to say the "O-word"...

setting: Office, then a conference room interview table
situation: The Boss puts Dilbert on a recruiting task force and instructs him to lie often to the smartest college seniors while not mocking their naivety. In the interview, a naive candidate asks whether meetings are like parties, and Dilbert, following orders to lie, can't bring himself to say the word that would truly answer the question.
punchline: Dilbert is forbidden from saying the 'O-word' (orgy), implying that meetings are nothing like parties, which highlights how recruiting relies on deceiving naive graduates.
summary: Told to deceive fresh graduates during recruiting, Dilbert awkwardly dodges a young candidate's hopeful comparison of meetings to parties.

file: 1997/1997-09-07_disconnect you_abrupt disconnect_please hold_wrong button_kevorkian disconnect_annoying message.gif
title: Dogbert Offers Ways to Disconnect

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert's technical support. How may I disconnect you?

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: What are my choices?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend the abrupt disconnect; simple, gets the job done.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I had that last time. What else do you have?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You might like our "please hold," followed by the "wrong button," disconnect.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Too predictable. Do you have anything new?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try our "Kevorkian disconnect." I put you on hold and play an annoying message until you disconnect yourself.

transcript.speaker: Recorded message
transcript.text: Your call is important. Please hold while we ignore it ... Your call is important ...

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Not bad.

setting: Dogbert's technical support call center desk
situation: Dogbert answers a tech support line by asking how he may disconnect the caller, then offers a menu of ways to get rid of them. The caller, who has apparently been through this before, rejects the abrupt disconnect and the predictable hold-then-wrong-button trick. Dogbert's newest option leaves the caller on hold with an irritating recorded message.
punchline: Dogbert treats tech support as the art of getting rid of customers rather than helping them, and the caller, a seasoned connoisseur of bad support, judges the insulting hold message as 'not bad'.
summary: A support line that exists to shed callers presents a menu of creative hang-up techniques, and the jaded customer critiques each one like a reviewer.

file: 1997/1997-07-05_dial number_known idiots_loser_donosaur_rat_telemarketers_idiots to call_calling people_phone tings.gif
title: Telemarketers Calling Known Idiots

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You two will be my telemarketers. Here's a list of known idiots to call.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I'll go first, Bob. Let's see... I dial the number. And wait for an idiot to answer...

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Ring ring ring

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: C'mon, you loser. Pick up the phone.

setting: Dogbert's telemarketing office, seated at a desk with phones
situation: Dogbert, acting as boss, assigns two employees to work as telemarketers and hands them a list of known idiots to call. The yellow, headset-wearing telemarketer dials and, while waiting for an answer, insults the person he is calling before they have even picked up.
punchline: The telemarketer has already decided the person he is calling is an idiot, and is impatient and insulting before they even answer, which reflects the contempt telemarketers have for their targets.
summary: A scheming dog puts two underlings on phone duty with a roster of marks, and one of them is rude to his target before the line even connects.

file: 1997/1997-08-16_recyclable_trash container_two containers.gif
title: Dilbert Questions Janitor's Single Trash Can

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I notice you only have one trash container with you...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whereas I have two containers — one for trash and one for recyclable materials.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One theory is that you make two separate trips to each cubicle...

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Could you turn around for a second?

situation: Dilbert walks through the cubicles carrying separate bins for trash and recyclables and confronts the janitor, who only pushes a single trash container. Dilbert theorizes that the janitor must make two trips to each cubicle. The janitor, unbothered, asks Dilbert to turn around.
punchline: The janitor implies he simply dumps the recyclables in with the trash, and asking Dilbert to turn around suggests he is about to do something unpleasant, like dumping the trash on Dilbert or kicking him.
summary: A conscientious employee lectures the cleaning worker about sorting waste, only to get a menacing request in response.

file: 1997/1997-08-22_ratbert_pager_vibrate_yeehaaa_no one paged_vibrating body.gif
title: Ratbert Loves the Vibrating Pager

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, I want you to wear this pager at all times. I'll set it to vibrate.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yeehaa!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No one has actually paged you yet.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It gets better?!!

setting: A room with a blue wall, a dresser with a lamp, and a carpeted floor
situation: Dogbert straps a pager onto Ratbert and sets it to vibrate. Ratbert shakes and squeals with delight, so Dogbert points out that nobody has paged him yet, meaning the vibration came from something else.
punchline: Ratbert is already thrilled by the pager's constant vibration, so learning that it will get even better when someone actually pages him is an unexpectedly funny escalation of his joy.
summary: A small creature is so delighted by the buzzing of a freshly strapped-on pager that he is stunned to learn the real fun has not even started.

file: 1997/1997-06-01_boss_umbrella_doaked_clothes microwave_dry off_tricked alice_boss naked_breakroom.gif
title: Boss Microwaved After Soggy Advice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I forgot my umbrella. I'm soaked.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why don't you toss your clothes in the microwave and dry them off?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would that work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sixty minutes ought to do it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We'll guard the door to the break room.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You know, ever since the downsizing began, I've felt much less company loyalty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why are you two so happy?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There are free goodies in the break room.

situation: The soaking-wet boss complains about forgetting his umbrella, and Wally suggests he dry his clothes in the microwave. The boss takes the advice and goes into the break room, where Dilbert and Wally guard the door for an hour while he is presumably cooking himself. Later they cheerfully tell Alice about the free goodies in the break room.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally knowingly send the boss to his death in the microwave, and their cheerfulness is explained by the free food left behind, a reaction to the downsizing that has eroded their loyalty.
summary: Two employees cheerfully talk their drenched boss into a deadly microwave drying scheme and then stand guard so no one interrupts.

file: 1997/1997-10-02_stupid people_insulted_formed mob_take abuse_survive_water_drink water_portesters_signs.gif
title: Mob Drinks Dogbert's Water Supply

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. All of the stupid people you've insulted have formed a mob and surrounded our house.

transcript.speaker: Protesters
transcript.text: We don't have to take this abuse. Let's see how long he can survive without water!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're taking turns putting our hose in their mouths. I think they're trying to drink all of our water.

setting: Inside Dilbert's house, looking out the window at a crowd of protesters
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that a mob of people he has insulted has surrounded the house. The protesters, holding signs reading 'Down with Dogbert', announce a plan to cut off the house's water. Dilbert then watches them take turns sticking the garden hose in their mouths and realizes they are drinking the water instead.
punchline: The mob's plan to deprive Dogbert of water by drinking all of it is hopelessly muddled, which confirms that the people he insulted really are stupid.
summary: A crowd of people insulted by Dogbert besiege the house with a plan so muddled that they try to starve him of water by drinking it from the hose.

file: 1997/1997-05-02_design product brochure_criminal fraud_marketing_not worng_conscience_marketing epople_business.gif
title: Marketing: Fraud With a Conscience Jar

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to work with our marketing people to design a product brochure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Groan.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Remember, what we do here might seem like criminal fraud but it's not. It's marketing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, as long as it's not wrong...

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Here's a jar to keep your conscience in. I'll put it in the closet with mine.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to work with the marketing department on a product brochure, and Dilbert groans inwardly. A marketing colleague warns him that their work may look like criminal fraud but is just marketing. When Dilbert says he'll help as long as it isn't wrong, the marketer hands him a jar for his conscience and says he'll store it in the closet alongside his own.
punchline: Marketing openly requires employees to set aside their ethics, and the closet is already full of the marketing staff's discarded consciences.
summary: A marketer cheerfully explains that deceptive-looking brochure work is fine and offers Dilbert a container in which to stash his scruples.

file: 1997/1997-09-12_presumed dead_like to work_finished three projects_lost five pounds_gave up coffee_seven patents_everyone prodcutive_life without mangement_paradise_spoon hug.gif
title: Paradise Without the Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now that our boss is presumed dead, I found out I like to work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished three projects today!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I lost five pounds, gave up coffee, and applied for seven patents!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Go, Alice!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Life without management is like paradise!

transcript.speaker: Woman in yellow hair
transcript.text: Who wants to spoon-hug?

situation: With the Boss presumed dead, the employees are thriving. Wally admits he actually likes to work, Dilbert finishes three projects in a day, and Alice reports weight loss, quitting coffee, and filing seven patents. In the last panel Wally calls it paradise and a coworker cheerfully offers spoon-hugs.
punchline: Without management around, everyone becomes happy, healthy and productive, implying the boss was the only thing holding the workplace back.
summary: Freed from a missing manager, the whole office blossoms into cheerful productivity and even affection.

file: 1997/1997-02-23_dread_staff meeting_describe accomplishments_amazing success_wally ville_ass fell asleep.gif
title: Wally's Sleeping Buns Meeting Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I dread this part of the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's go around the table and describe our accomplishments for the week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was another week of amazing success in Wallyville.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: On Monday I realized my left bun had fallen asleep.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was shocked. The "boys" had always worked as a team before.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thinking quickly, I shifted my weight to my right bun and hoped for the best.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's your left side, not your right.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's the other thing; apparently the boys switched sides sometime during the night.

setting: Conference room during a weekly staff meeting
situation: The Boss dreads the part of the staff meeting where everyone reports their weekly accomplishments. Wally, who is called on first, describes in elaborate detail how his left buttock fell asleep and how he coped by shifting his weight. Alice points out he has his sides mixed up, and Wally adds that his buttocks apparently swapped sides overnight.
punchline: Wally turns his weekly accomplishment report into a rambling, absurd tale about his sleeping buttock, showing he accomplished nothing of value while still presenting it as a success.
summary: Asked to report his weekly achievements, Wally instead narrates a ridiculous saga about a numb bottom and his confusion over left and right.

file: 1997/1997-08-07_analysts_got a raise_growth_lazy ones_open book management_smooth earnigs_stock market_money.gif
title: Smooth Earnings Justify Denied Raise

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Open Book Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So you see, if you got a raise, our earnings growth wouldn't be smooth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And smooth earnings are good for who?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stock market analysts?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Specifically, the lazy ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm fine, now that I understand.

situation: Under the banner of 'open book management,' the Boss explains to Dilbert that giving him a raise would make the company's earnings growth uneven. He asks who benefits from smooth earnings, and Dilbert guesses stock market analysts. The Boss adds that it's specifically the lazy ones, and Dilbert says he's fine with the decision now.
punchline: The Boss's 'transparent' explanation for denying a raise is that it would inconvenience lazy stock analysts, and Dilbert sarcastically claims to be satisfied with this absurd rationale.
summary: A boss justifies refusing a pay increase by arguing that steady quarterly numbers matter more, mainly to idle Wall Street analysts.

file: 1997/1997-06-09_applying critical thinking_children teaching_critical thinking_end of story_father_parenting_park bench_right and wrong_teach children_family.gif
title: Dogbert Questions Dogmatic Parenting

transcript.speaker: Man on bench
transcript.text: I teach my kids that these things are right and these things are wrong. Period. End of story.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that teach them to believe anything they're told without applying any critical thinking?

transcript.speaker: Man on bench
transcript.text: I don't think about that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Duh.

situation: A man sits on a park bench next to Dogbert and announces that he simply tells his kids what is right and wrong, with no discussion. Dogbert points out that this teaches children to accept whatever they are told without thinking critically. The man admits he doesn't think about that, and Dogbert replies with a one-word jab.
punchline: The man's admission that he doesn't think about the consequences of unquestioned teaching proves Dogbert's point, as he himself demonstrates a lack of critical thinking.
summary: A dogmatic father is gently skewered by a dog who notes that his rigid parenting style discourages independent thought, and the father unwittingly confirms it.

file: 1997/1997-12-17_company lawyer_secret military project_north elbonians_communits_guilty of treason_executed_pull a lever.gif
title: Lawyer Eager to Watch Dilbert's Execution

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The company lawyer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm working on a top secret military project. My boss hired some North Elbonians to help me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're communists. If I give them any information, I could be guilty of treason. I could be executed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you help?

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Sure. What would I have to do - pull a lever?

situation: Dilbert visits the company lawyer to explain that his boss has assigned North Elbonian communists to help on a top secret military project. He worries that sharing information with them could amount to treason and get him executed, and asks for help. The lawyer cheerfully asks what he would have to do, assuming his role is to carry out the execution.
punchline: The lawyer hears Dilbert's worry about being executed and offers to help by eagerly asking if he'd be the one pulling the lever, showing lawyers' stereotypical callousness.
summary: A worried engineer seeks legal protection from a treason charge, but the lawyer cheerfully volunteers to operate the execution lever instead.

file: 1997/1997-09-30_new personal crusade_hunt down people_strong opinions_bop them_everyone on earth.gif
title: Dogbert's Crusade Against Uninformed Opinions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have a new personal crusade.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to hunt down the people who have strong opinions on subjects they don't understand. Then I'll bop them with this cardboard tube.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would include everyone on Earth except you and me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lean over here.

situation: Dogbert, holding a cardboard tube, announces a new crusade to hunt down and bop people who hold strong opinions about subjects they don't understand. Dilbert points out that this would cover practically everyone on Earth except the two of them. Dogbert responds by asking Dilbert to lean over, implying he is about to be bopped.
punchline: Dogbert doesn't accept Dilbert's flattering exemption and tells him to lean closer, implying Dilbert himself has strong opinions on things he doesn't understand and gets the cardboard tube too.
summary: A self-appointed vigilante dog plans to whack every know-it-all with a cardboard tube, and his human companion's attempt to claim an exemption backfires.

file: 1997/1997-12-15_contract employees_evil totalitarian_military technology_north elbonia_project_regime_top secret.gif
title: Free Labor From Evil Regime

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I hired some contract employees from North Elbonia to help on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: North Elbonia is an evil totalitarian regime. My project will create top secret military technology to use against them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure, but you have to weigh that against the fact that they're willing to work for free.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has hired contract workers from North Elbonia to help on Dilbert's project. Dilbert objects that North Elbonia is an evil totalitarian regime and that his project is top secret military technology meant to be used against them. The Boss dismisses the concern, pointing out that they will work for free.
punchline: The Boss treats the cost savings of free labor as outweighing the obvious security and ethical problem of giving an enemy regime access to a secret military project.
summary: A manager staffs a classified weapons project with workers from the very enemy state it targets, because they cost nothing.

file: 1997/1997-07-03_benchmarking initiative_crying with joy_mother_phone call_asok_calls mother_family.gif
title: Mom Cries Over Benchmarking Title

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hi, Mom! Guess what.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm the process owner for our benchmarking initiative!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: She's crying with joy ...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I used to think that too.

situation: Asok phones his mother to proudly announce that he has been made process owner of the company's benchmarking initiative. As she cries on the line, he assumes it is happiness. A balding coworker holding a paper says he used to think that too, implying the mother's tears are really sorrow over a dead-end job.
punchline: The coworker's remark implies the mother is crying out of disappointment or pity, because the impressive-sounding title is actually a thankless, meaningless assignment.
summary: A young employee brags to his mother about a grand-sounding job title, and a weary colleague hints the tears are not what he thinks.

file: 1997/1997-09-03_dogbert_corporate emperor_downsizing_sounds negative_wedgiesizing_clean desk and shoo.gif
title: Wedgiesizing Instead of Downsizing

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Corporate Emperor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't like to call what I'm doing "downsizing." It sounds too negative.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like to call it "wedgiesizing." Now clean out your desk and shoo!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Yank!

transcript.speaker: Green dinosaur
transcript.text: He didn't take that very well.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't please everyone, Bob.

setting: Dogbert's office, where he sits atop a desk or computer as emperor
situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and holding a scepter, announces he dislikes the term "downsizing" because it sounds negative. His enforcer, the green dinosaur Bob, then gives a laid-off employee a violent wedgie while Dogbert tells him to clean out his desk. Afterward, Bob remarks that the employee didn't take it well, and Dogbert shrugs it off.
punchline: Dogbert replaces the euphemism "downsizing" with the literal and painful "wedgiesizing," mocking how management softens the language of layoffs while still treating employees cruelly.
summary: A crowned Dogbert rebrands his layoffs with a painfully literal new name, and his dinosaur henchman delivers it to the fired worker.

file: 1997/1997-07-26_article_boss_alice_highlighted_save time_page numbers_dont notice.gif
title: Boss Highlights Only Page Numbers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I found this article in a magazine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I highlighted the most important stuff to save you time.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You highlighted the page numbers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It takes forever if you don't notice those.

situation: The Boss hands Alice a magazine article, proudly saying he highlighted the most important parts to save her time. Alice looks it over and points out that the only thing he highlighted was the page numbers. The Boss responds that it takes forever if you don't notice that.
punchline: The Boss's claim to save time is absurd because his highlighting is useless, and he deflects with a nonsensical excuse that treats his own mistake as a pitfall for the reader.
summary: A manager proudly hands over a marked-up article, but the only thing he marked was the page numbers, and he blames the reader's attention for any wasted time.

file: 1997/1997-02-25_frazzled_meet deadlines_all day meeting off site_theroy_more time to explin.gif
title: All-Day Meeting About Deadline Importance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm totally frazzled. There simply isn't enough time in the day to meet my upcoming deadlines.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's have an all-day meeting off-site so I can explain why the deadlines are so important.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, your theory is that I'll have more time in the day if you explain something I already know?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have a lot of tools here.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he is overwhelmed and cannot fit his upcoming deadlines into the time available. The boss responds by scheduling an all-day off-site meeting to explain why the deadlines matter. Dilbert points out the flaw in this logic, and the boss admits he has no other solutions.
punchline: The boss's only remedy for a time shortage is a long meeting that consumes even more time, and he admits he has nothing else to offer.
summary: Faced with an employee who has too little time, a manager prescribes a full day of meetings and then concedes he is out of ideas.

file: 1997/1997-09-29_document marked proprietary_find anyone_gain experience_logical questions_insubordination.gif
title: Logical Questions Equal Insubordination

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have a question about this document marked "proprietary."

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: If I spent my entire life searching, do you think I could find ANYONE who would care about this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you gain experience, you'll realize that all logical questions are considered insubordination.

setting: Office cubicle area, then a conference room
situation: Asok, a young employee, holds a document stamped "proprietary" and sarcastically asks The Boss whether anyone anywhere could possibly care about it. In the final panel, at a meeting table, Dilbert gives the newcomer a world-weary piece of advice while Alice sits nearby.
punchline: Dilbert warns that in this company any sensible question gets treated as insubordination, so honest curiosity about pointless rules is punished.
summary: A junior employee mocks the pointless secrecy of a confidential document and is told by a veteran that sensible questioning is treated as defiance.

file: 1997/1997-08-15_ceo_telewedgie_relocating_compnay_phone behind_belt level_albeit.gif
title: Dinosaur Gives CEO a Telewedgie

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've asked Bob the Dinosaur to call your CEO and give him a telewedgie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will that stop him from relocating the company?

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: ...Now hold the phone behind you at belt level.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stranger things have happened, albeit not often.

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: Yank

transcript.speaker: CEO (on phone)
transcript.text: Aaiee!!

situation: Dogbert has enlisted Bob the Dinosaur to phone the CEO and deliver a 'telewedgie' as a way to stop him relocating the company. Dilbert doubts it will work, while Bob instructs the CEO to hold the phone behind himself at belt level and then yanks the cord. The CEO yelps in pain over the line.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd scheme to save the company is a long-distance wedgie over the phone, and his deadpan admission that stranger things have happened, though not often, shows how unlikely it is to succeed.
summary: A purple dinosaur pranks a distant executive by phone in a far-fetched plan to keep the firm from moving.

file: 1997/1997-10-11_ask for little_dilbert_empty cucbicle_gets little_gets what asks for.gif
title: Asking for Little, Getting Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I ask for so little.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: Dilbert sits alone in his empty cubicle.)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And boy do I get it.

situation: Dilbert sits alone in his cubicle, thinking to himself that he asks for very little from his job. After a silent beat staring at nothing, he concludes that he receives exactly that: very little in return.
punchline: Dilbert's modest expectations are met with equally meager rewards, a wry, deadpan acknowledgment that his job gives him almost nothing.
summary: A lone engineer muses that his demands are minimal, then glumly admits the workplace delivers precisely that minimal amount.

file: 1997/1997-02-03_every department_create web page_internal network_include enough info_security precaution.gif
title: Intranet Pages Too Dull to Read

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every department is required to create a web page for our internal network.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It should include enough information to be difficult to maintain, but not so much that it's useful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As a security precaution, we'll make it too dull and unorganized to read.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is pornography in or out?

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss tells the assembled team that every department must build a page for the internal network. He specifies that the pages should be burdensome to maintain yet not actually useful, and deliberately dull and disorganized as a 'security precaution'. A coworker then asks whether pornography should be included.
punchline: The Boss's absurd requirements make the intranet deliberately useless, and the coworker's deadpan question about pornography shows that the only content anyone would actually want to read is the forbidden kind.
summary: A manager orders pointless, deliberately unreadable intranet pages for every department, and a meeting attendee asks a cheeky question about inappropriate content.

file: 1997/1997-04-09_new org chart_graphical lay out_mentor.gif
title: Org Chart Ranking Is Just Layout

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The new org chart has my name lower than yours, but it doesn't mean anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See? It wouldn't all fit across the page. It's just a graphical layout thing, that's all.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hey, Dil-Boy, put a head on this and fetch my mail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: Are you asking me to be your mentor?

situation: Dilbert shows a bald, bespectacled coworker the new org chart, which places Dilbert's name below the coworker's, and insists the placement is only a page-layout quirk. Then Carol, with her huge hair, arrives and orders 'Dil-Boy' to fetch her mail. The coworker sitting at his desk asks whether she wants him to be her mentor.
punchline: Dilbert's reassurance that his lower position on the org chart means nothing is contradicted when he is immediately treated as a subordinate and ordered to fetch mail.
summary: A man brushes off his lower spot on the new org chart as mere formatting, only to be sent on a mail errand by a superior.

file: 1997/1997-12-19_project_little snag_north elbonian contractor_military technology_belligerent homelenad_huge laser_vaporize_contract employees_building workshop.gif
title: Contractors Build Laser, Boss Blames Workshop

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My project has hit a little snag.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our North Elbonian contractors stole our military technology for their belligerent homeland. They're building a huge laser to vaporize us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next year, remind me to include contract employees in the team-building workshop.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The floor is warm!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss admits his project has a little snag, then reveals that the North Elbonian contractors stole military technology and are building a giant laser to vaporize the company. His only proposed fix is to include contractors in next year's team-building workshop. Alice notices the floor is warming up, hinting that the laser is already powering up beneath them.
punchline: The Boss casually downplays a catastrophic security disaster as a 'snag' and thinks team-building would have prevented it, while the floor heating up shows the laser is about to destroy them.
summary: A manager shrugs off the news that outsourced foreign workers are about to incinerate the office, suggesting a bonding exercise as the lesson learned.

file: 1997/1997-03-07_boss_coincidence_fallen under spell_morons_must_pay inexperienced strangers.gif
title: Boss Hypnotized by Consultant Spell

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our boss has fallen under the spell of a consultant.

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Must... make assumptions.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Must... write... large checks to consultant... because... employees... are... morons.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Just because we pay inexperienced strangers to tell us how to do our jobs, that doesn't mean we're morons!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah! It's a coincidence.

setting: Office, hallway or break area with coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert and Wally watch the Boss shuffle along in a trance, mumbling that he must write big checks to a consultant because employees are morons. Wally indignantly insists that paying inexperienced outsiders to tell them how to do their jobs doesn't make them morons, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: Their loud insistence that it's all a coincidence shows they are indeed being treated as morons, since the company pays outsiders to do what they could do themselves.
summary: Two employees complain that their zombie-like manager is handing money to an outside expert, then sarcastically protest that their own incompetence has nothing to do with it.

file: 1997/1997-09-24_stock holder meeting_wake up_certification_jokes_tech jokes.gif
title: Boss's Dull ISO Joke Material

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of getting ISO 14000 certification.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the difference between that and ISO 9000?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, about 6000. Ha ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, I think I'll use that one at the stockholder meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, that'll wake them up.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to obtain ISO 14000 certification. When Dilbert asks how it differs from ISO 9000, the Boss gives a weak arithmetic pun and laughs heartily at it. He then decides to use the joke at the stockholder meeting, and Dilbert sarcastically agrees.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically says the Boss's lame, nerdy standards-number joke will 'wake up' the stockholders, implying it is so boring it would put them to sleep.
summary: A manager proudly delivers a dreadful pun about quality standards and plans to repeat it to investors, while his employee dryly mocks it.

file: 1997/1997-02-10_bullet point_monthly accomplishments_leveraged synergy_technology platforms.gif
title: Wally's Synergy Is a Journey

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a bullet point for your monthly accomplishments, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Put me down for, "Leveraged synergy across all technology platforms."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was your accomplishment last month.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's more of a journey than a destination.

situation: Dilbert, holding a notepad, asks Wally for a bullet point summarizing his monthly accomplishments. Wally offers a buzzword-laden phrase about leveraged synergy, and Dilbert points out it is the same accomplishment he reported last month. Wally deflects by calling it an ongoing journey.
punchline: Wally reuses the same meaningless buzzword accomplishment every month and, when caught, excuses it with a vague motivational cliché so he never has to actually do anything new.
summary: Wally pads his progress report with empty jargon he already used before, then dodges accountability by dressing up his inaction as a never-ending journey.

file: 1997/1997-07-19_famous person_sandra bullock_kevin spacey_eats bacon_kevin who eats bacon_one degree away_close to fascinating.gif
title: Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon-Eating

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Give me the name of any famous person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sandra Bullock.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Sandra Bullock was in a movie with Kevin Spacey... and Kevin Spacey eats bacon.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: See that? Everyone on Earth is only one degree away from someone named Kevin who eats bacon!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is so close to being fascinating.

situation: Ratbert asks Dilbert to name any famous person, then links Sandra Bullock to Kevin Spacey and finally to the fact that Spacey eats bacon. He proudly announces that everyone is one degree from a Kevin who eats bacon, and Dilbert dryly responds.
punchline: Ratbert's absurd, trivial 'discovery' parodies the Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon game, and Dilbert sarcastically says it falls just short of being fascinating.
summary: Ratbert plays a mangled version of the Kevin Bacon trivia game and is proud of a connection that is utterly pointless.

file: 1997/1997-04-08_alice and wallys_box lower_every year_new org chart_rearrange layout_secretaries day card_same one.gif
title: Org Chart Box Placement Suspicion

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Here's the new org chart. I had to rearrange the layout to make it fit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is my box lower than Alice and Wally's?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It means nothing... nothing at all.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, who told you that every year I fish your secretaries' day card out of your trash and save it for next time?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What?

situation: Carol, the boss's secretary, hands him the new org chart. He notices his box is drawn lower than Alice and Wally's and demands to know why. After she says it means nothing, he paranoidly accuses her of knowing his secret habit of recycling her Secretaries' Day card.
punchline: The boss assumes her nervous-sounding reassurance is a veiled dig, and in defending his ego he accidentally confesses that he reuses the same Secretaries' Day card every year.
summary: A boss fixated on his place in the org chart blurts out an embarrassing confession about his cheap gift habits.

file: 1997/1997-01-12_buying car_touch negotiator_suggested retail price_invisible spary_scurvy_tax audits_airbag_gravel_lease terms_engraved_hood ornamnet.gif
title: Tough Negotiator Buys Overpriced Add-Ons

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Buying a car

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: You're one tough negotiator.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: It only took you four hours to get me all the way down to the manufacturer's suggested retail price.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: There's no profit left!! My family will go hungry!! Bwaa! Bwaa!

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: Sorry. I assume you want the rust inhibitor coating for only $500.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Yeah. Rust is bad.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: Yes!! Ka-ching. Ka-ching.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: Sorry. We also have an invisible spray that protects against scurvy and tax audits.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... okay.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: Initial here if you want your airbag to be full of fresh aspen air instead of gravel.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: Only $600.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: And the lease terms are engraved on this free hood ornament!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Be glad they didn't install it.

situation: Dilbert proudly haggles a car salesman down to the manufacturer's suggested retail price over four hours. The salesman fakes despair, then happily sells him a series of absurd, overpriced add-ons like rust coating, an invisible spray against scurvy and tax audits, and a gravel-free airbag. Dilbert goes along with each one, and Dogbert ends with a quip about the hood ornament.
punchline: Dilbert thinks he won the negotiation, but the salesman recoups all the profit and more by upselling ridiculous extras that Dilbert agrees to without resistance.
summary: After a long haggle that he believes he won, a car buyer gets fleeced by a salesman peddling nonsense add-ons at inflated prices.

file: 1997/1997-07-07_title of book_gives away plaot_hemingway_imagination_chick magnet.gif
title: Dogbert Declines to Catch Frisbee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate it when the title of a book gives away the whole plot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Take Hemingway's "Old Man and the Sea." Geez, talk about leaving nothing to the imagination.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess the odds were very low that you would leap in the air and catch that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm only here to be a chick magnet.

situation: Dilbert walks across a lawn carrying a frisbee while complaining to Dogbert that book titles give away the plot, using Hemingway's Old Man and the Sea as an example. He throws the frisbee absent-mindedly, and it sails past Dogbert and lands in the grass. Dilbert wryly remarks on the low odds of Dogbert catching it, and Dogbert says he's there only to attract women.
punchline: Dilbert's literary rant turns out to be a setup for his dog to ignore the frisbee, with Dogbert openly admitting his role is merely decorative, a chick magnet rather than a frisbee-catching pet.
summary: While grumbling about spoiler-heavy book titles, Dilbert tosses a frisbee that his dog cheerfully refuses to fetch, claiming his only job is to attract admirers.

file: 1997/1997-12-01_interns_imprtant_mink coat_good eatin_analogy police.gif
title: Interns Are Like Minks, Boss Says

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, at this company, we think our interns are as important as minks to a mink coat.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Um... minks do not enjoy any of the benefits of the mink coat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they're good eatin', too!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I must report you to the analogy police.

situation: The Boss tells intern Asok that interns are as important to the company as minks are to a mink coat. Asok points out that minks get no benefits from the coat, and the Boss cheerfully doubles down by adding that minks are good to eat. Asok responds that he must report the Boss to the analogy police.
punchline: The Boss's analogy accidentally reveals that interns are exploited and expendable, and he makes it worse by saying they are good eating, prompting Asok's deadpan 'analogy police' remark.
summary: A manager's attempt to flatter an intern with a fur-based comparison backfires when the intern notes the flaw and the manager makes it even more sinister.

file: 1997/1997-02-18_all grown up_intern_unanswerable_whiny_decison.gif
title: Intern Masters Whiny Meeting Opener

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I'd like to start the meeting with a whiny, unanswerable question.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Why can't anyone make a decision around here?!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: That was good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My little intern is all grown up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sniff

situation: A young intern announces he will open the meeting with a whiny, unanswerable question, then complains that nobody can make a decision. A coworker with big hair compliments the performance, while Dilbert proudly sniffles that his intern has grown up.
punchline: Dilbert is touchingly proud that the intern has learned the classic corporate skill of complaining about indecision, treating a whiny rant as a professional milestone.
summary: A junior employee proves he has absorbed office culture by delivering a perfect complaint, and his mentor tears up with pride.

file: 1997/1997-11-28_authentic baby_week old_explain absence_mickey rooney.gif
title: Authentic Baby Doesn't Excuse Absence

transcript.speaker: Off-panel employee
transcript.text: This is an authentic baby, less than one week old.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel employee
transcript.text: As I feed this authentic baby in front of you, recall how big my stomach was last week.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel employee
transcript.text: So, do I still need a note from my doctor to explain my absence?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, unless you can prove where Mickey Rooney is right now.

situation: An employee, seen only as an arm holding a swaddled newborn, presents the baby to the Boss as proof she just gave birth and was absent for that reason. She even feeds the baby while reminding him how large her stomach was the week before. She asks if she still needs a doctor's note, and the Boss insists she does.
punchline: The Boss is so suspicious and bureaucratic that even a newborn baby isn't sufficient evidence for an absence, comparing it to being unable to prove where Mickey Rooney is, implying the baby could be anyone's or a fake.
summary: A new mother brings her newborn to work as undeniable evidence for her absence, yet her skeptical boss still demands official paperwork.

file: 1997/1997-11-24_cable guy_electrician_hole in wall_install_installer_phone line_wire.gif
title: Twenty Minutes Unless Something Unexpected Happens

transcript.speaker: Installer
transcript.text: I'm here to install your ISDN phone line.

transcript.speaker: Installer
transcript.text: This will only take twenty minutes... unless something unexpected happens.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great, because I need it tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Installer
transcript.text: Uh-oh... your wire goes into a little hole in the wall.

setting: Dilbert's home doorway and interior, with the installer's van parked outside
situation: A telephone installer arrives at Dilbert's door to put in an ISDN line and promises it will take only twenty minutes, with a caveat about unexpected problems. When Dilbert says he needs it done by tomorrow, the installer immediately discovers a complication: the wire disappears into a small hole in the wall.
punchline: The installer's cautious estimate is instantly undermined, as the 'unexpected' problem is simply the wire going into a hole in the wall, which is an utterly ordinary part of any installation, implying he is clueless or stalling.
summary: A phone technician hedges his time estimate, then treats a perfectly normal wall hole as a baffling complication the moment the customer mentions a deadline.

file: 1997/1997-11-01_manger training_comment_contain nonsense_implementation.gif
title: Manager Training in Meaningless Buzzwords

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Manager training

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: You will often be asked to comment on things you don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: These handouts contain nonsense phrases that can be used in any situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... So, let's dominate our industry... with quality implementation of methodologies.

transcript.speaker: Man in green tie
transcript.text: I'll get right on it.

setting: Corporate training room and a conference room
situation: A trainer teaches new managers that they will often have to comment on things they don't understand, and hands out sheets of generic nonsense phrases usable in any situation. In the final panel, the boss recites one of these phrases in a meeting, and an employee solemnly agrees to act on it.
punchline: The boss's empty buzzword sentence means nothing, yet the employee takes it seriously and promises to get right on it, showing how management jargon passes for substance.
summary: Newly minted managers are given cheat sheets of meaningless jargon, and a boss promptly uses one to inspire a gullible subordinate.
keywords: comment on things you don't understand

file: 1997/1997-07-23_catbert_evil hr director_abuse people_reduce turnover_job titles_convicted felon.gif
title: Catbert Changes Everyone's Job Title

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can't abuse people if they quit the company. I'd better find a way to reduce turnover.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All job titles will be changed as follows...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My new title is... "Convicted felon."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That'll look good on the ol' résumé.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, then an employee's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, worries that employees who quit can no longer be abused, so he decides to reduce turnover. He announces a company-wide change of job titles, and Wally learns his new title is "Convicted Felon" while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: Catbert keeps people from leaving by giving them job titles so damaging that no other employer would hire them, and Dilbert sarcastically notes how good it will look on a résumé.
summary: A malicious personnel chief makes sure his victims can never leave by saddling them with career-ruining official titles.

file: 1997/1997-12-22_illogical scientist_much smarter_scientists_invented things_don't understand sceince.gif
title: The Illogical Scientist's Flawed Argument

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Hi. I'm Dan the Illogical Scientist.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: I'm much smarter than you because scientists have invented many things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But those are other scientists, not you.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Apparently you don't understand science.

situation: A mustached scientist named Dan walks up to Dilbert at his desk and introduces himself as the illogical scientist. He claims he is smarter than Dilbert because scientists have invented many things. When Dilbert points out that those inventions were made by other scientists, Dan dismisses him by saying he doesn't understand science.
punchline: Dan's argument is a fallacy of borrowed credit, and when Dilbert rightly points this out, Dan responds with a circular insult that proves he really is illogical.
summary: A self-declared illogical scientist boasts of superiority by claiming other people's achievements, then brushes off the obvious objection by insulting his critic.

file: 1997/1997-12-04_phil_ruler of heck_pitchspoon_minor sins_merging company_non alcoholic beer_synergy_bad pun.gif
title: Devil Ousted After Merging with Non-Alcoholic Beer

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I used to be Phil, the ruler of Heck. My pitchspoon was feared by all who committed minor sins.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Then I made the mistake of merging with a company that makes non-alcoholic beer.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I was ousted.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: They said we'd have synergy!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it was just a bad pun.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, with Phil in a red devil costume
situation: Phil, dressed as a devil and holding an oversized pitchspoon, explains to Dilbert that he once ruled Heck, feared for punishing minor sins. He then merged with a company that makes non-alcoholic beer and was ousted. Phil angrily complains that the merger was promised to bring synergy.
punchline: Phil's merger partner makes non-alcoholic beer, a watered-down product that fits the 'Heck' pun, and Dilbert deadpans that the promised 'synergy' was just a bad pun.
summary: A demoted devil blames a disastrous merger with a near-beer maker for losing his throne, while a coworker suggests the whole deal was a wordplay gone wrong.

file: 1997/1997-02-24_promise the customer_build in month_timing probelm_shifting blame_engineering_spending huge bonus_blame transfer.gif
title: Sales Guy Plans Blame Transfer

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I had to promise the customer we could build the thing in a month even though you said it was impossible.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I'll solve the timing problem by shifting blame to engineering while spending the huge bonus I got for the sale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your planning has improved.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Beginning blame transfer now...

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Rrr

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Rrr

situation: A salesman tells Dilbert and the engineers he promised a customer an impossible one-month delivery. He announces his plan to blame engineering for the delay while he spends his large sales bonus. Dilbert dryly notes his planning has improved as the salesman starts the blame transfer and the engineers growl in anger.
punchline: The salesman's 'planning' consists of collecting the bonus for an impossible promise and then pinning the inevitable failure on engineering, and Dilbert sarcastically praises it.
summary: A salesman cheerfully lays out how he will pocket a bonus for an impossible promise and then dump the fallout on the engineers.

file: 1997/1997-06-10_biggest prospect_brain overload_kenny sales weasel_tech specs_uses electricity_car.gif
title: Salesweasel Can't Handle Technical Specs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you'll work with "Kenny the Salesweasel" on our biggest prospect.

transcript.speaker: Kenny
transcript.text: Tell me all of our product's technical specs on the way. I like to be prepared.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our product is beige. It uses electricity.

transcript.speaker: Kenny
transcript.text: Whoa! Brain overload!

setting: Office, then inside a red car on the way to a client
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a salesman named Kenny, who will pitch the company's biggest prospect with him. Kenny asks Dilbert to brief him on the product's technical specs during the car ride so he can be prepared. Dilbert gives the barest description, and Kenny claims it is already too much to take in.
punchline: The salesman who insists on being prepared is so uninterested in technical detail that even the most trivial specs overwhelm him, suggesting he will sell a product he doesn't understand.
summary: A sales rep who demands a technical briefing before a big client visit is overwhelmed by the two simplest facts about the product.

file: 1997/1997-03-13_excellent negotiator_insulted_need help_negotiator_relentlessly irrational_too logical_telecommuting.gif
title: Hiring an Irrational Negotiator

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your help to negotiate with my boss for more telecommuting days.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm too logical to be a good negotiator. You need someone who is relentlessly irrational.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert says you're an excellent negotiator, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm insulted!!

setting: Dilbert's office, with Dogbert on a filing cabinet
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert to help him negotiate with his boss for more telecommuting days. Dogbert declines because he is too logical and says Dilbert needs someone relentlessly irrational. Dilbert then approaches Ratbert, telling him Dogbert called him an excellent negotiator, and Ratbert takes offense.
punchline: Dogbert's recommendation of Ratbert as the ideal negotiator is really a statement that Ratbert is relentlessly irrational, which Ratbert correctly interprets as an insult.
summary: Dogbert passes on a negotiating job because rationality is a handicap, so Dilbert turns to Ratbert, who is offended to learn why he was chosen.

file: 1997/1997-12-09_coached well_date_date analyzer_cubicle fibers_office job.gif
title: Grunting Through a Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grunt grunt. You're absolutely right. Grunt grunt grunt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grunt grunt grunt

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Someone coached you well for this date. You haven't said anything I object to yet.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I see cubicle fibers...you have an office job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grunt

setting: A doorway at the start of a date, then a lab with a Date-Alyzer machine
situation: Dilbert arrives for a date and responds to everything with agreeable grunts, apparently coached to say nothing objectionable. His date notices he has been coached, then uses a machine called the Date-Alyzer, which has Dilbert bent over its base, to analyze him and deduce from cubicle fibers that he has an office job.
punchline: Dilbert's only way to avoid saying anything offensive is to grunt, and his date's high-tech scrutiny still instantly pegs him as a cubicle-bound office drone.
summary: A man who has been coached to stay agreeable on a date can only grunt, and a gadget analyzing him reveals his dull office job anyway.

file: 1997/1997-03-25_avoid boss_proved worng_boss disequilibrium_photocopies_proofread.gif
title: Boss Disequilibrium After Being Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Avoid the Pointy-Haired Boss today. I proved him wrong about something.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, terrific. Now he's in a state of boss disequilibrium until he proves he's right about something.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They're photocopies! You don't need to proofread each one!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll see about that.

setting: Office cubicles and a conference room or desk
situation: Dilbert warns Alice to avoid the Boss because Dilbert proved him wrong about something. Alice reacts with dismay, explaining the Boss will now be unsettled until he can prove himself right about anything. In the last panel a coworker protests that photocopies don't need proofreading, while the Boss stubbornly insists on doing it anyway.
punchline: The Boss needs a win so badly after being proven wrong that he insists on pointless, wasteful proofreading of photocopies just to feel right about something.
summary: After being corrected, the boss desperately hunts for any chance to be right, even by insisting on checking copies of documents.

file: 1997/1997-05-20_stupid_ignorant_being narrow minded.gif
title: Stupid, Ignorant, or Both

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was trying to decide if you're stupid or just very ignorant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I thought, "Whoa, Dogbert, you're being narrow-minded about this."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could easily be both.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It only looks easy.

situation: Dogbert sits on the floor next to Dilbert's desk while Dilbert works at his computer. Dogbert muses aloud about whether Dilbert is stupid or merely very ignorant, then corrects himself for being narrow-minded and concludes Dilbert could be both. Dilbert, still facing his monitor, retorts that it only looks easy.
punchline: Dogbert pretends to be open-minded by widening his insult to cover both stupidity and ignorance, and Dilbert's reply turns it back on him by implying being both takes real effort.
summary: Dogbert politely expands his insult of Dilbert from one flaw to two, and Dilbert fires back that such a feat is harder than it appears.

file: 1997/1997-01-05_input_fist of death_corporate culture_find cause_caused by managers_culture problem.gif
title: Boss Blames Mailroom Guy for Culture

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'd like your input on something.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh... my intuition is activating the Fist of Death.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our corporate culture is bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm trying to find the cause.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, obviously the problem isn't caused by managers who have no self-awareness... so what could it be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The culture problem must be coming from the other direction. Some employee must be causing this problem!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think it's the guy in the mail room. His bad culture is infecting the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: Mailroom Guy
transcript.text: If this is about that conference room full of mail, I don't know how it got there.

setting: The Boss's office, then the mail room
situation: The Boss asks Alice for input on why the corporate culture is bad. Alice sarcastically points out that it surely isn't self-unaware managers, and the Boss concludes that the real problem must be an employee, settling on the mailroom guy. The mailroom worker, sorting mail, nervously denies knowing how a conference room got filled with mail.
punchline: The oblivious Boss pins the company's bad culture on the lowest-level employee, who coincidentally seems guilty of something else entirely.
summary: A clueless manager hunts for the source of toxic workplace culture and decides a mailroom clerk must be the infectious culprit.

file: 1997/1997-06-05_dogbert_bearer_bad news_doctor_six months to live_nose job_mix up_hospital_medical.gif
title: Dogbert Delivers Wrong Medical News

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Professional bearer of bad news

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your doctor asked me to tell you that you have six months to live.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: There must be a mistake. I'm here for a nose job.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, you're right... I wondered why that last guy was so happy when I told him he'd have one huge nostril for the next forty years.

situation: Dogbert, working as a professional bearer of bad news, tells a hospital patient that his doctor says he has six months to live. The patient protests that he is only there for a nose job. Dogbert realizes he has mixed up his patients and had given the previous man the wrong news about his nose.
