punchline: Dogbert casually admits he gave the previous patient the nose-surgery disaster news, and that man's happiness at hearing it shows the bad news was delivered to the wrong people.
summary: A hired messenger of grim tidings mixes up two patients, telling a man with a minor procedure that he is dying while a dying man was told something trivial.

file: 1997/1997-04-25_business plan_disarray_free time_deliverables_joy_perverse sources_alternative.gif
title: Joy From Business Plan Disarray

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good news! Our business plan is in complete disarray!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Free time!! No deliverables!!! And it's not our fault!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yippee!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you realize that all our joy comes from perverse sources?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't know there was an alternative.

situation: Wally pops around a cubicle wall to announce that the company's business plan has collapsed. He and Dilbert celebrate because it means free time, no deliverables, and no blame. Dilbert then observes that all their joy comes from perverse sources, and Wally says he never knew any other kind existed.
punchline: Wally's deadpan reply reveals that he has never experienced happiness from anything other than the company's misfortune, highlighting how miserable the work environment is.
summary: Two cubicle workers cheer the collapse of their company's plans because it frees them from work, then realize that dysfunction is their only source of happiness.

file: 1997/1997-05-08_flashback_practical joke_college kid_bushel of money_photographers.gif
title: Dogbert Invents Web Browser as Prank

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flashback: Dogbert and the world's smartest garbageman invent the first web browser as a practical joke.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's out of control.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wonder what will happen to that college kid we framed.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: He'll be okay.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: Where would you like this bushel of money?

transcript.speaker: Young Billionaire
transcript.text: Stack it next to the photographers.

setting: A flashback scene by a garbage can, then a wealthy man's grooming session
situation: In a flashback, Dogbert and the world's smartest garbageman realize that the web browser they created as a practical joke has grown out of control. They wonder what happened to the college kid they framed for it. The final panel shows that kid, now fabulously rich, being groomed by a stylist while an assistant carries in a bushel of money and photographers wait nearby.
punchline: The college kid they framed as a prank became a wildly wealthy celebrity thanks to the web browser, so being framed turned out to be the best thing that ever happened to him.
summary: Two pranksters who accidentally unleashed the internet learn that their scapegoat has become a pampered, money-drowned star.

file: 1997/1997-03-06_rather the consultant_consulting spell_overly complicated_matices_diagrams_intellectual superirority.gif
title: Ratbert's Consulting Spell Controls Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I am under your consulting spell.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your overly complicated matrices and diagrams have convinced me of your intellectual superiority.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I am afraid to act without your approval.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Did I say you could put your arms up like that?

setting: The Boss's office, with Ratbert standing on the desk
situation: The Boss, arms stretched out in front of him like a hypnotized zombie, announces that he is under Ratbert's consulting spell. He explains that Ratbert's complicated matrices and diagrams have convinced him of the consultant's superiority, so he is afraid to act without approval. Ratbert then scolds him for raising his arms without permission.
punchline: The Boss is so awed by the consultant's jargon and diagrams that he literally behaves like a mind-controlled puppet, needing permission for even the smallest movement.
summary: A manager entranced by a tiny consultant's baffling charts becomes so dependent on his approval that he needs permission to move his own arms.

file: 1997/1997-01-06_advertisement_elbonia_grainy photos_pig_mail order bride_animals.gif
title: Elbonian Mail-Order Bride Surprise

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've decided to end my loneliness by getting a mail-order bride from Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The photos were grainy, but the advertisement guarantees that she's cute.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Blonde.

setting: Office cubicles, then a muddy village in Elbonia
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker tells Dilbert he plans to end his loneliness by ordering a bride from Elbonia, assuring him she must be cute despite the grainy photos. In Elbonia, a man in a tall dark hat checks a box of wigs and says 'Blonde' while another Elbonian holds a yellow wig up to a pig dressed in a frilly outfit.
punchline: The 'cute' mail-order bride is actually a pig in a blonde wig, so the grainy photos and the guarantee were a scam.
summary: A lonely man confidently orders an Elbonian bride from a blurry ad, unaware that the Elbonians are about to pass off a wigged pig as his sweetheart.

file: 1997/1997-12-06_career counseling_job involving sin_bingo field_budget work_no marketing_no auditing_no garnet manuafacturing.gif
title: Career Counseling for a Devil

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Career counseling

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: I'd be good at any job involving sin.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Perhaps something in the bingo field... or maybe budget work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about marketing?

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: I HAVE a soul. It's just a small one.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gotcha. No marketing... no auditing... no garment manufacturing.

situation: A man dressed as a devil tells Dogbert, his career counselor, that he would excel at any job involving sin. Dogbert suggests marketing, but the devil objects that he does have a soul, just a small one. Dogbert concludes that he must also be excluded from auditing and garment manufacturing.
punchline: Dogbert implies that marketing, auditing and garment manufacturing are such morally corrupt professions that even a devil with a small soul is too decent to work in them.
summary: A devil seeking career advice is steered away from several professions that apparently demand even less conscience than he has.

file: 1997/1997-04-07_good perfromance_deal with ambiguity_indecisive leadership_flexible_not indecisive.gif
title: Blamed for Boss's Indecisive Leadership

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, your performance is good, but you must learn to deal with ambiguity.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did I just get blamed for your indecisive leadership?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not indecisive; I'm flexible.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That would explain how your head got where it is.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Alice during a review that her performance is good but she needs to cope better with ambiguity. Alice realizes he is really blaming her for his own indecisiveness. When he claims he is merely flexible, she retorts with an insult implying his head is lodged somewhere unpleasant.
punchline: Alice sarcastically suggests the Boss is so 'flexible' that he has contorted himself enough to get his head stuck in his own rear end.
summary: A manager's complaint about an employee's trouble with ambiguity gets turned back on him when she calls out his wishy-washy leadership and mocks his claimed flexibility.

file: 1997/1997-09-11_boss plane crash_leave early_mixed feelings_plane crash_want cake_mourn_celebrate.gif
title: Boss's Plane Crash Prompts Cake

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I just heard that our Pointy-Haired Boss's plane crashed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I must admit I have mixed feelings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't know if you should mourn or celebrate, right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I mean celebrate or leave early.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hurry if you want some cake.

situation: Carol announces to the meeting that the Pointy-Haired Boss's plane has crashed. Wally admits to mixed feelings, and Dilbert guesses he is torn between mourning and celebrating. Wally clarifies that his dilemma is only whether to celebrate or leave early, and a coworker in a party hat invites them to hurry for cake.
punchline: Nobody mourns the boss's apparent death; the only question is whether to celebrate with cake or just take the afternoon off.
summary: News of the boss's plane going down is met with party hats and dessert instead of grief.

file: 1997/1997-09-20_dinosaurs_downsized_fate_vote by email_jimmy carter_monitor voting.gif
title: Dinosaurs Face Downsizing Reader Vote

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Should the dinosaurs be downsized? You decide their fate.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vote by e-mail: dinosaurs@unitedmedia.com

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A. I love the dinosaurs!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: B. Stick to office jokes!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: C. No talking animals!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: D. I don't have any opinions but I like to vote!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: E. Get rid of everyone so I can use the blank space for notes.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There's a Jimmy Carter here to monitor the voting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

setting: Dogbert's desk, with a reader-poll panel in between
situation: Dogbert, sitting at his desk, announces that readers can decide by e-mail whether the strip's dinosaur characters should be downsized. The middle panel lists the voting options, with a final joke option to get rid of everyone. Catbert then announces that a Jimmy Carter has arrived to monitor the voting, which makes Dogbert nervous.
punchline: Having an election monitor like Jimmy Carter, famous for overseeing elections in troubled countries, implies the vote is suspected of being rigged, which is why Dogbert says uh-oh.
summary: A cartoon reader poll on the fate of some dinosaur characters turns suspicious when an international election observer shows up to supervise it.

file: 1997/1997-07-04_dogbert_lord_master_worthless cretin_telemarketing_voice mail.gif
title: Dogbert Telemarketing His Own Master

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Beep beep boop beep

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am Dogbert, your lord and master! Submit to my will, you worthless cretin!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does telemarketing work for that sort of thing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll know tomorrow; that was your voice mail.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch dialing a phone, then delivers a domineering pitch demanding submission from whoever answers. He asks whether telemarketing works for this kind of request, and Dilbert, sitting beside him, points out that the call went to Dogbert's own voice mail.
punchline: Dogbert's world-domination telemarketing scheme starts with him unwittingly calling his own voice mail, so the only person he has tried to command is himself.
summary: A would-be tyrant phones in his demand for obedience and realizes too late that nobody was listening but his own answering machine.

file: 1997/1997-06-02_guiding prciples_network architecture_obvious ideas_techno jargon_unclear writing_suspenders_muddles thinking.gif
title: Network Architecture Principles Meet Suspenders Insult

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: I put together some guiding principles for our network architecture.

transcript.speaker: Woman with Big Red Hair
transcript.text: I sure hope this isn't a bunch of obvious ideas disguised with techno-jargon and unclear writing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let the games begin.

transcript.speaker: Woman with Big Red Hair
transcript.text: So tell me, do suspenders cause muddled thinking, or is it the other way around?

situation: A bearded engineer in suspenders hands out a paper of guiding principles for the company's network architecture. A large-haired woman at the table says she hopes it isn't obvious ideas dressed up in jargon and poor writing, and Dilbert, watching from the table, announces that the games are starting. She then insults the author by asking whether suspenders cause muddled thinking.
punchline: A meeting that begins with professional critique of the document turns into a petty personal jab at the author's clothing, and Dilbert knows to expect the sniping.
summary: A technical presentation turns into a spat when a colleague mocks the author's document and then his suspenders.

file: 1997/1997-05-11_carl_cubicle dwellers_hard worker_coffee cup_walk around_downsized_co workers resntment_snarky.gif
title: Carl and the Coffee Cup

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: I am Carl, the cubicle dwellers' friend.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: I travel from cubicle to cubicle to tell people how hard I'm working.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: I am working so-o-o-o hard. Work, work, work. It's all I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How is that possible?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You walk around all day with that coffee cup resting on your belly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does your job description say "transport coffee cup on belly"?

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: He's a terrible conversationalist.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How many miles per gallon do you get?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hypothetically, if you were downsized, how would the cup get around?

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: What's wrong with these people?

situation: Carl, a coworker, wanders from cubicle to cubicle holding a coffee cup on his belly while boasting to everyone about how hard he works. Dilbert points out that all he actually does is carry the cup around, and Alice piles on with her own jabs. Carl is baffled by their hostility.
punchline: Carl's whole job appears to be walking around loudly claiming to be busy, and his coworkers sarcastically mock the fact that he does nothing, while he is oblivious to why they're annoyed.
summary: A stroll-about slacker who advertises his busyness gets roasted by coworkers for doing nothing but lugging a mug around, and he can't understand why they're so rude.

file: 1997/1997-04-15_catbert_evil hr director_life insurance policy_pay premiums_collect insurance_valuable_company_don't like cats_business.gif
title: Wally Is Worth More Dead

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company has taken out a life insurance policy on you, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We pay the premiums and we collect the insurance when you die.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is this because I'm so valuable to the company?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's because we think you'll be more valuable dead.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is exactly why I don't like cats.

setting: Catbert's human resources office, across a desk
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Wally the company has taken out a life insurance policy on him and will collect when he dies. Wally hopefully assumes it reflects his value to the company, but Catbert says they simply expect him to be worth more dead than alive.
punchline: The company's insurance policy on Wally isn't a sign of appreciation; it reveals that management considers him more profitable dead than working, which Wally blames on cats.
summary: An H.R. cat informs a lazy employee that the firm has bet on his death and stands to profit from it.

file: 1997/1997-08-03_employee rock climbing seminar_valuable teamwork_skills_rock climbing_open jars.gif
title: Rock-Climbing Teamwork Seminar Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Welcome to the employee rock-climbing seminar.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: You'll learn valuable teamwork skills by doing dangerous things unrelated to your jobs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Isn't rock climbing a solo activity?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll help identify your body.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It seems like you'd need a strong grip to climb rocks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't even open jars unless I use special tools.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Cramp!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm disoriented by the pain!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey!

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Here are your diplomas. Now get out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Go team!

setting: Rock-climbing gym during a corporate training seminar
situation: An instructor welcomes employees to a team-building rock-climbing seminar. Wally points out that climbing is a solo activity and that he lacks the grip strength for it, then gets a hand cramp. Wally ends up tangled in a heap with Dilbert and Alice, and the instructor hands out diplomas and throws them out.
punchline: The seminar teaches no real teamwork or climbing; the only thing the 'team' accomplishes is collapsing in a painful tangle, and Wally's weak 'Go team!' cheer is ironic.
summary: A pointless corporate climbing workshop dissolves into a groaning pile of coworkers who are handed certificates and shown the door.

file: 1997/1997-05-23_labor saving software_no labor_dead office_nothing on screen_computer software_wally_dilbert.gif
title: Labor-Saving Software Proves Itself By Idleness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wrote this labor-saving software. Watch it do its thing.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: Dilbert and Wally watch the computer in silence.)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you tell if it's working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You don't see any labor happening around here, do you?

situation: Wally, seated at his desk, proudly announces that he has written labor-saving software and invites Dilbert, who stands holding a coffee mug, to watch it work. They stare at the computer in silence until Dilbert asks how he can tell if it's working. Wally points out that nobody in the office is doing any work, which he takes as proof of success.
punchline: Wally claims the lack of any visible work around the office is evidence his software is working, which is really just a cover for his and his coworkers' chronic idleness.
summary: A lazy engineer takes credit for a program that saves effort, citing the office's general absence of effort as proof it functions.

file: 1997/1997-07-09_feel for engineers_tired of pretty boys_appreciate dancing_exotic dancing_passion_phyiscs_scratch ear_can't get enough.gif
title: Dogbert Steals Dilbert's Date

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Until I met you, Dogbert, I always fell for engineers.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: But I'm tired of pretty boys. I want a guy who will appreciate my exotic dancing as much as my passion for physics.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Scratch under this ear for a minute.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Sure. I can't get enough touching.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sob

situation: A woman with long black hair sits on the grass petting Dogbert and tells him she is tired of pretty boys and wants someone who will appreciate her exotic dancing and love of physics. Dilbert, an engineer, sits off to the side ignored. By the end she is happily scratching Dogbert's ear while Dilbert sobs in the background.
punchline: The woman who used to date engineers prefers a dog who will happily be petted over Dilbert, leaving the engineer heartbroken and rejected.
summary: A physics-loving dancer passes over the lovelorn engineer in favor of Dogbert, whose appeal comes down to being scratched.

file: 1997/1997-12-26_role model_using deception_time management_wally is dead_daily planning session_ideal role model.gif
title: Asok Imitates Wally's Deceptive Time Management

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My role model is using deception to improve his time management.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wally is dead. Sorry.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And now the daily planning session.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, I don't think you've picked an ideal role model.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Asok is dead.

situation: Asok thinks admiringly about Wally, who dodges a request by telling a caller on the phone that he is dead. Asok then peeks over a cubicle wall at Wally napping at his desk. Alice tells Asok that Wally is a poor role model, and Asok copies the trick by claiming he is dead too.
punchline: Asok has absorbed Wally's laziness and dishonesty so thoroughly that he reuses the 'I'm dead' excuse immediately, proving Alice's point about bad role models.
summary: An eager young engineer adopts his slacker coworker's habit of lying and napping, and instantly demonstrates why that was a mistake.

file: 1997/1997-08-26_work during vacation_supposed to work_concept_empathy.gif
title: Wally's Failed Vacation Empathy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a shame you have to work during your vacation. The same thing happened to me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Actually, in my case I went on vacation when I was supposed to be working. But the concept is the same.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently she wasn't looking for empathy.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, approaches Alice at her computer and sympathizes with her having to work during her vacation, claiming the same thing happened to him. He then admits that he actually went on vacation when he was supposed to be working. Alice is left unimpressed and Wally is shown with a mug on his face and a coffee spill on his shirt, while Dilbert comments.
punchline: Wally's supposed empathy is really the opposite of Alice's situation, since he skipped work to take vacation, and his comparison is so tone-deaf that Alice reacts with violence, leaving Dilbert to note she wasn't seeking empathy.
summary: A lazy coworker tries to commiserate with a colleague whose vacation was interrupted by work, but his own story turns out to be about shirking work for leisure, and it ends badly for him.

file: 1997/1997-12-31_line of probablity_illusion of gravity_consciousness.gif
title: Ratbert Misunderstands "The Norm" Physics Lecture

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: ...As your consciousness passes through each universe, you tend to follow a line of probability.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Got it.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: And since it's more probable that matter is near other matter, you have the illusion of gravity as your consciousness moves toward the norm.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Did you get all that, Ratbert?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hey, I'm not stupid.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Does this Norm guy have a last name?

setting: Outdoors on a grassy lawn near a post
situation: A garbage man sits on the grass and explains a theory about consciousness moving through parallel universes along a line of probability, claiming gravity is merely an illusion. Ratbert, taking notes, says he follows it. At the end he reveals he took "the norm" to be a person and asks for Norm's last name.
punchline: Ratbert insists he's not stupid but proves he misunderstood the physics lecture by assuming "the norm" refers to a guy named Norm.
summary: A man's lofty lecture on parallel universes and the illusion of gravity ends with a note-taking Ratbert wondering about the surname of someone called Norm.

file: 1997/1997-09-13_boss_down in jet_minor injuries_saved by padding_saved by prayer_work great_minor hair injuries_100 nuns onboard_nunnery_not a lot of aerobics.gif
title: Boss Survives Crash Thanks to Nuns

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Work has been great since our boss went down on the jet!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I survived with only minor hair injuries. I was lucky to be on a flight that had a hundred nuns onboard!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You were saved by prayer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, padding. They don't do a lot of aerobics at the nunnery.

situation: Carol, wearing an enormous mass of hair, happily says work has improved since the boss's plane went down, just as the boss walks up. The boss explains that he survived the crash with only minor hair injuries because the plane was full of nuns. When Dilbert asks if prayer saved him, the boss says it was the nuns' padding that cushioned him.
punchline: The boss credits his survival not to prayer but to the soft, out-of-shape bodies of a hundred nuns who cushioned the crash, a tasteless remark that fits his obliviousness.
summary: After a plane crash, a boss shrugs off his survival by crediting the cushioning bodies of the nuns around him instead of any divine intervention.

file: 1997/1997-12-24_illogical scientist_software_prove a negative_trained scientist_involve electric shocks_engineering.gif
title: The Illogical Scientist Proves Negatives

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Hi. I'm Dan, the illogical scientist. That software you're writing will never work, and I can prove it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't mean to be rude, but it's not logically possible to prove something can't be done.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: It's impossible for most people, but I'm a trained scientist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did the training involve electric shocks?

situation: A scientist named Dan introduces himself as illogical and claims he can prove that Dilbert's software will never work. Dilbert points out that it is logically impossible to prove something cannot be done. Dan says his scientific training makes him the exception, and Dilbert suggests the training must have involved electric shocks.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that Dan's absurd claim of defying logic must be the result of brain damage from electric shock treatment.
summary: A self-declared illogical scientist insists he can do the logically impossible, and Dilbert wryly wonders what odd training could explain such confidence.

file: 1997/1997-10-01_ads_bad opinions_capatalism_cardboard tube_free_internet_people_something free_greedy corporations_technology.gif
title: Free Internet Lesson With Cardboard Tube

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: People with bad opinions

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: The Internet should be free. Why should I have to pay some greedy corporation or look at ads??!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will now use this cardboard tube to explain the intricacies of capitalism.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lesson one: THIS was something that should be free.

setting: An office or desk area, under a 'People With Bad Opinions' header
situation: A man angrily complains that the Internet should be free and that he shouldn't have to pay a greedy corporation or look at ads. Dogbert announces he will use a cardboard tube to explain capitalism, then whacks the man with it, knocking him flat on his back with stars circling his head.
punchline: Dogbert's lesson in capitalism is to hit the man with a tube he didn't pay for, noting that the beating was something that should have been free, showing that nothing of value comes without cost.
summary: A man grumbling about paying for online access gets a painful, wordless economics lesson from a dog wielding a tube.

file: 1997/1997-04-30_stock options_sign agreement_yada yada.gif
title: Dogbert Reads Employment Agreement: Yada Yada

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company won't give me my stock options unless I sign this new employment agreement.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yada, yada, yada, yada, yada, yada, yada, yada, yada, yada.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm not reading it. I just like to look at documents and go yada, yada, yada.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on a couch
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, who is acting as an advisor, to look over a new employment agreement his company is making him sign to get his stock options. Dogbert takes the document and recites 'yada, yada' as if reading it. When Dilbert asks for his opinion, Dogbert admits he never read it and just enjoys looking at documents.
punchline: Dogbert's useless 'review' of the legal document mocks professional advice that amounts to nothing, and the fact that nobody really reads the fine print of contracts.
summary: Dilbert seeks Dogbert's counsel on a contract, only to learn the pooch is just babbling nonsense at the pages for fun.

file: 1997/1997-10-12_quick phone call_make small talk_brought a magazine_alice_panty hose.gif
title: Dilbert Blackmails Coworker With Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to make a quick phone call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want to make small talk?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I brought a magazine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you tear out a few pages for me to read?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That wouldn't be right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me some pages or else I'll ask Alice about panty hose.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You wouldn't dare.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, Alice, what do you think of the concept of panty hose?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Aargh!! What moron invented leg covers that can be destroyed by touching a twig?!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Here! Make it stop!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too late.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Look at this!!!

setting: Conference room, waiting for a meeting to start
situation: While waiting for the boss, who has stepped out to make a phone call, Dilbert is stuck with a coworker who refuses small talk and won't share his magazine. Dilbert threatens to ask Alice about panty hose, and when the coworker calls his bluff, Dilbert does it anyway and Alice erupts in a rage.
punchline: Dilbert's threat of asking Alice a harmless-sounding question was a real weapon, and he carried it out anyway, unleashing Alice's fury over a ruined pair of panty hose.
summary: Bored while waiting for a late meeting, Dilbert sets off Alice's temper on purpose when a coworker won't share his reading material.

file: 1997/1997-06-25_alice_bonus_capitalism_flawed premise_less work_wally bonus_worked less_implications staggering_frightening bonus.gif
title: Less Work, Bigger Bonus Paradox

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I did less work than usual this quarter and I got a bonus.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The implications are staggering. The entire system of capitalism has a flawed premise.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's only ONE thing that could make this bonus more frightening.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got one, too.

situation: Alice announces at a meeting that she received a bonus despite doing less work than usual. She worries that this undermines the whole premise of capitalism. Wally, who is famous for doing almost no work, then reveals that he got a bonus as well.
punchline: If even lazy Wally is rewarded with a bonus, it confirms that bonuses have no connection to actual work, which is the truly frightening conclusion.
summary: Alice is alarmed that slacking off earned her a bonus, and her unease deepens when the office's laziest employee is also paid one.

file: 1997/1997-06-26_business consulatnts_common sense_debunks effectiveness_logically flwaed_no common sense_writing book_mass market.gif
title: Consultant Writes Book Debunking Consultants

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing a book that debunks the effectiveness of business consultants.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But common sense would say that you're being a consultant yourself, so your opinion is logically flawed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Only people with no common sense will buy your book.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I prefer to call them the mass market.

setting: Dilbert's home office, at a desk with a computer
situation: Dogbert sits at a computer typing and announces he is writing a book debunking business consultants. Dilbert points out that Dogbert is himself a consultant, so his opinion is logically flawed. Dogbert replies that only people with no common sense will buy the book, and then reframes those people as the mass market.
punchline: Dogbert cynically admits his book will only appeal to people lacking common sense, but sees that as a huge and profitable audience.
summary: A self-interested consultant brushes off a charge of hypocrisy by noting that gullible readers make up the biggest market of all.

file: 1997/1997-06-15_attractive_body language_employee satisfaction_extent of feelings_fake happiness_impending reorganization_lottery_marketing feild_new rules_not motivated_paycheck_sarcastic_survey_unprofessional_work.gif
title: Asok Explains Office Body Language

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Asok the intern explains the new rules of body language.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Fake happiness.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This means: I am not motivated by the size of my paycheck.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ahh!! Wahh! Wahh!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This means: I am slightly concerned about the impending reorganization.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This means: I have decided to work in the marketing field.

transcript.speaker: Label
transcript.text: Counter-clockwise spin

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This means: I am being sarcastic.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Oh, THERE'S a good plan.

transcript.speaker: Label
transcript.text: Note lips

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This means: The recent employee satisfaction survey has not captured the extent of my feelings.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This means: I think you are attractive but it would be very unprofessional to show it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This means: My lottery investment paid off.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yank!

situation: Asok the intern demonstrates a series of exaggerated body-language poses and explains the hidden workplace meaning of each. They range from crying over a paycheck to hanging himself over a satisfaction survey. In the last panel he yanks the Boss's tie to mean his lottery investment paid off.
punchline: Body language is reduced to blunt, dark gags about miserable pay, reorganizations and surveys, ending with Asok yanking the Boss's tie to show he has won the lottery and can quit.
summary: An intern acts out silent office gestures, each one secretly translating into a grim complaint about pay, reorganizations or surveys.

file: 1997/1997-12-12_go home early_exempt employee_unimportant document_shuffle around_quiet desparation.gif
title: Exempt From Having a Life

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished all of my work. Can I go home early?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're an "exempt" employee. That means you're exempt from having a life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I could clench an unimportant document and shuffle around in quiet desperation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the spirit!

setting: Office, in front of the Boss's doorway
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has finished all his work and asks to go home early. The Boss refuses, explaining that as an exempt employee he is exempt from having a life. Dilbert resignedly offers to pretend to be busy by carrying a document around, and the Boss cheers him on.
punchline: The Boss twists the legal term 'exempt' to mean employees have no right to a personal life, and he approves of Dilbert faking busyness in quiet misery rather than letting him leave.
summary: A worker with nothing left to do is denied time off and told to look busy instead, which his boss warmly applauds.

file: 1997/1997-01-23_layer of management_meeting disaster_senior management_warning the layer above_dont mention problems.gif
title: Layers of Management Warn Each Other

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't mention any problems when you do your presentation to senior management, Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They might try to solve the problems during the meeting. That would be a disaster.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: As far as I can tell, every layer of management exists for the sole purpose of warning us about the layer above.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying they have a purpose?

setting: The Boss's office and a hallway at the office
situation: The Boss instructs Alice not to mention any problems in her presentation to senior management, fearing they might actually try to fix them. Afterward, Alice tells Dilbert that every layer of management seems to exist only to warn employees about the layer above. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether she is saying management has a purpose.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic question suggests that management layers serve no real purpose at all, and that warning about the next layer up is the closest thing to one.
summary: After being told to hide problems from the executives, Alice observes that middle managers mostly serve as lookouts for the level above, prompting a snarky remark about management's usefulness.

file: 1997/1997-03-30_security system_cost fortune_camera_every room_criminal activity_fortress portected_show kids_stuff stolen.gif
title: Burglar Steals Dilbert's Camera-Protected Home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This security system cost a fortune but it's worth it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I put a camera in every room to deter any criminal activity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We may now go to the park knowing our fortress is protected.

transcript.speaker: Burglar
transcript.text: I can't wait to show my kids what I do at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can only think of one thing worse than having all of my stuff stolen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that is having some of it returned.

transcript.speaker: Burglar
transcript.text: This thing is hideous in good light.

setting: Dilbert's home, then a park bench
situation: Dilbert installs a costly security system with a camera in every room, then goes to the park with Dogbert, confident his home is safe. A burglar walks past carrying Dilbert's lamp, camera equipment and couch, happily thinking about showing his kids his work. Dilbert grumbles about his stuff being stolen, and the burglar returns a hideous couch.
punchline: The security cameras only recorded the burglary rather than preventing it, and the thief returns the one item he found too ugly to keep, making Dilbert's loss even more insulting.
summary: A man's pricey surveillance setup fails to stop a thief who strolls past him carrying the whole house, then drops back the ugliest piece.

file: 1997/1997-11-07_catbert_evil hr director_reward employees_reward_skip staff meeting_alice.gif
title: Skipping Meetings as Employee Reward

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You don't need to reward employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Just torture them less. It will feel the same as a reward.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You may skip my staff meeting this week, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thank you thank you thank you.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, advises the Boss that he doesn't need to reward employees. Instead, he should simply reduce the torment they normally endure, which will feel just as good. The Boss tries it by letting Alice skip his staff meeting, and she gushes with gratitude.
punchline: Employees are so badly mistreated that merely being spared a routine miserable meeting feels like a generous reward.
summary: A scheming H.R. cat teaches a manager that easing up on mistreatment is a cheap substitute for real perks, and a grateful employee proves it works.

file: 1997/1997-04-20_tips from headquarters_long distance_short words_cheap boss_save money_dumb ideas_swiss trip_curse words.gif
title: Penny-Pinching Tips, Expensive Swiss Trip

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here are some money-saving tips from headquarters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "When calling long distance, use short words."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "If everyone did this, our fifty-billion-dollar company could save nine hundred dollars per year."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Tip two: For faxes, use sans serif fonts. They transmit faster. Annual savings could exceed three hundred dollars."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next on the agenda, remember I'll be in Switzerland next week on a fact-finding trip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you need to call me at my four star hotel, be sure to use short words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might want to save those short words until he's on his clue-finding trip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Those are NOT all short words.

setting: Conference room, then a Swiss hotel room
situation: The Boss reads out silly cost-cutting tips from headquarters, like using short words on long-distance calls and sans serif fonts on faxes, each saving only a few hundred dollars for a fifty-billion-dollar company. He then announces a pricey fact-finding trip to Switzerland and a four-star hotel. Dilbert suggests saving short words for when the boss goes looking for clues, and in Switzerland the boss gets an angry call full of curse symbols.
punchline: The company obsesses over trivial savings while management spends lavishly, and the staff respond with a call of short, rude words that the boss pedantically says are not all short.
summary: Management preaches absurdly tiny economies to the staff while the boss jets off to a luxury hotel abroad, and gets cursed out by phone for his hypocrisy.

file: 1997/1997-08-24_employee communications survey_negative news_come to insult_communication problems.gif
title: Fear of Telling Boss Bad News

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: We have the results of the employee communications survey.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: The number one problem is "fear of giving negative news to managers."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?! Why haven't I heard this before?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Well... maybe because it's negative news?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a solution or did you just come to insult me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't get involved.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Ooh. Um... maybe if we wait a few days it will take care of itself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine. Next.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Happily, there are no other communication problems whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Heh heh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder why so many problems go away on their own.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have no comment at this time.

situation: A presenter reports that the top finding of an employee communications survey is fear of giving bad news to managers. The Boss is shocked he never heard this and, when the presenter honestly explains why, demands a solution or accuses him of insulting him. The presenter backs down, claims there are no other problems, and the Boss is left puzzled.
punchline: The survey result is proven true on the spot: the presenter is so afraid of the Boss's reaction that he suppresses the bad news, and the Boss remains oblivious to why problems 'go away on their own.'
summary: A survey reveals employees fear telling managers bad news, and the manager's reaction to the report instantly demonstrates why.

file: 1997/1997-05-24_consultant_meeting_obvious generalities_revenue for profit_run by artits_small businesses_business.gif
title: Consulting in Obvious Generalities

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become a consultant in the field of obvious generalities.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll work for small businesses that are run by artists. They'll think I'm brilliant, which I am.

transcript.speaker: Artist (man)
transcript.text: Whoa! Are you saying we need revenue to make profit??

transcript.speaker: Artist (woman)
transcript.text: Ouch! I've got a headache on one side.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then a small business conference room
situation: Dogbert, sitting on the couch next to a reading Dilbert, announces he will become a consultant specializing in obvious generalities and will target small businesses run by artists. In the last panel he is at a table with two artist clients, who react with shock and pain to the idea that a business needs revenue to make a profit.
punchline: Dogbert's consulting is nothing more than stating the obvious, but the artist clients are so business-naive that basic truths like needing revenue for profit blow their minds.
summary: A scheming dog picks gullible creative types as clients for his advice-free consulting practice and wows them with the most basic business facts.

file: 1997/1997-09-21_bad clothes_casula clothes_catbert_evil hr director_explain logic_hawaiian shirt_impact on earnings_one casual day.gif
title: Casual Friday Banned Over Hawaiian Shirts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Another evil policy. I'm a happy cat.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purr purr

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "Casual clothes will not be allowed this Friday..."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "...because we had Hawaiian shirt day on Wednesday."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Um... can you explain the logic here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're only allowed one casual day per week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we had two casual days, obviously it would have an impact on earnings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does stupidity have an impact on our earnings, too, or is it just bad clothes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're only sure about bad clothes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you're killing us with that outfit.

setting: Conference room and Catbert's HR office
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. Director, announces that casual clothes will be banned this Friday because there was a Hawaiian shirt day on Wednesday. Alice and Dilbert question the logic, and the Boss claims that more than one casual day per week would hurt earnings. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether stupidity also hurts earnings, and the Boss says they're only sure about bad clothes, then blames Alice's outfit.
punchline: The company obsesses over the supposed financial harm of casual clothing while ignoring the far greater damage of its own stupid policies, and then singles out Alice's outfit instead.
summary: An HR policy bans casual attire on the grounds of an earlier Hawaiian shirt day, and the justification collapses when an employee's sarcastic question is turned into a criticism of her clothes.

file: 1997/1997-06-14_advice_clone boss_email message_no knowledge_perspective_possible_no experience.gif
title: Cloning the Boss Adds Perspective

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Someday it will be possible to clone our boss.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But the clone would have no experience and no knowledge.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just sent an e-mail message to Japan. I don't know the language so I took your advice and typed it all in caps.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. That put it all in perspective.

situation: Dilbert muses that technology might one day clone their boss, and Wally objects that the clone would lack experience and knowledge. The Boss then walks up and cheerfully says he emailed Japan in all caps because he doesn't know the language. Dilbert realizes the boss already lacks knowledge and experience.
punchline: The Boss's absurd belief that typing in capital letters translates an email into Japanese shows he already has no knowledge or experience, so a clone would be no worse than the original.
summary: After coworkers joke that a cloned boss would be clueless, the real boss proves he is just as clueless by shouting in English at Japan.

file: 1997/1997-06-07_despotic nations_software license_submit strip searches_opening package.gif
title: Software License Demands Strip Searches

transcript.speaker: Software License
transcript.text: Software license: By opening this package, you agree...

transcript.speaker: Software License
transcript.text: ...You will not make copies or export to despotic nations. You will submit to strip searches in your home...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: RRRIP

transcript.speaker: Licensing Inspector
transcript.text: Frankly, both of us would have been happier if you had just walked away.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer opening a software package while a voice reads out the license terms, which escalate to absurd demands like strip searches in your home. As he tears the package open, a man in a hospital gown and a yellow rubber glove appears to carry out the search. He tells Dilbert they would both have been happier if he had just walked away.
punchline: The ridiculous license terms are enforced literally by an inspector who arrives for the invasive search, and even he wishes Dilbert had never opened the package.
summary: Tearing open shrink-wrapped software triggers the arrival of a gloved inspector ready to enforce an outrageously invasive license agreement.

file: 1997/1997-06-28_added billions_create system_employee of the week_hire experts_product process_stock value_new internet product.gif
title: Hire Experts Instead of Building Product

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've identified the people who will create the system to develop a product process.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: While we were doing that, our competitor created a new Internet product that added a billion dollars to their stock value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Experts attribute the company's success to their "Employee of the Week" program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Quick! Hire those experts!

situation: Dilbert reports that his team has only just identified who will build a process for developing products, while a competitor has already launched a hugely valuable internet product. He reads a newspaper article crediting the rival's success to an Employee of the Week program. The Boss immediately orders him to hire those experts.
punchline: The Boss ignores the real lesson that his company is slow and process-obsessed, and instead reacts to a trivial, dubious expert opinion by hiring the pundits.
summary: While one firm drowns in planning its planning, a rival strikes it rich, and the boss's answer is to hire the commentators who credited a gimmick.

file: 1997/1997-06-06_dogbert_bearer bad news_wally fired_videos_stealing stuff_one percent raise.gif
title: Dogbert Delivers Bad News Gleefully

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Professional bearer of bad news

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wally, your boss asked me to tell you...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're fired!!! And they have secret videos of you stealing stuff!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This can't be true.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's not. But watch how happy you are when I tell you about your one-percent raise.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a professional bearer of bad news, tells Wally that he has been fired and that the company has secret videos of him stealing. Wally is horrified, then Dogbert admits it was a lie. He explains it was a setup so that Wally will be relieved when he hears about his paltry one-percent raise.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately terrifies Wally with false news so that a miserly one-percent raise feels like good news by comparison.
summary: A canine messenger frightens an employee with invented disasters just so a stingy pay bump will seem like a gift.

file: 1997/1997-07-01_goal is to be happy_more successful_annoy_rat_dilbert_lecture_compare.gif
title: Ratbert Gloats About Being Happier

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: If the goal of all creatures is to be happy... and I'm happier than you are...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: We can conclude that I'm more successful than you are. Isn't that right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are really starting to annoy me now.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The gap widens.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes!

setting: Dilbert's living room, on a blue couch
situation: Ratbert sits on the couch next to Dilbert and argues that because happiness is the goal of all creatures and he is happier, he is more successful than Dilbert. Dilbert grows visibly angrier at the smug logic. When Dilbert says Ratbert is annoying him, Ratbert celebrates because his irritation proves the point.
punchline: Dilbert's growing annoyance makes him even less happy, so Ratbert's claim of being happier and more successful becomes even more true, which Ratbert cheerfully points out.
summary: A smug little pet uses a neat bit of logic to declare himself the winner in life, then delights in how his victory margin grows as his owner gets angrier.

file: 1997/1997-08-28_old job_network systems_asminstrator_reckless abuse_power_new ethernet card_solve problem_big pile_office.gif
title: Dogbert Relishes Sysadmin Power Abuse

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going back to my old job as a network systems administrator.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm attracted by the potential for reckless abuse of power.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This new Ethernet card could solve your problem. Would you like a sniff before I throw it in a big pile in my office?

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then an office cubicle
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert, who is relaxing on the couch with a bag of chips, that he is returning to his old job as a network systems administrator. When Dilbert asks why, Dogbert says he likes the chance to abuse power. In the office, Dogbert dangles a new Ethernet card before a stressed-looking user, teasing him before tossing it onto a pile.
punchline: Dogbert admits he wants the sysadmin job because it lets him lord scarce hardware over desperate users, offering a taunting 'sniff' of a solution before hoarding it.
summary: A scheming dog returns to IT administration for the thrill of tormenting users who depend on him for equipment.

file: 1997/1997-06-08_clean cubicle award_matthew_traveler check_10 dollars_downsized_shredded documents_motivational impact.gif
title: Clean Cubicle Award for Downsized Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm happy to award the "Clean Cubicle Award" to Matthew.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a ten-dollar "Travelers Check."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where's Matthew?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He was cruelly downsized last month.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: His cubicle was clean because he shredded his important documents out of spite.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All of his furniture and equipment were scavenged by bitter employees who have to do his work now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is not having the motivational impact I had hoped for.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay... the "Travelers Check" will go to whoever knows what number I'm thinking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They sure were sore losers.

setting: Office meeting room, then a restaurant
situation: The Boss tries to present a ten-dollar travelers check as a 'Clean Cubicle Award' to Matthew, only to learn that Matthew was downsized last month. His employees explain that the cubicle was clean only because Matthew shredded his documents out of spite and coworkers stripped his furniture. Unmotivated, the Boss switches to a number-guessing game for the prize, and ends up alone at a restaurant table musing about sore losers.
punchline: The Boss blames the 'sore losers' for the failure of his award program, oblivious to the fact that his own downsizing caused the resentment and ruined the cubicle contest.
summary: A manager's cheap office-cleanliness prize backfires when the winner turns out to have been laid off and left behind a gutted workspace.

file: 1997/1997-05-10_industry survey_our industry_hugh technology_textile workers_teen agersm dead people.gif
title: Salary Survey With Broadened Industry

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We did an industry survey to see how your salaries compared to the average.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We didn't get the numbers we hoped for, so we broadened the definition of "our industry."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm so happy to be in the industry of "high technology, textile workers, teen-agers, and dead people."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel over-paid.

situation: The Boss sits at a conference table with Dilbert and Wally and reads from a paper about a salary survey comparing their pay to the industry average. He admits the results were disappointing, so the company redefined 'our industry' to include much lower-paid groups. Wally sarcastically repeats the new definition and Dilbert dryly concludes he must be overpaid.
punchline: Management manipulated the data by widening the definition of the industry to include low-paid groups like teenagers and dead people, so employees look overpaid and can justify low salaries.
summary: To make employee pay look generous, management redefines the comparison group until the staff appear to be overpaid.

file: 1997/1997-06-20_project caribou_walls project_final design_now_wally_thimble_morale in thimble.gif
title: Boss Reassigns Wally's Project to Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give me a final design for Project Caribou by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's Wally's project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know, but I'm thinking about it now and Wally isn't in the room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell Wally it's your project now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you see this thimble? I keep my morale in it.

situation: The Boss demands a final design for Project Caribou by Tuesday. Dilbert points out the project belongs to Wally, but the Boss says Wally isn't in the room and simply hands the project to Dilbert, who is left to break the news to Wally. Dilbert responds by holding up a thimble and saying it contains all his morale.
punchline: Dilbert's morale is so depleted that it would fit inside a thimble, a sarcastic reaction to being randomly saddled with a coworker's project.
summary: A manager arbitrarily hands a colleague's assignment to whoever happens to be standing in front of him, and the worn-down employee shows how little motivation he has left.

file: 1997/1997-01-26_moms birthday_wants nothing_home entertainment theater_50 inch screen_surround sound_satellite link_toaster oven.gif
title: Mom's Surprising Birthday Wish List

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you want for your birthday this year, Mom?

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Oh, nothing. I have everything I need.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, c'mon. There must be something you want.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Well, one thing. But it's silly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You just name it.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: I'd like a home entertainment theatre with a fifty-inch screen, "THX" surround sound and a 600 kbps satellite link to the net so I can view adult pictures during the commercials.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was thinking more along the lines of a new toaster oven.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Oh, that's exciting. I'll put it next to my other one and watch them fight it out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a real dark side to the information age.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Oh, and about the gift of life I gave you; you're welcome.

setting: Dilbert's mother's kitchen and living room
situation: Dilbert asks his elderly mother what she wants for her birthday. She claims she needs nothing, then admits to a silly wish and requests a high-end home theater with fast satellite internet so she can watch adult pictures during commercials. Dilbert had only expected to buy a toaster oven, and she snarks back about the gift of life.
punchline: The sweet-looking little old lady asks for a high-tech setup for watching porn, then sarcastically reminds Dilbert that she gave him the gift of life, implying he owes her more than a toaster oven.
summary: A son's modest birthday gift plans for his grandmotherly mom are upended when she demands a lavish media setup for her own racy viewing habits.
keywords: dark side of the information age

file: 1997/1997-02-15_wendy_new secretary_time to process_pay increase_on desk_three months_more is not better.gif
title: Secretary's Secretary Laughs at Raise

transcript.speaker: Alice's colleague (secretary)
transcript.text: This is Wendy, my new secretary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't know secretaries could have secretaries.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now will you have time to process my pay increase? It's been on your desk for three months.

transcript.speaker: Secretary and Wendy
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Here's another case where more is not better.

setting: Office reception area at a secretary's desk
situation: Dilbert visits a secretary who introduces her new assistant, Wendy, and he remarks that secretaries now have secretaries. Hoping the extra help will speed things up, he asks her to finally process his pay increase, which has sat on her desk for three months. Both women burst into laughter, and Dilbert concludes that doubling the staff hasn't helped.
punchline: Adding a second secretary doesn't make the first one any more willing to process paperwork, so the extra headcount just means twice as many people laughing at his pending raise.
summary: Dilbert hopes a secretary's new assistant will finally free up time to approve his overdue raise, but both of them just laugh at him.

file: 1997/1997-03-20_engineer_gulty_insufficient light_major sin_prince_tech writer_unnatural attraction_leverage synergies_engineering.gif
title: Tech Writer Sentenced to Buzzword Hell

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You are guilty of being a technical writer with an unnatural attraction to an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: It's not a major sin, so you only go to Heck. I'm Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Sit down and type, "I proactively leverage my synergies," a hundred times.

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: No-o-o!!!

setting: The entrance to Heck, a cave in the afterlife
situation: Phil, dressed as a horned devil and carrying a giant spoon, judges a newly arrived technical writer. Her offense is an unnatural attraction to an engineer, which only earns her a stay in Heck rather than Hell. Her punishment is to type a meaningless corporate buzzword sentence a hundred times, and she screams in horror.
punchline: Being forced to write empty management jargon is treated as a torment worse than fire and brimstone, which shows how awful corporate buzzwords are.
summary: A devilish Phil condemns a lovestruck technical writer to an eternity of typing meaningless business jargon.

file: 1997/1997-11-05_cobol_cobol code_glaciers_vast experience_rewrite_incharge_dinosaur_intern_meteor kill.gif
title: Dinosaur Expert Awaits Y2K Meteor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You two will be in charge of rewriting our COBOL code to fix the millenium problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I realize you've never worked with COBOL before, Asok. That's why I'm teaming you with Bob, so you can learn from his vast experience.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So, you recommend waiting for a meteor to kill us all.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: The glaciers are way too slow.

situation: The Boss assigns Asok and Bob, a green dinosaur, to rewrite the company's COBOL code to fix the millennium problem. He explains that Bob's vast experience with COBOL will help Asok learn. Later, Asok asks Bob for his recommendation and the dinosaur suggests waiting for a meteor to wipe everyone out.
punchline: Bob is literally a dinosaur, so his 'vast experience' is prehistoric, and his only solution to the Y2K problem is the extinction event that killed his own kind.
summary: A manager pairs a young programmer with an ancient dinosaur colleague as a mentor for a legacy-code deadline, and the mentor's advice is cosmic annihilation.

file: 1997/1997-07-30_dogbert_integrate_bad technology_idiot boss_good etchnology_throw away_bad tech_pure veil.gif
title: Praising the Boss's Bad Purchase

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's my job to integrate the bad technology that our idiot boss bought with the good technology we already own. Your advice?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Throw away the bad technology. Goof off until the next planned upgrade of the good technology. Tell your boss the improvements are a result of his brilliant buying decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. That's almost pure evil.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert how to integrate the poor technology his boss purchased with the good systems the company already has. Dogbert advises discarding the bad equipment, slacking off until the scheduled upgrade of the good system, and then crediting the boss's purchase for the improvement. Dilbert is impressed by how evil the plan is, and Dogbert takes it as a compliment.
punchline: Dogbert's plan dodges the work and flatters the boss with false credit, and he treats Dilbert's remark that it is almost pure evil as thanks.
summary: Dogbert coaches Dilbert to bin a clueless manager's bad purchase, loaf around, and then hand the manager credit for upgrades that were coming anyway.

file: 1997/1997-10-09_telecommunters_eat anytime_wild animals_tranquilizer darts_flatbed_giant shoehorn.gif
title: Telecommuter Treated Like Wild Animal

transcript.speaker: Telecommuter
transcript.text: Telecommuters can eat any time they want, just like wild animals.

transcript.speaker: Telecommuter
transcript.text: There's only one way they'll ever get me back in the cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the plan. You'll need tranquilizer darts, a flatbed truck and a giant shoehorn.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No harpoon?

setting: A telecommuter's home (kitchen and living room), then the boss's office
situation: A telecommuter in a bathrobe stands at her open fridge, then lounges on her couch, thinking that the only way she'll go back to the office cubicle is by force. In the final panel the boss lays out a plan to a coworker involving tranquilizer darts, a flatbed truck and a giant shoehorn, treating her like a wild animal that must be captured and hauled in.
punchline: The boss's plan to retrieve the telecommuter is literally an animal-capture operation, and the coworker's only concern is that it lacks a harpoon, as if she were a whale.
summary: A homebound worker muses that only force could return her to the office, and her manager promptly drafts a wildlife-capture scheme to do exactly that.

file: 1997/1997-01-15_software license_rumble_prepare for assimilation.gif
title: Software License Makes Dilbert Gates' Servant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ... So you didn't read the software license and you inadvertently agreed to be Bill Gates' towel boy in his huge new house. When do we move?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: RRRUMBLE!

transcript.speaker: Bill Gates' House
transcript.text: Prepare for assimilation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The house has come for me.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that by not reading a software license he unknowingly agreed to become Bill Gates' towel boy in Gates' huge new house, and cheerfully asks when they move. The room begins to shake, and a giant, menacing machine-like house bursts through the wall announcing assimilation, so Dilbert realizes the house has come to collect him.
punchline: Bill Gates' mansion is portrayed as a Borg-like machine that forcibly assimilates Dilbert, mocking Microsoft's domineering power and the unread fine print of software licenses.
summary: A buried clause in an unread software agreement summons a monstrous, Borg-style mansion that crashes into Dilbert's home to claim its new servant.

file: 1997/1997-02-19_union job_file or grievance_moving ten feet_johnny cash_wait for union person.gif
title: Union Worker Blocks Moving PC

transcript.speaker: Union Worker
transcript.text: Hey, that's a union job. Put it down or I'll file a grievance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm only moving it ten feet. If I wait for a union person, I'll be unable to do my job for a week.

transcript.speaker: Union Worker
transcript.text: Watch me not care.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If anyone sees you move the PC tonight, try saying you're Johnny Cash.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should just use the elevator.

setting: Office cubicle area, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert is carrying a computer when a union worker with a tool belt stops him, insisting that moving equipment is a union job and threatening a grievance. Dilbert explains he'd lose a week of work waiting for a union employee, and the worker shrugs it off. That night Dogbert advises him to claim to be Johnny Cash if caught, and a robed Dilbert with a hooked rope considers using the elevator instead.
punchline: The union worker's indifference to the productivity cost of waiting a week is so complete that Dilbert resorts to sneaking around at night in disguise, and the 'Johnny Cash' advice implies a bizarre cover story is the only way to dodge the rules.
summary: A territorial union worker forbids a simple ten-foot computer move, pushing Dilbert toward covert nighttime relocation with an absurd alibi.

file: 1997/1997-05-12_cactus shreiks_cold_freezing_other warm_raise temp_wally shirtless.gif
title: Thermostat War Over Office Temperature

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's freezing in here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll just give the thermostat a little bump.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can we at least agree that when my cactus shrieks in agony, it's too warm?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It wasn't shrieking BEFORE you took your shirt off.

transcript.speaker: Cactus
transcript.text: Aaagh!!

situation: Alice shivers in the office and decides to turn up the thermostat. A coworker, shirtless and holding a cactus, complains that the cactus shrieks in agony from the heat. Alice retorts that it only started shrieking after he took his shirt off.
punchline: Alice implies the cactus is reacting to the sight of the coworker's shirtless body, not the temperature.
summary: A chilly office worker cranks up the heat, and a half-dressed colleague blames the warmth for his suffering plant, only to be told the real culprit is his bare torso.

file: 1997/1997-10-31_manager training_same room_decison_illustrate point_puppet show_blamesville_manager meg.gif
title: Journey to Blameville Puppet Show

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Manager training

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Never be in the same room as a decision.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: I'll illustrate my point with a puppet show that I call...

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: "Journey to Blameville," starring "Suggestion Sam" and "Manager Meg."

setting: Conference room during a manager training session
situation: A trainer stands beside a flip chart showing a stick figure labeled "You" running away from the word "Decision" and tells the managers-in-training never to be in the same room as a decision. He announces a puppet show to illustrate the point, then appears with two hand puppets, Suggestion Sam and Manager Meg, for a skit titled "Journey to Blameville."
punchline: The manager training teaches that the best career strategy is avoiding responsibility for decisions so that blame lands on someone else, and it does so with a condescending puppet show.
summary: A management seminar instructor teaches his students to dodge decisions entirely, then breaks out puppets for a skit about shifting blame.

file: 1997/1997-08-27_work ethic_alice_working during vacation_remain motivated_glass ceiling_never break.gif
title: Alice Breaks the Glass Ceiling

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I admire your work ethic, Alice. You're even working during your vacation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be hard to remain motivated when you know you can never break through the glass ceiling.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, it looks like it's just tile after all.

situation: Dilbert compliments Alice for working even while on vacation, then sympathetically notes how discouraging it must be to never break through the glass ceiling. Alice angrily punches through the ceiling, and a man in a blue shirt and tie dangles from the hole as ceiling debris falls. She remarks that the ceiling is just tile.
punchline: Alice takes the glass ceiling metaphor literally, smashes through the actual ceiling, and reveals that the barrier to advancement was never as solid as it seemed, while also taking out an unfortunate man above.
summary: Prompted by a coworker's pitying remark about the glass ceiling, an irritated employee literally punches through the office ceiling to test it.

file: 1997/1997-01-07_mail order bride_elbonian_exact date_garage.gif
title: Mail-Order Bride Kept in Garage

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My Elbonian mail-order bride will arrive any day now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you know the exact date?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Because they're sending her by mail. I wasn't willing to pay for overnight delivery.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's one lucky gal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll probably keep her in the garage. It has a sink.

setting: Office break room table during lunch
situation: Wally tells Dilbert over lunch that his Elbonian mail-order bride will arrive any day. When asked why he doesn't know the exact date, he explains he refused to pay for overnight shipping. He then casually says he plans to house her in the garage because it has a sink.
punchline: Wally treats his future wife like a cheap parcel, skimping on shipping and planning to store her in the garage, and Dilbert's sarcastic 'lucky gal' underscores how badly he'll treat her.
summary: Wally cheerfully reveals he's shipping in a bride the cheapest way possible and intends to lodge her wherever the plumbing is convenient.

file: 1997/1997-01-13_work_anti work_unit of work_generated unnecessary work.gif
title: Wally's Work and Anti-Work Balance

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I did equal amounts of work and anti-work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For every unit of work I did, I generated an equal amount of unnecessary work for co-workers. I figure I broke even.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, come see me after the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oh, great. You're driving me into negative territory!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: At a staff meeting, Wally cheerfully reports that he did as much anti-work as work this week, creating an equal amount of unnecessary work for his co-workers, so he considers himself even. The Boss then tells him to come see him after the meeting. Wally complains that this extra task pushes him into negative territory.
punchline: Wally treats creating pointless work for others as a legitimate offset to his own output, and then objects that the Boss's request for a meeting is itself unwanted work that ruins his supposedly balanced ledger.
summary: A lazy employee boasts that the busywork he inflicts on colleagues cancels out his own output, then protests when his boss adds to his workload.

file: 1997/1997-10-26_editable wax fruit_live at desk_no social life_social activity_vending machine food_marketing network.gif
title: Boss Hunts the Employee With Friends

transcript.speaker: The Boss
