transcript.text: It has come to my attention that one of you has a social life.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There must be some mistake.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't be successful until our social lives are worse than the industry average.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our competitors spend the nights in their cubicles. They eat from vending machines.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone here has not shown the same level of competitive spirit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone had a social activity last night!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm sorry! I thought they were friends... But they were only recruiting for a multi-level marketing network!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What were they selling?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Edible wax fruit...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Brochure?

situation: The Boss gathers the team and announces that one of them has a social life, which he considers a competitive weakness because rivals live at their desks and eat vending machine food. He singles out Asok for having done something social the previous night. Asok confesses, then explains the supposed friends were only recruiting him into a multi-level marketing scheme selling edible wax fruit.
punchline: Asok's one social outing turns out to be a sales pitch rather than real friendship, so even his guilt is pathetic, and he still tries to sell Dilbert a brochure.
summary: A manager hunts down the one employee who dared to socialize, only to learn the outing was a pyramid-scheme recruitment pitch.

file: 1997/1997-10-30_contact_important documents_listening_managers_mandatory classes_subordinates_time mangement_prerequisite class.gif
title: Mandatory Classes for Managers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There are several mandatory classes for managers.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Avoiding contact with subordinates.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Misplacing important documents.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The joy of listening to your own voice.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Have you taken the prerequisite class in time management?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Twice.

situation: Catbert, acting as the evil H.R. director, reads The Boss a list of mandatory management classes from a sheet of paper. The classes teach bad managerial habits such as avoiding employees and losing documents. He then asks whether The Boss has taken the prerequisite time management class.
punchline: The Boss admits he has taken the time management class twice, implying he is so bad at managing time that he needed to repeat it, which fits the absurd curriculum of bad management habits.
summary: An H.R. cat recites a syllabus of dysfunctional management skills to his boss and learns that even the basic prerequisite had to be taken repeatedly.

file: 1997/1997-08-21_recruiting on campus_judging me_job interview_engineering knowledge_ancient_confidence_people skills.gif
title: Campus Interviewee Insults the Interviewer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Recruiting on campus

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: It's funny that YOU'RE judging ME. My engineering knowledge is current and yours is ancient.

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: I think I impressed him with my confidence.

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: Ooh! People skills! I forgot!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bonk bonk bonk

situation: Dilbert is conducting a recruiting interview at a college campus. The young engineering student sitting across from him boasts that his knowledge is current while Dilbert's is ancient. The student then thinks he made a good impression, and only later realizes he forgot to show people skills and bonks himself on the head.
punchline: The student mistakes insulting his interviewer for confidence, and only afterward realizes he neglected the people skills that would have made the insult unwise.
summary: A cocky job candidate belittles the engineer interviewing him, then belatedly realizes he skipped the courtesy part of interviewing and punishes himself.

file: 1997/1997-04-26_business plan_disarray_three hour lunch_turn around_distinguish_dedication_insanity.gif
title: Dedication Versus Insanity at Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Alice, our business plan is in complete disarray so we're taking a three-hour lunch. Want to join us?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, I've got to work harder than ever to turn this situation around!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sometimes it's hard to distinguish between dedication and insanity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which one are we?

situation: Wally leans into Alice's cubicle to announce that the failing business plan means he and Dilbert are taking a three-hour lunch, and invites her along. Alice, her hair even more wild than usual, refuses and says she must work harder than ever to fix the situation. Wally then muses that dedication and insanity are hard to tell apart, and Dilbert asks which one they are.
punchline: Alice's frantic overwork looks like dedication or insanity, and Dilbert's question implies that he and Wally, who are skipping out on a crisis for a long lunch, are the ones who are neither dedicated nor sane.
summary: While Wally and Dilbert slip away for a marathon lunch in the face of a failing plan, Alice stays behind to slave over the problem, prompting a wry reflection on who is truly committed or crazy.

file: 1997/1997-07-29_engineers_secret code_little probelms_technology_managers_agreed_comapny.gif
title: Vendor Engineer Laughs in Binary

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell me the truth. Use the engineer's secret code if you must.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are there any little problems with the technology that my managers agreed to buy from your company?

transcript.speaker: Vendor Engineer
transcript.text: Ha ha snort snort ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 1100111... Good. Go on.

setting: Office desk with a laptop, during a meeting with a vendor's engineer
situation: Dilbert asks a vendor's engineer to be honest about problems with technology his managers already agreed to buy. The engineer bursts into snorting laughter. Dilbert, typing on his laptop, interprets the laughter as a binary-style confirmation and tells him to continue.
punchline: The engineer's uncontrollable laughter is itself the honest answer, implying the purchased technology is riddled with serious problems that management never bothered to check.
summary: An engineer's hysterical laughter reveals that the product Dilbert's bosses bought is far worse than 'little problems.'

file: 1997/1997-10-07_fun talking_little bored_shut you down_conversation_self centered girl_yawn.gif
title: Self-Absorbed Date Yawns at Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I had fun talking to you tonight, Gilbert.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: It got a little boring when you tried to steer the conversation away from me. But I managed to shut you down by looking uninterested.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's Dilbert, not Gilbert.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Yawn!

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hill, walking after a date
situation: Dilbert walks with a woman at the end of a date. She cheerfully says she enjoyed their talk, then explains she had to look uninterested to stop him from steering the conversation away from her. When Dilbert corrects her mistake about his name, she yawns.
punchline: The self-centered date gets his name wrong, admits she suppressed any conversation not about her, and then proves her indifference by yawning at his correction.
summary: A narcissistic date compliments an evening that was entirely about herself, botches Dilbert's name, and yawns when he objects.

file: 1997/1997-04-27_fake acronyms_staff meeting_straight face_action items_cod meeting_marketing_could lie_business.gif
title: Fake Acronyms Dodge Boss's Action Items

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Here's your list of fake acronyms for the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Try to keep a straight face when you use them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got a few action items. Who isn't busy?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd be all over it but I need to prepare a BTR for the CPD meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd love to help but this is XRP week for the entire LBQ.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My spoo has too much fleem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Rrrrr

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That was smooth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, if I could lie I'd be in marketing.

setting: Office conference room during a staff meeting
situation: Wally hands Dilbert a list of made-up acronyms to use as excuses at the staff meeting. When the Boss asks who isn't busy to take on action items, Wally, Dilbert and Alice each deflect with meaningless jargon. The Boss is baffled and the three walk away having dodged all the work.
punchline: Dilbert admits he got away with lying so easily that the only job he's missing is in marketing, implying marketing people routinely bluff with nonsense.
summary: Armed with a cheat sheet of invented jargon, three coworkers fend off a manager's request for volunteers by sounding too busy to question.

file: 1997/1997-12-16_communist north elbonian contractors_top secret military project_executed for treason_legal department_execution instead.gif
title: Hiring Enemy Contractors Risks Treason

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a little concerned about your hiring communist North Elbonian contractors to help on my top secret military project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry. What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could be executed for treason.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Talk to our legal department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could I opt for the execution instead?

situation: Dilbert objects that his boss has hired communist North Elbonian contractors to work on his top secret military project. The boss breezily asks what the worst outcome could be, and Dilbert says he could be executed for treason. The boss tells him to take it up with the legal department, and Dilbert asks whether he can choose the execution instead.
punchline: Dilbert would rather be executed than deal with the company's legal department, implying the bureaucracy is a fate worse than death.
summary: A worker warns his careless manager that outsourcing a classified project to a hostile foreign nation could get him executed, then decides that facing the lawyers sounds even worse.

file: 1997/1997-12-25_role model_despite pressure_frustration_can't break_no spine_philosopher_wally_asok admires wally.gif
title: Wally's Spineless Motto

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're my role model, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Despite all the pressure and frustration, you press on. You bend but you do not break.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My motto is "They can't break you if you don't have a spine."

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wow. You're like a philosopher!

setting: Office break room or cafeteria table
situation: Asok sits across from Wally at a lunch table and tells him he admires him as a role model, praising how Wally endures workplace pressure and frustration without breaking. Wally explains that his secret is simply having no spine, and Asok, still starry-eyed, calls him a philosopher.
punchline: Wally's admirable resilience is really just spinelessness, and naive Asok mistakes his cynical lack of backbone for profound wisdom.
summary: A young intern idolizes a veteran coworker's toughness, only to learn it comes from having no backbone at all.

file: 1997/1997-06-22_save money_copier ink_add water_copies light_compensate_darken_implement_dilbert_creative thinker_implantation task_bigger raise_creative way.gif
title: Watered-Down Copier Ink Scheme

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have a great idea to save money.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We can make the photocopier ink last longer by adding water to it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wouldn't that make the copies too light?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ordinarily, yes. But we can compensate by setting the copier to "Darken."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll need someone to implement this idea ... let's see.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, how about Dilbert? He isn't doing much work lately.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd do it myself but there's no reason to waste a creative thinker on an implementation task.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you still mad that I got a bigger raise than you did?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I found a creative way to deal with it.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and Wally's cubicle
situation: Wally pitches the Boss a cost-saving idea: dilute the photocopier ink with water and compensate by setting the copier to 'Darken'. Wally then volunteers Dilbert to implement it, claiming he is too much of a creative thinker for such a task. Dilbert asks if Wally is still upset about Dilbert's bigger raise, and Wally reveals that dumping the work on him was his creative revenge.
punchline: Wally's nonsensical money-saving idea was really a petty way to get back at Dilbert for his bigger raise by saddling him with a pointless chore.
summary: A scheme to stretch copier ink with water turns out to be a coworker's sneaky payback for a pay-raise grudge.

file: 1997/1997-04-05_company training_hope to learn_bad toupee_dead animal_freak of nature_general.gif
title: Training Goals: Insulting the Trainer's Hair

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company training

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Let's go around the room and we'll each say what we hope to learn.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: I hope to learn whether that thing on your head is a bad toupee, a dead animal, or a hideous freak of nature.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Can I call that "general"?

setting: Company training room with a flip chart
situation: A trainer asks each attendee to state what they hope to learn from the session. A woman with enormous hair uses her turn to insult the trainer's head of hair, asking if it is a toupee, a dead animal or a freak of nature. The trainer flatly responds by asking whether he can record her comment on the flip chart under the heading "general."
punchline: The trainer treats a blatant personal insult as an ordinary training objective, dismissively filing it under the vague category "general."
summary: A seminar leader answers a rude question about his hairpiece by cheerfully asking to categorize it as a generic learning goal.

file: 1997/1997-07-12_assignment done_copies_black and white_colors_irrelevant changes_printing.gif
title: Black and White Are Colors

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought I asked for that to be in color.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Black and white are both colors. So technically... Oh, wait, I see what you mean.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that all it took to satisfy his need for irrelevant changes?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I did it while the color copies were printing.

situation: Wally hands the Boss a finished report, and the Boss complains he asked for it in color. Wally starts to argue that black and white count as colors, then realizes what the Boss means. Dilbert asks whether that was all the Boss wanted, and Wally reveals he made the change while the color copies were already printing.
punchline: Wally's trivial, effortless workaround shows the Boss's demand was meaningless, yet it satisfied him, and Wally got away with essentially no extra work.
summary: A pedantic quibble over what counts as a color ends with Wally satisfying his boss's pointless request without lifting a finger.

file: 1997/1997-10-23_autographs for sale_check back_martin luther_martin luther king jr._religious leader_softball signed.gif
title: Forged Autographs Ready in Ten Minutes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Autographs for sale

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Wow... a softball signed by Martin Luther, leader of the Protestant Reformation.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'm impressed, but what I'm looking for is something signed by Martin Luther King Jr.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Too bad you don't have anything from him.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Check back in ten minutes.

setting: Dogbert's autograph shop, at a counter with a display case
situation: A customer browsing Dogbert's memorabilia shop admires a softball supposedly signed by Martin Luther, the Protestant Reformation leader. He says he is really after something signed by Martin Luther King Jr. and laments that Dogbert has nothing from him, and Dogbert replies that he should check back in ten minutes.
punchline: Dogbert's offer to have the item ready in ten minutes reveals that his autographs are forged on demand, which means the Martin Luther softball is a fake too.
summary: A shopper asks a dealer for a different historical signature and learns the merchandise is manufactured to order.

file: 1997/1997-06-16_two hour meeting_friday night_tina_no personal life_useless meetings_void_insane_have a meeting.gif
title: Tina Schedules Meetings to Fill Her Void

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I scheduled a two-hour T.H.N.P.L. meeting for seven o'clock on Friday night.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: T.H.N.P.L. stands for "Tina has no personal life." I'm scheduling useless meetings to fill the void in my life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tina, this is insane.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Are you suggesting we have a meeting to discuss it? Is Saturday okay?

situation: Tina approaches Dilbert's cubicle and announces a two-hour meeting for Friday evening. She cheerfully explains the acronym means her own lack of a personal life, and that she books pointless meetings to fill the emptiness. When Dilbert calls it insane, she responds by proposing yet another meeting to discuss it.
punchline: Tina is so desperate to fill her empty personal life with meetings that she answers a complaint about the pointless meeting by scheduling another one on Saturday.
summary: A lonely coworker admits she books needless after-hours meetings to fill her empty social calendar, then offers to hold another one to talk about the objection.

file: 1997/1997-09-22_rolex watch_corporate limit_vendor gifts_limit 50 dollars.gif
title: Wally's Fake Rolex Vendor Gift

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Look at the "Rolex" watch I got from a vendor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know there's a corporate limit of fifty dollars for vendor gifts?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you know that's a maximum not a minimum.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh. Maybe that's why he whined when I took it off his arm.

situation: Wally shows Dilbert a "Rolex" watch he says he got from a vendor. Dilbert reminds him of the corporate fifty-dollar limit on vendor gifts and clarifies that it is a maximum, not a minimum. Wally then reveals he actually took the watch right off the vendor's arm.
punchline: Wally's "gift" wasn't given at all; he took it off the vendor's arm, so he has missed the point of the gift limit and arguably committed theft.
summary: A coworker flaunts an expensive-looking watch from a supplier, then casually admits he simply removed it from the man's wrist.
